LEAD_PARAGRAPH: CHICAGO, Dec. 31. -- One of the largest audiences ever seen in the Garrick Theatre, which is on the same street as the Iroquois and less than one block distant, sat in complete ignorance of the awful tragedy which was being enacted 200 feet away.

COLON, Dec. 31. -- Information reached Gov. Melendez last night from Carti, a tiny village near the Island of Pines, in Panama territory, that Colombian troops landed there on Dec. 21 and conferred with the Indian Chief, Inanaquina, who was afterward taken aboard a vessel, and, it is thought, conveyed to Cartagena.

CHICAGO, Dec. 31. -- Although the Iroquois Theatre was undoubtedly the safest theatre in Chicago, it became evident today that the City Building Department had not strictly enforced one or two sections of the building ordinances.

ASHTABULA. Dec. 31. -- The east-bound limited train No. 22 on the Lake Shore Road was wrecked two miles west of this place to-day while running at a high rate of speed. The train ran into an open switch, and three persons were killed and several others injured.
HAVANA, Dec. 31. -- Fargo Squiers, the eldest son of United States Minister Squiers, was accidentally shot and killed to-day by Gaston Michaud, a French chauffeur employed by his father.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 31. -- Senator Smoot, with the assistance of his attorneys, is engaged in preparing to defend himself against the charges which challenge his eligibility. Ex-Senator Cannon, who publishes a newspaper in Utah, in a recent issue charged that Mr. Smoot was here to represent the Mormon Church.
LONDON, Jan. 1. -- King Edward and Queen Alexandra have sent telegrams of sympathy to the United States Government through Lord Lansdowne, the Foreign Secretary, to the sufferers of the Chicago fire.
LONDON, Dec. 31. -- The Treasury Department to-night issued an account of the revenue of the United Kingdom for the first nine months of the fiscal year of 1903-4.

LONDON, Dec. 31. -- Japan has renamed the war ships she has purchased from the Argentine Republic the Kassaga and the Nishni. It is expected that they will sail from Genoa for Japan next week.

Some of the colonists who returned to town early in the season have opened their cottages for the occasion.

Travis, was victorious both morning and afternoon, his second match with E.A. Freeman of the Montclair Golf Club was close enough to keep his mind on the game.

DALLAS, Texas, Jan. 1 -- The tenth annual New Year's rabbit hunt of the Texas Rabbit Hunters' Club was held to-day at Lucas Prairie, thirty miles north of Dallas, beginning at 8 o'clock in the morning and closing at 4, o'clock in the afternoon. Forty-eight hunters from different sections of the State participated, and 1,143 rabbits were killed during the day.

LONDON, Jan. 2. -- In reviewing the past year in China the Peking correspondent of The Times says there have been no great changes. The Court has not changed, and is showing no indication of reform, which, indeed, is impossible under the Dowager Empress as she is now advised.

GALVESTON, Texas, Jan. 1. -- Gold which assays $3,000 a ton has been discovered in Gonzales County, in Southwest Texas, near the town of Harwood. The story is that the head driller of the Bay Shore Oil Company discovered the gold in sands of wells while drilling for oil three miles south of Harwood.

LAKEWOOD, N.J., Jan. 1. -- With the golf links of the Country Club in excellent condition, practically free from snow, the members and many of their friends opened the year to-day with an interesting day's play in the special two-day New Year's tournament. Thirty-five competitors drove off in the eighteen-hole qualifying round for three cups, the players being divided into sets of eight, according to their scores.

Green of Chicago, a brother of the testator, in the petition accompanying the will, says that the estate in New York State amounts to about $940,000, of which $900,000 is personal property. Hearst caused the Democratic National Committee to select St. Louis as the site for the next National Convention, which is to be held on July 6. Driggs was yesterday sentenced by Judge Edward B. Thomas in the United States Circuit Court, Brooklyn, to one day's imprisonment in the Kings County Jail and to pay a fine of $10,000.

ALBANY, Jan. 12. -- Gov. Odell went to New York at 8 o'clock this morning and returned early this evening, in time to attend the dinner given at the Executive Mansion to the State officers and their wives.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 12. -- Sir Chentung Liang-Cheng, the Chinese Minister here, called upon Acting Secretary of State Loomis late this afternoon and informed him that he had received a cable dispatch from Peking stating that the Emperor had fixed his seal to the Chinese-American treaty and had acceded to the request of the American Government through Minister Conger for the immediate exchange of ratifications.

ALBANY, Jan. 12. -- Coincident with the launching here to-day of a boom of State Senator George R. Malby for the Republican nomination for Governor, statements were made by intimate friends of Gov. Odell that there was no probability that the Governor would consider a renomination.

PITTSBURG, Penn., Jan. 12. -- The Pittsburg Coal Company's stocks were hammered on the Pittsburg Exchange to-day. It was the general opinion that the dividend on the preferred stock would be taken off. The Directors issued scrip redeemable within a year, paying 6 per cent. The preferred stock recovered three points before the closing, and a rapid advance is expected to-morrow owing to the placing of a $25,000,000 loan with the Union Trust Company.

ROME, N.Y., Jan. 12. -- After serving as cashier of the Farmers' National Bank in this city since 1875, the date of its organization, Samuel Wardwell, aged eighty-one, retired to-day. He is succeeded by George Clarabut.

LONDON, Jan. 13. -- Details regarding the conference of the elder statesmen, Cabinet Ministers, and chiefs of the naval and military staffs on Monday are given by the Tokio correspondent of The Times. The conference lasted five hours. It is understood that it merely drafted the reply to Russia's last note, inasmuch as the latter, though unsatisfactory in substance, was conciliatory in tone, thereby inviting a continuance of the negotiations.

ALBANY, Jan. 12. -- William C. Gotshall, President of the Port Chester Railroad Company, who was here to-night, when shown a dispatch announcing the intention of the New York, Westchester and Boston Railway Company to build a railway from the Harlem River to Port Chester, paralleling the proposed Port Chester Railroad, said that officials of the Port Chester company felt no concern about any prospective rival railway.

ST. PETERSBURG, Jan. 12. -- The Russian budget for 1904 estimates the ordinary receipts at $990,047,246, against $948,816,339 for 1903. The expenditures are estimated at $983,229,125, against $940,232,611 for 1903.

ALBANY, Jan. 12. -- The law prohibiting the employment of bakers for more than sixty hours per week or more than ten hours per day was declared to be constitutional to-day by the Court of Appeals. The law is held to be a constitutional measure to protect the public health, and the court holds that the Legislature did not exceed its police powers in making it.

Nothing could be more indicative of the estimation in which the history of the Pension Bureau has caused that institution to be held than the announcement that the surviving teamsters of the civil war have formed an organization to secure pensions for themselves. It is only those teamsters who swore and bled their horses and mules on the Union side, we infer, who have associated in this movement.

WATERTOWN, N.Y., Jan. 13. -- At the Carthage ice races yesterday Carrina, owned by Hutchins Fritz of Carthage, paced a mile in 2:15, breaking the world's ice record for pacers by a quarter of a second.

LONDON, Jan. 14. -- A dispatch from Tokio to Reuter's Telegram Company says that Japan's answer to the latest Russian note was handed yesterday afternoon to Baron de Rosen, the Russian Minister, and that negotiations will be continued without any time limit being set for their termination.

Grosvenor and Hepburn, resulting in striking out the paragraph from the Legislative Appropriation bill which provides for the salaries and expenses of the Civil Service Commission by a vote of 78 to 65.

LONDON, Jan. 14 -- The Times's Peking correspondent says that the terms of Russia's proposals to Japan, as announced in Berlin, are regarded as substantially correct. It is believed that Russia selected this way of giving publicity to them in order to test the opinion of the world.

LONDON, Jan. 13. -- Herbert Spencer's will is a curious document. It directs that his body shall be placed in a coffin with a loose lid and easily opened from below, and that the body shall be cremated and the ashes buried, all without any species of religious ceremony.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- It can be stated on authority that the Administration does not contemplate paying a dollar out of the United States Treasury to Colombia on account of the secession of Panama. Nor will it go before The Hague tribunal as a party to any proceedings growing out of that secession.

CONSTANTINOPLE, Jan. 13. -- The Porte has notified the Austro-Hungarian and Russian Ambassadors of its full acceptance of the Macedonian reform scheme and of its consent to the repatriation of the Macedonian refugees.

The work on the rapid transit subway now nearing completion is threatened with serious delay through a general strike scheduled to take place at noon to-day on the Fifty-ninth Street power house, to be extended to the entire subway unless non-union men who are doing the equipment work are discharged.
Staten Island business men are to organize a trust company for Richmond Borough, and, as soon as the preliminaries are arranged, application will be made for a special charter.

ALBANY, Jan. 13. -- A memorial calling for the impeachment of Justice Warren B. Hooker of Chautauqua County was reported here to-day as being in the course of preparation by the Chautauqua County Republicans, who have recently taken occasion to denounce Justice Hooker and Tax Commissioner Lester F. Stearns, for their alleged connection with certain Post Office scandals in that county.

PARIS, Jan. 13. -- No action has yet been taken in the direction of mediation between Russia and Japan, but it is learned that the Powers desirous of peace in the Far East are considering the desirability of such a step. Whether the proposed action will be joint or independent, remains to be determined.

GOSHEN, N.Y., Jan. 13. -- Two hundred people gathered at the trolley station in this village to-day and watched Dr. James Nicholas Vann start for Middletown, eight miles away, in a cutter hitched to a trolley car. Dr. Vann claims to be ninety-seven years old and thirteen times a widower.

WELLAND, Ontario, Jan. 13. -- Judge Wells this afternoon gave his decision in the case of James N. Abeel, under arrest here for extradition to New York for alleged forgery in connection with his alleged impersonation of "J. Ogden Goelet."

SUPERIOR, Wis., Jan. 13. -- A run on the savings department of the First National Bank entirely subsided this afternoon, two hours before the regular closing time. A quarter of a million dollars was paid out yesterday, and about $75,000 to-day. Deposits to-day were in excess of withdrawals.

ALBANY, Jan. 13. -- Dr. Peterson of the State Commission in Lunacy will make an investigation of the abuses complained of in a published article by a woman who spent three weeks as a nurse at the Ward's Island institution of the Manhattan State Hospital.

PITTSBURG, Jan. 13. -- The will of Mrs. Mary E. Schenley was filed for probate today. It creates a trust with three trustees. The American trustees will sell her property in Pennsylvania and send the money to the trustees in England. Only one stipulation is made. The Schenley mansion in Pittsburg is not to be sold until all the rest of the estate here has passed out of the hands of the trustees.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- An American "group" to be affiliated with the Inter-Parliamentary Union for International Arbitration was organized to-night at a meeting in the lobby of the House of Representatives. About forty members of the Senate and House became members. Representative Bartholdt of Missouri was made Chairman and Representative Rodenberg of Illinois temporary Secretary.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- Delay of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations in reporting the Panama treaty for passage has resulted in placing the Administration forces in the upper house in a most embarrassing position. Of their weakness the opposition forces have taken advantage by making attacks, on the President and his course in the entire Panama matter.
ST. PETERSBURG, Jan. 13. -- The reports to the effect that M. Bezobrazoff (a leader of the war party, whom the Czar recently made a Secretary of State,) has fallen into disfavor appear to be untrue.

BABYLON, L. I., Jan. 13.--The Amagansett express of the Long Island Railroad, east bound, in charge of Engineer Murray and Conductor Olin and consisting of the engine, baggage car, parlor car, smoker, and one ordinary day car, this afternoon jumped the track at Belmont Junction, a mile west of here. Higgins, the President of the Senate; Speaker Nixon, and the Republican as well as the Democratic leaders of both houses will be invited.

The features of the Assembly session were the announcement of committee designations by Speaker Nixon and of appointments by the Speaker and the Clerk and the memorial addresses in honor of Assemblyman Hughes of Washington, whose death, since the last session of the Legislature, was formally announced.

"Then," he said, "if a man disagrees with his party he can retire without risking his bread and butter.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., Jan. 13. -- Edwin Warfield was inaugurated Governor of Maryland to-day. The Governor-elect was escorted to the executive mansion by a legislative committee, and thence the party proceeded to the State House, where a big audience listened to the addresses of the retiring Governor, John Walter Smith, and Gov. WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- Three bills relating to National banks and the currency were acted on to-day by the Sub-Committee of the House Banking Committee having charge of the measures.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- The treaty between the United State and China is now law in both countries. Ratifications, which had been authorized by cable, were exchanged in this city to-day, and President Roosevelt signed the proclamation putting the treaty into effect.

ITHACA, N.Y., Jan. 13. -- The Princeton relay team has withdrawn its entry at the indoor sports to be held in Boston early in February, under the auspices of the Boston Athletic Association. Princeton was to have run against the Cornell team. The Cornell management to-day notified that Princeton could not, on account of examinations, prepare for the event.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Jan. 13. -- Application was made in the United States District Court to-day for a receiver under the Feder bankruptcy laws for the C.H. Gill Lumber Company.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, Jan. 18. -- In the presence of the joint assembly of the members of the Ohio Senate and House, Lieut. Gov. Harding to-day declared Marcus A. Hanna re-elected United States Senator of Ohio for the term of six years, beginning March 4, 1905. The two branches in separate session had given Senator Hanna the largest majority ever given a Senator from this State.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 13. -- The Baroness Hengelmuller, wife of the Ambassador from Austria, entertained this afternoon at a small musical when her friends were invited to hear Miss Unschuld de Melasfeld, the young Austrian pianist who is spending a season in America. The invitations were limited to the seating capacity of the Embassy drawing rooms.

About five thousand men are affected by the reduction. The company headquarters are here but its fifteen plants are scattered throughout the country.

ROCHESTER, N.Y., Jan. 14. -- To-day's storm has obstructed traffic more than any other storm this Winter. The Auburn branch of the New York Central was blocked all day, owing to drifts in a deep cut at Victor, and the Rochester and Eastern trolley road was also tied up. Through trains from the West were hours late on the New York Central.

Vandegrift Co. of Philadelphia for free entry for a Shetland pony, imported for the American Museum of Natural History. MARIETTA, Ohio, Jan. 14. -- The Pure Oil Company of Pittsburg to-day purchased the Cameron oil interests in this county, 1,200 barrels production and 6,000 acres of leases, paying $1,300,000.

PRETORIA, Jan. 20. -- The Asiatic Labor bill passed its second reading in the Legislative Council to-day.

PARIS, Jan. 20. -- Although no official authority is obtainable for the statement, there is strong reason to believe that exchanges of communications are now going on between France and Russia concerning the position Russia will finally adopt in response to the latest Japanese note.

LONG BRANCH, N.J., Jan. 20. -- Charles P. Irwin's ice yacht Georgie won the first of a series of three races to-day for the championship pennant of the North and South Shrewsbury Rivers, sailed on the South Shrewsbury River. Four boats entered the contest, the others being Commodore Morris's Mildred, William R. Joline's Hazel L., and George J. Gilling's Wizard.

Business upon the Stock Exchange continues satisfactory to the bulls, not disturbing to the bears, and of no considerable interest or importance to anybody not falling into those classes. The bulls say the prices speak for themselves. It may be asked why prices should rise, and it may be thought that they should not rise, but that they do rise is indisputable.

The special meeting of the stockholders of the Eastern Trust Company, held yesterday afternoon, in connection with the annual meeting of the company, was looked forward to with considerable interest. About two weeks ago a committee of stockholders sent out a notice to the effect that the Eastern Trust, while perfectly solvent, was not making such money as justified its existence, and had, therefore, better be put in liquidation.

CHICAGO, Jan. 20. -- A cablegram received this afternoon by Prof. Harper of the University of Chicago announced the death of Prof. Hermann Eduard von Holst at his residence in Freiberg, Germany, where for three years he had been on leave of absence from the university, seeking to regain his health.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- At to-day's meeting of the National Board of Trade the report of the Committee on Rivers and Harbors, presented by George Anderson of Pittsburg, caused considerable feeling, and at one stage of the discussion Mr. Anderson declared that he was not sure there ever would be another meeting of the board.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 20. -- The Treasury experts who have been investigating the office of Secretary Edward A. Mosely of the Inter-State Commerce Commission, have made a partial report.

AUSTIN, Texas, Jan. 20. -- The Mexican Railway Commission has just issued a statement showing that foreign railroad companies operating in Mexico own 11,712 kilometers of railway and Mexican companies own 3,173 kilometers. The capital represented by the foreign railway companies operating in the republic, including bonds and stock at its par value, is $854,563,067 Mexican money.

The suit brought by Miss Emma Walker, a public school teacher, in Part I. of the Supreme Court, Brooklyn, against Dr. William H. Maxwell, Superintendent of Schools, and Lyman A. Best, Principal of Public School No. 108, for $10,000 damages for libel, was given to the jury last night, after Mr. Maxwell had been on the stand.

WHITE PLAINS, N.Y., Jan. 20. -- Marie Gerren, a German servant, died in the hospital here to-day from the effects of burns received at Hartsdale on Monday last. She was employed as maid by Mrs. Harvey Bassford, who, in trying to save the girl when the latter's dress caught fire from the kitchen range, was herself fatally burned, dying in the hospital here on Monday afternoon.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 20. -- The first tf two subscription dances under very smart auspices took place this evening at the Willard, where a company of 300 gathered in the Red Ballroom. Mrs. William S. Cowles, the sister of President Roosevelt, acted as hostess for the committee, with Major Charles L. McCawley to present the guests.
Charles Stich has bought from James M. Horton the plot of six lots 75 by 200 running through from One Hundred and Thirty-eighth to One Hundred and Thirty-ninth Street, 425 feet east of Lenox Avenue.
When a cry of fire rang through the crowded tenement at 419 East Sixty-fourth Street startled tenants ran about seeking where it was, and their quest led to the discovery of a triple tragedy.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., Jan. 20. -- It is asserted to-night that Senator Gorman has the power to end the bitter fight in the Legislature over the election of a successor to Senator McComas. It is also apparent that if he does not soon exercise that power his influence as the head of his party in Maryland will be weakened.

KAVANA, Jan. 20. -- Acting Secretary of Agriculture Diaz has appointed John W. Flanagan, an American, Cuban Commissioner to the St. Louis Exposition. Mr. Flanagan is agent here of the Southern Pacific Railroad. In company with a party of Havana editors he has left for St. Louis.

If, as has so often been charged, the American playgoing public is fickle and forgetful of its familiar favorites, then it has made an exception, and a most honorable exception, in the case of Miss Ada Rehan and the choice pieces of the old Daly repertory which she is reviving at the Lyric Theatre.

CHICAGO, Jan. 20. -- It is probable that the City Council next Monday night will again consider and revise the new theatre ordinance. A meeting between the theatre managers and a special committee of the Aldermen will be held later in the week. There is a general feeling among the Aldermen that the essentials demanded of the theatres are too stringent.

The Atlantic Association of the Amateur Athletic Union has had considerable discussion over the competition of members of boat clubs in athletic events open to several boat clubs, the Atlantic Association maintaining that such a competition being open to two or more organizations, is an open event and therefore comes under the rule of the Amateur Athletic Union requiring sanction.

BERLIN, Jan. 20. -- The Budget Commission of the Reichstag, which is made up of the leaders of all parties, to-day approved the additional appropriation of $50,000 for the German exhibit at the St. Louis Exposition, making a total of $875,000. The vote, with one exception, was unanimous.

ALBANY, Jan. 20. -- For the purpose of giving school teachers already employed in New York City the preference when appointments to be Principals and Assistant Principals are made, Senator McCabe today presented a bill which is construed as attacking the methods of Superintendent of Schools Maxwell.

ALBANY, Jan. 20. -- Gov. Odell spoke to the toast "The State of New York" at the banquet of the State Bar Association to-night. His remarks caused considerable stir as certain parts were taken as bearing directly upon the action of the Bar Association to-day relative to the Justice Hooker charges.

Crazed by overwork. Lena Antoss, twenty-one years old, an embroidery worker of 2,920 Eighth Avenue, attempted to take her life yesterday afternoon by jumping into the North River at One Hundred and Twelfth Street, the police say. She was rescued by Dudley Trenifried, a boatman of One Hundred and Eighth Street and the North River, in a spectacular manner.

ELIZABTH, N.J., Jan. 20. -- Apologizing to the public for the bad trolley service in this part of New Jersey, the Public Service Corporation carried two columns of advertising matter in the columns of the local newspapers to-night in the form of a statement signed by President Thomas N. McCarter.

Racing dates for the year at the Eastern tracks were arranged yesterday by the Stewards of The Jockey Club at a meeting held in the rooms of James R. Keene, at the Waldorf-Astoria. Besides Mr. Keene there were present August Belmont, F.R. Hitchcock, J.H. Bradford, and Andrew Miller.
LONDON, Jan. 21. -- A dispatch to The Times from Vladivostok says that among Russian naval men war feeling is intense, but the public seems indifferent.
CHICAGO, Jan. 20. -- May wheat touched a new high mark -- 92 1/8@92 1/4 cents -- to-day, a net gain for the day of 2 1/4 cents, and 16 cents higher than the average price last Fall.

The London Times of Jan. 11 devotes two columns and a half to the correspondence between the Duke of DEVONSHIRE and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN on the subject of the Liberal Unionist Association. The correspondence begins with a letter from the Duke, who is President of the association, dated Oct. 23, and closes with a letter from Mr. CHAMBERLAIN dated Jan. 4.

It was a busy day at the automobile show yesterday for the demonstrating automobiles that virtually make up the open-air exhibit just outside of Madison Square Garden. While the big show is in progress inside the building there is a very active feature of the exhibit outside. These demonstrating cars are the vehicles kept in readiness, with skilled chauffeurs, to take parties who seem inclined to buy on a short tour about the city.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 20. -- The House Committee on Judiciary gave a preliminary hearing on the Hepburn-Dolliver bill in the interest of Prohobition to-day. The bill is intended to overcome the United States Court decision denying the State the right to prohibit sales of liquor from other States while it remains in the original package, and empowers the States to apply their excise laws whether in the package or not.

We are now informed by The Tribune's Washington dispatches that the unanimity which he has from time to time described in the councils of the Republican Party in support of Mr. ROOSEVELT has undergone "an appreciable change," and has become unanimous. That sounds like nonsense, but it is not our fault.

Mrs. Clara H. Stranahan, the widow of James S.T. Stranahan, the Brooklyn philanthropist, yesterday applied to Chancellor William J. Magie in Jersey City for an order to compel her nephew, Capt. Addison Ely, a well-known lawyer of Rutherford, N.J., to render an accounting in a transaction involving about $65,000 belonging to the complainant, and also to restrain him from transferring or disposing of certain securities, stocks, bonds, and mortgages owned by his aunt.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 20. -- Many important changes will occur in the army during the next few days resulting from the retirement of Lieut. Gen. Young and the promotion of Major Gen. Chaffee to be a Lieutenant General.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- Before leaving for Florida to-day, Senator Quay set at rest the mooted question as to whether he would favor instructing the delegates from Pennsylvania to the Chicago Convention for Roosevelt. He said that if it should become necessary he would go on the floor of the State Convention, of which body he will be a member, and make a motion that the delegates at large be instructed to support Roosevelt.

Mr. and Mrs. M. Orme Wilson gave last evening in their new home, 3 East Sixty-fourth Street, a musicale preceded by a dinner. The function was the first large entertainment in their new home, and served as a housewarming.

Wall Street heard yesterday that trouble has been brewing between the Corn Products Company, commonly known as the Glucose Trust, and the Standard Oil interests which control the New York Glucose Company. There have been rumors of a disagreement for some weeks, and they are now said to be reaching an acute stage because of the approaching annual meeting of the New York Glucose Company, which takes place the second Monday in February.

ELIZABETH, N.J., Jan. 21. -- The Rev. Bartholomew Zindzius, rector of St. Peter and Paul's Roman Catholic Church here, appeared in police court to-day against three of his parishioners, whom he accused of defaming him. They had previously sued the priest for slander in the District Court because he had reprimanded them from the pulpit for attending a meeting held here by an Anarchist.

ALBANY, Jan. 21. -- The plan of educational unification favored by Superintendent Charles R. Skinner of the Department of Public Instruction is embodied in a bill introduced to-day in the Assembly by Mr. Davis of Warren County. The bill provides for a selection by lot within ten days of nine of the present Regents, who thereupon shall become the Board of Regents, the terms of office of all the others thereupon ceasing.

LONDON, Jan. 22. -- The Times's Moscow correspondent says that the Grand Duke Vladimir Alexandrovitch, the Czar's eldest uncle and Commander in Chief of the St. Petersburg Military Division, and the Grand Duke Serge Alexandrovitch, another uncle of the Czar and Commander in Chief of the Moscow Military Division, are strongly supporting Admiral Alexieff, the Viceroy of the Far East, (who is believed to be in favor of war.)

William E. Dodge, who died Aug. 9 last, left an estate which State Appraiser Robert Mazet, in a report filed in the Surrogates' office yesterday, values at $7,114,298.92. Of this amount $6,693,898.92 is personal property and $420,400 real estate. Deductions of subscriptions to several church and other organizations, expenses of administration, and commissions of the executors amount to $365,187.80, leaving the net estate $6,749,111.12.

In consequence of a series of severe tests of a fireproofing compound, colorless and transparent, in which the actor, "Nat" Wills, and his manager, W.C. Cameron, became interested, all the so-called Frohman theatres in New York have their scenery already soaked in the substance. These houses include the Herald Square, the Garrick, Daly's, Knickerbocker, Savoy, Empire, Criterion, Lyceum, Garden, and Hudson.

GREENSBOROUGH, N.C., Jan. 21. -- The main dining room, dormitory, and laundry of the State Normal College were destroyed by fire to-day. The three hundred and fifty young women students were rescued. The girls were forced to flee in their night clothes.

AUSTIN, Texas, Jan. 21. -- It is reported on trustworthy authority that Capt. Harry Brown of Philadelphia and interests which are closely identified with the Standard Oil have acquired a large interest in the Mexican Petroleum Company, which is developing an extensive oilfield near Tampico, Mexico. The company has been given encouragement by the Mexican Government under the belief that it was to become a rival of the Standard Oil for Mexican business.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., Jan. 21. -- Arrested on his honeymoon was the sad fate of young Maxie Cameron McGee, whom Detective Richard Joyce and Special Officer J.P. Finan recognized at the Southern Hotel from the description of him telegraphed from New York City. Grand larceny is charged against McGee by the dry goods firm of Tefft, Weller Co. of New York.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., Jan. 21. -- Senator German is either losing his grip or playing a big political bluff in the three-cornered fight for United States Senator. Isidor Rayner, the anti-machine candidate, lost two votes in to-day's ballot, and ex-Gov. Smith gained one. All outward appearances indicate that Gorman and his lieutenants are for Bernard Carter, the Baltimore corporation lawyer.

It is up to the National Democratic Convention to nominate a man who will have the magnetic force to draw the conservative element of the country to support him and thereby insure his election. There are thousands of Republicans itching for a change of Government, who will not hesitate to tender their support to the Democratic candidate if he is considered safe, but will not be inveigled to support a claptrap nominee or platform.

The original love letters of Sarah Margaret Fuller, the friend of Greeley, Emerson, Hawthorne and Channing, written while she was literary critic of The New York Tribune, 1845-6, to James Nathan, about fifty in number, were sold yesterday by the Anderson Auction Company, 5 West Twenty-ninth Street. They were the letters whose recent publication in this city excited so much interest. They were sold as a lot and fetched $110.

William Jennings Bryan was the guest of honor at the nineteenth annual dinner of the Holland Society of New York, held last night in the grand ballroom of the Waldorf-Astoria, and made the principal address of the evening to nearly 500 men who were described by one of the speakers as "remnants of the old Dutch civilization of New Amsterdam."

PINEHURST, N.C., Jan. 21. -- The new tower trap, a recent addition to the equipment of the Pinehurst Gun Club, was used to-day for the first time in a tournament, and a unique contest resulted. C.A. Lockwood of New York won, with 35 targets. H. Nelson Burroughs of Philadelphia was second, with 31.

LONDON, Jan. 22. -- Dispatches from St. Petersburg to The Daily Telegraph and The Daily Mail assert that Russia's reply to the latest Japanese note was drawn up at a Ministerial council held yesterday, at which the Czar presided.

BALTIMORE, Jan. 21. -- The parents and other relatives of Miss Evelyn Bash in this city, who have not seen or heard anything of her since she boarded a Pennsylvania Railroad train at Union Station Jan. 2 to go to Englewood, N.J., are much distressed over her strange disappearance. Her father, Edward H. Bash, said to-night that he feared she had been abducted or had met with foul play.

The prospects for peace between Russia and Japan are distinctly better than they have for some weeks been. And this is not to be imputed to general popular ignorance of the former course of the negotiations. There has been such Ignorance. But it has not prevented the knowledge that the Russian dispatches were couched in language which was so far from conciliatory as to be peremptory and even provocative.

Giant powder in sufficient quantity, according to experts, to blow an entire city block into fragments, was taken yesterday by the police of the West Forty-seventh Street Station from a vacant flat in the tenement at 594 Eleventh Avenue, not far from the places where, within a month, attempts to blow up two large structures in process of erection have been discovered.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, Jan. 21. -- An almost continuous fall of rain for the last thirty-six hours, carrying off the snow, has caused freshets in practically all Ohio streams. The danger at many places has been greatly increased by the breaking up of ice in the streams and the formation of gorges.

The Board of Directors of the Foreign Trade Association yesterday afternoon appointed a committee to inquire into the subject of the alleged exorbitant freight rates to Cuba and Porto Rico now exacted and to propose a plan of relief.

Active, Strong Market. -- For the first time in many weeks transactions on the New York Stock Exchange yesterday approached the million-share mark, falling short of that amount by only a few thousand shares. Almost without exception the course of prices was upward, and in nearly all the prominent issues the closing prices were practically the highest of the day.

In every detail the members of Squadron A simply eclipsed their previous efforts at military display in their armory, Ninety-fourth Street and Madison Avenue, last night. They assembled for a review by Major-General Corbin, who recently has taken command of the Department of the East.

LONDON, Jan. 22. -- The Shanghai correspondent of The Times says that Sheng Ta-Jen (Director of Railways) has telegraphed to Wu Ting-Fang (Vice President of the Foreign Office) requesting him to remind United States Minister Conger that the American syndicate is violating the contract for the Canton -- Han-Kow Railway.

Hockey, basketball games, relay and pursuit races and a potato race, in addition to the usual speed events, made a varied and attractive programme of ice sports at the ice carnival held in the Clermont Skating Rink, Brooklyn, last night, and was greatly enjoyed by a crowd of spectators which filled the building to the extent of its capacity.

THE HAGUE, Jan. 21. -- Queen Wilhelmina inaugurated the festivities attending the Queen mother's jubilee with a gala dinner to-night. Speaking for herself and for the Prince Consort, she proposed the health of the Queen mother.

An attempt to escape of three boys imprisoned in the juvenile ward of the Queens County Jail in Long Island City was frustrated yesterday by the jailers, when the boys had almost worked their way through the sixteen-foot wall. This is the jail which President Jaeckel of the State Prison Commission recently characterized as "the worst jail I ever visited."

Belasco and De Mille's old Lyceum success of "The Wife" was revived yesterday afternoon by the pupils of the Empire Dramatic School. In its combination of mature and juvenile lovers, of serious emotion, and comic relief, it has infinite variety -- but not of the kind that age cannot wither nor custom stale.
CHICAGO, Jan. 21. -- Joseph L. Ferrell of Philadelphia has thrown handsful of excelsior on a hot gas fire in the rooms of the Western Society of Engineers. It smoked, but it did not blaze.

ALBANY, Jan. 21. -- Gov. Senator PLATT of Connecticut has plucked out the heart of the mystery that beclouds the opposition to the Panama treaty. Everything was cleared up, he said in the Senate debate on Wednesday, "by the admission of Senators PATTERSON and CARMACK that the true reason for opposing the treaty was the desire to have the canal constructed at Nicaragua rather than at Panama."

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. 21. -- While the Southern Pacific's "Sunset Limited" train was climbing the mountains between San Luis Obispo and San Ardo last night, a Wells-Fargo treasure box was mysteriously stolen out of the express car.

CHICAGO, Jan. 21. -- A storm of liquidation broke over the grain pits to-day. Nevertheless, after a fall of 2 1/2 cents in July and 1 3/4 cents in May, the markets closed at little under the extraordinary high record set in yesterday's final quotations for May, the leading option. July, however, failed to rebound equally with May.

TOKIO, Jan. 21. -- The Japanese Government is closely watching the spread of disorder in Korea, and, while considering the possible necessity of intervention for the protection of the Japanese and other foreign residents, hesitates to dispatch a larger force than that there now, on account of the delicacy of the general situation.

Announcement was made yesterday by the Erie Railroad that the proposed plan of running the trains of the Northern Railroad of New Jersey into the Weehawken terminal of the West Shore Railroad had been abandoned. This plan was suggested by President Underwood of the Erie in order to relieve the congestion at the Erie terminals in Jersey City and in order to give the Northern New Jersey commuters a better train service.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- The Senate Philippines Committee room was crowded to the doors all day during the hearing on the Frye bill to extend the coastwise navigation laws of the United States to the Philippines, so that all commerce between this country and the islands shall be carried in American vessels.

ALBANY, Jan. 21. -- The visit to this city to-day of Charles A. Towne, formerly United States Senator from Minnesota, to call on Judge Parker and David B. Hill, brought out an interesting story of how Representative Ira E. Rider of New York City balked Charles F. Murphy in the execution of a plan which the Tammany leader had in mind as a means of dazzling the Democracy in Congress.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- The President and Mrs. Roosevelt held their second large reception of the season this evening. The function was in honor of the judiciary, the guests invited to the Blue Room being largely representative of that portion of the official world.

Mr. BRYAN has defined his position. It is time for the leaders of the Democratic Party to define theirs. In his homecoming speech at Lincoln Mr. BRYAN declared that the Kansas City platform must be reaffirmed this year, and that the candidate must be a man who would accept that platform and stand upon it.

ALBANY, Jan. 21. -- Despite the criticism which Gov. Odell's plan to save the State $40,000,000 on the cost of canal construction has evoked, the Governor has no intention of abandoning it and predicts that legislation will be enacted before the session is over which will supply the $5,000,000 additional revenue annually which will be necessary to carry his scheme into effect.

BOSTON, Jan. 21. -- Nance O'Neill, the young California actress who came practically unheralded to the Columbia Theatre two weeks ago, has met with such pronounced success that she will next week give a series of special matinee performances at the Tremont Theatre. To-night Miss O'Neill appeared in Sudermann's "Fires of St. John," which is new to this country.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- An interesting incident of the trial of August W. Machen, the Groff Brothers, and the Lorenzes on an indictment charging conspiracy to defraud the Government in connection with the sale of letter box fasteners, came to-day just before adjournment.

ALBANY, Jan. 21. -- The Grievance Committee of the State Bar Association, to which was referred the charges of the Jamestown Bar Association against Justice Warren B. Hooker, will probably organize here within the next two weeks. By that time it will have been formally notified by Secretary F.E. Wadhams of the memorial received from the Jamestown Association.

No diminution in interest or in the size of the crowd was noticeable yesterday at the automobile show in Madison Square Garden. Even in the afternoon the aisles were uncomfortably thronged and the demonstrating cars outside of the Garden were doing a rushing business carrying prospective purchasers on short trips about the city.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21. -- Senator Hanna, who had a severe attack of grip in New York several weeks ago, is suffering from a recurrence of that illness, and was confined to his bed to-day. He is under the care of a physician, who ordered that he must have rest, and not to be disturbed. It is said his illness is not serious, and that he is better to-night.

IT may be remembered that the late Miss Charlotte M. Yonge in certain papers presented many reminiscences of Lord Seaton, for the lady was of the same family that had for its leading representative John Colborne, who for his valor and many fine qualities is best known in English military annals as Lord Seaton.

The University of Chicago Press announces the early publication of the first four volumes of Part II. of the Ancient Record Series, which has been undertaken by Dr. James H. Breasted, the well-known lecturer and writer on Egyptian archaeology. This part deals with Egypt, and will consist of twelve volumes, divided into five classes.
LONDON, Jan. 22. -- A continuance of the ease of discount rates is anticipated in the market here.
NEW HAVEN, Conn., Jan. 22. -- Yale won from Princeton in the basket ball game here to-night, after a hard struggle, by a score of 16 to 10.

Any proposed infraction of the principle of free trade, made by a politician of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S importance, was sure enough to convert the "campaign of education" in which it was brought forward into a much more exciting season than the normal contests of Parliamentary elections.

CHICAGO, Jan. 22. -- Will J. Davis and Harry J. Powers, "resident owners" and managers of the Iroquois Theatre, made their appearance before the Coroner's jury to-day. Mr. Powers placed the responsibility for the management of the theatre upon Mr. Davis, who was the active manager, while he was but passive in the conduct of its affairs.

In the preface to his forthcoming book, "The Citizen: A Study of the Individual and the Government," which will be published in February by A.S. Barnes Co., Prof. N.S. Shaler gives an interesting result of his long experience as a teacher and his associations with many thousands of students.

" The Report of the United States National Muscum" for the year ended June 30, 1901, and submitted to Congress by the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution, is an octavo volume of 393 pages, 57 pages of index, over 200 full-page plates, and 25 text illustrations. Part I. is the report proper; Part II. consists of papers describing and illustrating collections in the muscum.

Apparently crazed because he had been deserted on account of his intemperate habits, Frederick Thomas Thrush, a lithographer employed by Julius Frank at 56 University Place, attempted last evening to murder his wife, Cora, and his son, Frederick, seventeen years old, in the vestibule of the flat house at 153 East Fifty-fourth Street.

BERLIN, Jan. 22. -- Under the Presidency of Duke Ernst Gunther of Schleswig-Holstein, Emperor William's brother-in-law, the Middle European Economic Society was formally founded here last night, after having been under discussion for about a year. It aims to procure the establishment of a Middle European Economic Alliance, on the lines proclaimed by Count Goluchowski, the Austro-Hungarian Minister for Foreign Affairs, several years ago.

While still maintaining that the courts could not compel the Interurban Street Railway Company to issue transfers at Twenty-third Street and Broadway or Twenty-third Street and Sixth Avenue, President Herbert H. Vreeland stated yesterday afternoon that he could cut out, if he wished, 125 other transfer points without any possibility of interference from the courts or anybody else, even though it might be decided finally that the two places mentioned must be transfer crossings.

LONDON, Jan. 22. -- Hall Caine's new novel, and the drama founded upon it, will not be published in the early Fall, as was expected. The delay is caused by the author's enforced abstinence from work for some time, on account of exhaustion due to overtaxing himself.

PARIS, Jan. 22. -- The Chamber of Deputies was the scene of much excitement to-day in connection with the case of the Abbe Delsor, the Alsatian priest who was expelled from France recently. His expulsion has revived the animosities growing out of the Franco-Prussian war, a considerable element of the press and public asserting that the expulsion of Delsor as a foreigner marked the final abandonment of Alsace to Germany.

The hockey team of the Crescent Athletic Club of Brooklyn, champions of the Amateur Hockey League, defeated the New York Athletic Club seven at the St. Nicholas Rink last night by a score of 2 to 0, both the points being made in the second period of the game.

Mr. BRYAN has again taken his place as the undisputed leader of the Democratic Party. He is full of confidence, he is defiant. "There will be no fight in the convention by the so-called reconstructionists," says Mr. BRYAN. "They will not be strong enough."

IF judgment from phrases and detached paragraphs, and some knowledge of an author's former work and personal character be valid, Mr. F.B. Sanborn's history of New Hampshire in the "American Commonwealths" series is as original in its merit as Miss Agnes Repplier's delightful "Philadelphia."
CLEVELAND, Jan. 22. -- The Produce Exchange Banking Company, at Broadway and Central Avenue, closed its doors to-day. The Insolvency Court has appointed the Cleveland Trust Company receiver.

Not only does gloomy weather have a very practical effect in moderating enthusiasm; when its effect is to disturb telegraphic communications with the country the market is left to limp along upon its own single leg.

BOSTON, Jan. 22. -- Senator Marcus A. Hanna of Ohio contributes to the February number of The National Magazine, published in this city, an article under the caption of "Socialism and the Labor Unions." It embodies in concrete form some conclusions drawn by Senator Hanna from his observations and experience in business and politics, and in a measure outlines his life work and indicates his personal ambition.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Jan. 22. -- An ice gorge broke above the city to-day and a flood of water swept down the Cuyahoga River, tearing away three big steamboats from their moorings. The vessels were carried down the stream and crashed into the drawbridge of the Superior Street viaduct.

TUSCALOOSA, Ala., Jan. 22. -- The most disastrous cyclone that ever visited this section swept over Moundville, Ala., a town of 300 inhabitants, fifteen miles south of Tuscaloosa, this morning at 1 o'clock, and as a result thirty-seven persons were killed, more than 100 injured, and every business house in the town, with the exception of a small drug store, was completely destroyed.

LOOKING back over the year that has just ended there seems to have been rather a dearth of really notable books. Mr. Morley's "Life of Gladstone," of course, heads the list, and the Carlyle letters might perhaps take the second place in importance.

Grosvenor, the Trow Directory, Printing, and Bookbinding Company announces this morning that it will sell at public auction at noon of Feb. 15 all the "plates, dies, paper, appliances, and other materials used" by them in the manufacture of the book.

There were 225 present, and among them were the President, members of the Cabinet, diplomats, Senators and Representatives, army and navy officers, and persons prominent in the business and literary world.

THE engagement of Enrico Caruso at the Metropolitan Opera House is near its close. He will end it next week, when, if the gods that preside over the health and vocal integrity of operatic artists permit, he will give a final performance of Edgardo in "Lucia di Lammermoor."
DALLAS, Texas, Jan. 30. -- The State of Texas has started in through its courts to "smoke out" the Standard Oil Company, if possible, from its hidden operations in the Texas oil fields.

ATLANTIC CITY, N.J., Jan. 30. -- If plans of local capitalists are carried out, $300,000 will be spent for the creation at Ventnor Heights of an amusement park. The park will embrace eighty acres, and if it is deemed wise a large convention hall will be erected. A gentleman's driving park will be laid out, with a one-mile track 100 feet wide.

AMERICAN trade with Cuba, Porto Rico, and other West Indian points has been seriously hampered by the high rates of freight charged by the American shipping lines which have a monopoly of this trade, and an ef fort is now being made by the Foreign Trade Association to break that monopoly, or at any rate to secure concessions from it.

Nineteen persons -- eighteen men and one woman -- will begin a fight in the Supreme Court this week to recover the twenty-five-thousand-dollar reward which the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company offered for information leading to the arrest and conviction of those responsible for the circulation in 1899 of the reports attacking the company's financial condition, which resulted in the most sensational stock "raid" known in Wall Street in recent years.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 30. -- The House today passed the Urgent Deficiency bill which carries an aggregate of $12,000,000. The paragraph providing for additional mileage was struck out in Committee of the Whole, not a single member having the courage to pass between the tellers in opposition to the motion.

LONDON, Jan. 31. -- Lloyd's Weekly Newspaper says this morning that Mrs. Florence Maybrick, the American woman who was serving a life sentence for having poisoned her husband, was released from the Aylesbury Female Convict Prison at 6:45 o'clock on the morning of Jan. 25 on special license.

Morris Wood, the Long Branch (N.J.) skater, who has held the one-mile skating championship of the United States for the past two years, not only successfully defended his title at that distance, but also gained the honors at one-half and five miles at the amateur speed skating championship meeting under the auspices of the Amateur Skating Association, held at Verona Lake, Verona, N.J., yesterday afternoon.

Some came in short, severely plain dark walking costumes, while others were in heavy trailing velvets, or filmy organdies. Warner of this city expressed the opinion to-night that the judgment of the Venezuelan Federal Hight Court had been influenced by the presence of United States warships in Venezuelan waters. NEWARK, N.J., Jan. 31. -- The E.E. Hogan Shoe Manufacturing Company, which recently failed, has arrived at an agreement with nearly all its creditors to settle at 25 cents on the dollar. The liabilities of the company are $68,985.85 and the nominal assets $34,480.20, including the factory and machinery.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 31. -- Iron and steel exports during the month of December, for which the Bureau of Statistics has just presented complete figures, show an increase of $1,597,938, compared with December of the preceding year. This increase is found especially in steel rails and locomotives.

Henry Stanley Allen, the announcement of whose death at Ballston, N.Y., appeared yesterday morning, was a successful and well-known publisher in this city for nearly half a century, very progressive and original in his methods. He encouraged authors to write books on subjects which he knew the public was interested in, and placed them upon the market by the subscription method.

Last night Miss Ada Rehan and Mr. Otis Skinner revived at the Lyric Theatre the Daly production of Shakespeare's chameleon play of "The Merchant of Venice" -- the play that conceived by its unknown Elizabethan originators as a farce-comedy of Jew-baiting, was so deeply psychologized and vitalized in Shakespeare's hands as to be accepted in the sentimental and humanity-mad nineteenth century as the tragic embodiment of the fate of a persecuted race.

The proposal to abridge the term of the evening schools and other modern educational expansions has evoked vigorous protests from various quarters: but the injustice of the double reduction planned for teachers' salaries seems to have escaped the attention of nearly all critics except the teachers themselves.

ALBANY, Feb. 1 -- Attorney General Cunneen, in his annual report, presented to the Legislature this evening, shows that the special franchise law adds nearly $200,000, 000 to the taxable property of the State, that the amount of taxes which have been assessed upon this, and the validity of which was involved in the cases which the Attorney General won in the Court of Appeals in 1903, was $18,412,884.

Tribou, a gardener employed by her stepfather. The young woman's exploit took place while her parents were visiting in New York, where Miss Whittaker formerly lived.

Philip Kearney of the New York Athletic Club won the one-mile metropolitan skating championship at Olympia Field, One Hundred and Thirty-fifth Street and Lenox Avenue, last night from a field of an even dozen skaters, including all the well-known speed skaters of the city and vicinity. P. Hayward of the Polytechnic Preparatory School of Brooklyn was second, and "Gus" Stoltz of the Euclid School, Brooklyn, was third.

Several years ago there was an agreement by which Klaw Erlanger built and booked in only the highpriced theatres, while Stair Havlin confined themselves to the cheaper houses.

HAVANA, Feb. 1. -- The Department of State and Justice has ordered the prosecution of the persons at Cienfuegos suspected of responsibility for the defacing of the escutcheon at the United States Consulate, and has notified United States Minister Squiers that an investigation and punishment have been ordered. This action followed a demand by Mr. Squiers for the punishment of the guilty persons.

This heir applied to the court for an annual allowance of $50,000, upon the ground that he could not live on less in the style which was expected of him.

BOSTON, Feb. 1. -- The decision in favor of the Amalgamated Copper Company caused an immediate buoyancy in trading when announced to-day on the Boston Stock Exchange. The entire market became active with a rush. Amalgamated was carried up to 50 5/8, an advance of 2 over Saturday. The other stocks sold higher in sympathy.

In a billiard match which was practically entirely at open table play the Canadian amateur champion, Arthur Marcotte of Quebec last night defeated J. De Mun Smith of St. Louis. The contest was the formal beginning of the fourth annual championship tournament of the National Association of Amateur Billiard Players.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 1. -- Secretary Shaw to-day informed the House, in answer to a resolution, that his department had six horses. The total cost of the carriages is $2,145. The "livery" of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing cost $1,028. Seven men care for and drive the "livery."

After a year's absence Mme. Emma Calve returned to the Metropolitan Opera House and made her first appearance last evening, being welcomed by an audience that crowded the house to the doors -- one of the largest, in fact, that has been seen there this season outside of the "Parsifal" performances.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., Feb. 1. -- The graduating exercises of the Midshipmen of the class of 1904 were held at the Naval Academy to-day, and were of an imposing nature. Secretary of the Navy Moody delivered an address and handed the diplomas to the graduates. The ceremonies were attended by a large number of the friends of the graduates.

It will be noted that the scheme is based on the assumption that legislation is necessary.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 2. -- Mr. Clarke, the new Democratic Senator from Arkansas, made his maiden speech in the Senate to-day. He announced his indorsement of every position taken by the President in connection with the Panama revolt and in the negotiating of the treaty with the new State.

TRENTON, N.J., Feb. 2. -- The Lawrenceville Preparatory School is stirred over the confessed operation of a roulette wheel and other forms of gambling in the upper house, or fourth form class, which is to graduate in June. The school sends its graduates to all the big universities, but more especially to Princeton. About sixty students are involved in the disclosure. The Faculty has confiscated the apparatus, and forbidden the players to leave the campus.

After long discussion a sub-committee consisting of Messrs. Goldfogle, Rider, Douglas, and Dunwell was appointed to formulate a plan of action and submit it to the delegation on Friday morning.

William Collins Whitney, Secretary of the Navy in President Cleveland's first Administration, street railway financier, and sportsman, died yesterday afternoon at 4 o'clock at his residence, 871 Fifth Avenue. His death was due to peritonitis and blood poisoning following an operation for appendicitis performed last Saturday evening.

Loree, and other leading financiers as stockholders of the Maryland Trust Company to enforce their statutory liabilities. The plaintiffs are George Gunther, the United States Fidelity and Guaranty Company, and tile Fidelity and Deposit Company of Maryland.

The sudden redoubling of Russian activity, as illustrated by the purchase of all the available coal in North China for Port Arthur, betokens the imminence of the danger.

NEW HAVEN, Feb. 2. -- Henry Miller at the Hyperion Theatre here to-night produced a new English comedy called "Man Proposes." The play is by Ernest Denny, is in four short acts, and met with warm approval by the audience. The piece deals with the difficulty a self-sacrificing nobleman encounters in defending his scapegrace younger brother, who assumes his title and falls in love with the girl he himself wishes to marry.

"Der Detektiv," a four-act piece from Berlin, by Ernst Gettke and Victor Leon, full of local slang and up-to-date hits at the virtues of typewriters and the stench of automobiles. Spalding of Peoria, Ill. A large audience listened to his discussions of "Democracy, Socialism, and Labor."

A genuine classical ballet, "Coppelia," will be presented at the Metropolitan Opera House. Senorita Varasi, who came over several weeks ago but has not yet had an opportunity to display her talents, will be the premiere danseuse, and will have the support of about forty dancers. "Cavalleria Rusticana" will precede "Coppelia" Friday night, as the ballet is only a little over an hour long.

PARIS, Feb. 9. -- The attitude of the French Government in view of the war is now definitely determined upon. France will maintain neutrality under any and all circumstances, the Franco-Russian alliance being construed as not requiring France to intervene in behalf of Russia, even should Great Britain or any other third power intervene in behalf of Japan.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 9. -- The central figure in the postal frauds trial, August W. Machen, ex-Superintendent of the Rural Free Delivery Division, occupied the stand to-day, when the last week of the trial began. He said he assumed responsibility for the acts of Miss Liebhardt, his Chief Clerk, who had initialed and signed letters from his division.

The splendid work of the detail from the New York fire brigade which went to Baltimore so willingly and even enthusiastically is a credit to the force. No doubt it contributed materially to check the spread of the conflagration, and without this timely assistance the area of destruction might have been very much greater.

Edward F. Croker took command of the New York Fire Department promptly at 10 o'clock yesterday morning, obeying the order of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, which restored him to his position as Fire Chief and upset the order of ex-Commissioner Sturgis dismissing him.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 9. -- Secretary Hay has addressed a note to the powers that participated in the suppression of the Chinese rebellion suggesting that they unite in insisting that the integrity of the Chinese Empire shall be maintained and that the field of hostilities shall be localized.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Feb. 9. -- Peace has been once more established between the bowlers of the East and the West, the American Bowling Congress at its session to-day offering inducements to the delegates of the New York Bowling Association which the latter could not very well refuse. The visitors gained one point outright by a rule restricting all future competing teams in the National tournament to accredited members of the city associations.

Erastus Wiman, who lifted Staten Island to its highest prosperity, from which it dropped into financial straits, died last night at his home at the corner of Wall and Jay streets, St. George. He had been ill three years, when he suffered a stroke of paralysis. He never fully recovered, and for more than a year had been almost helpless and his mind was no longer clear.

BALTIMORE, Feb. 9. -- Recovering from the first shock of disaster, Baltimore today sets its best thought to the great financial problems with which it is confronted. Counting round bales as half bales, the number is 9,485,537, which compares with 8,905,503 and 10,588,250 bales to Dec. 13, 1902, and to March 14, 1893, respectively.

Incidentally he broke all previous records in the dispatch of private pension bills. Under his guidance 320 of these measures of relief were passed by the House in 155 minutes.

It is something to be proud of to know that thirteen distinct communities, voluntarily united, created other organizations of equal rank and power with themselves, "until the newly created members of the family exceeded the original in number, in population and in political power."

Late yesterday afternoon the Mayor received information that an attempt would be made to rob the bank, and he immediately swore in a dozen citizens as officers and put them on guard.

The relations between science and literature, and especially between science and fiction, were the chief theme, very naturally, considering the scientific eminence of the guest and the literary character of the hosts.

SYDNEY, N.S.W., Jan. 11. -- Never within the memory of the oldest Australian resident has the season throughout the Commonwealth been so favorable as at the present time, and everywhere the work of pastoral and agricultural recuperation is making rapid progress.

LONDON, Jan. 30. -- Political dovecotes are fluttered in anticipation of the dinner to be given at the end of next week by Lord Wimborne, the principal guests being the Duke of Devonshire and Lord Rosebery. It is assumed that the arrangement is the preliminary to an understanding between the two statesmen that shall have important consequences for the political situation, more especially to the Liberal Party.

His rapid rally from the desperate condition in which he lay yesterday has cheered and gratified everybody. It is admitted that at one time yesterday he was on the verge of death, and hardly anybody dared to hope that he would be alive to-night.

Mr. Spooner began by saying that if the United States abandoned the treaty the French Government would have assumed our responsibilities, which this Nation would not have tolerated.

This pavilion is named after Dr. Abram Du Bois, who for fifty years was surgeon and Director of the Infirmary. He left a legacy of $80,000 for the institution, which endowed the pavilion.

For over three years this alligator has lived without known pain or ache in the city laboratory, but now it is feared by the city's physicians that he may not recover.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20. -- The Navy Department is making preparations to transfer the wireless telegraphy school for enlisted men from Newport, R.I., to the Navy Yard at New York, where better facilities are afforded for this work. It is intended to assemble there all men under electrical instruction, both in wireless telegraphy and other branches.

Hunnewell will play George H. Brooke of Philadelphia, and it appears to be settled that Shaw will again be the champion. Shaw showed easily his superiority over Joshua Crane, Jr., in this morning's game.

CHICAGO, Feb. 20. -- The exoneration of Mayor Harrison from criminal responsibility in connection with the loss of life in the Iroquois disaster and the voting of an indictment charging manslaughter against Manager Will J. Davis were the first fruits of the afternoon session of the special Grand Jury to-day.

A SCOTCH collie belonging to Joseph Thompson, four miles south of Milton, Ind., has become mail carrier for the family. He began the practice of watching for John DuGranrut, rural carrier on the route out of here, a week ago, and since then has been regular in going to meet the mail wagon each day when it came in sight.

There have recently developed indications that all is not harmony among the Western railroads, and also that discord is likely to spread East as well as West. Tariffs on grain have been the point over which contention has arisen, starting some time ago, when the Omaha-Chicago schedules were interfered with subsequent to the bid for business by the Great Western on opening its new line.

OGDEN, Utah, Feb. 20. -- The explosion of a carload of dynamite, caused by the collision of two Southern Pacific trains at Jackson yesterday, and resulting in the death of twenty-five persons and the injury of fifteen others, wrecked everything within a radius of half a mile. Of the forty-six persons in Jackson, only nine escaped death or injury.

The programme chosen by Mr. Gericke for the fourth afternoon concert of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, given yesterday in Carnegie Hall, seemed scarcely a happy one in its combination of styles and moods of music. It contained only three numbers: Brahms's E minor symphony, Lalo's concerto for violin to which he gave the name of "Spanish Symphony," and two movements from Georg Schumann's suite, "In Carnival Time," Opus 22.

The clay target contingent of the Crescent Athletic Club was in excellent shooting mood at the Bay Ridge traps yesterday, and aided by the favorable weather conditions, made good records in the eleven events decided. L.C. Hopkins was credited with another straight score in the third competition for the February Cup, and practically won the trophy, which calls for the three highest scores during the month.

CHICAGO, Feb. 20. -- Amid excitement unprecedented in the wheat pit since the Russo-Japanese war began, wheat to-day soared to $1.07, or more than 4 cents higher than yesterday's close. The advance was irresistible. Armour, who for months has been the almost undisputed monarch of the pit, sold millions of bushels of the grain, but for every bushel offered two were demanded by professional and outside traders, who frantically bought everything offered.

Smathers, the turfman, who is at present in Europe, has cabled to his attorneys in this city that he purposes to settle the claims against the firm.

WAYNE, N.J., Feb. 20. -- Three men were killed and many were injured this morning by an explosion that destroyed two buildings and damaged several others at the plant of the Laflin Rand Powder Company, about a mile from this place. A carload of powder standing on the railroad track also was blown up.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20. -- Postmaster General Payne to-day received the resignaton of Perry S. Heath as Secretary of the National Committee and announced that he would accept it immediately. The duties of Secretary will devolve on Elmer Dover, the Assistant Secretary of the committee, until the full committee meets a few days before the National Convention, when a Secretary will be elected to succeed Mr. Heath.

Rice of New York, will not be started to-morrow, as scheduled, owing to the failure of some of the prospective competitors, who did not play in the recently finished masters' event, to put in an appearance.

ST. PETERSBURG, Feb. 20. -- Military activity is proceeding on an ever-increasing scale, and all is in readiness for the mobilization of the entire Russian army should that become necessary. Officials say that in a fortnight 100,000 additional troops will be in Manchuria. Three army corps of Siberian Rifles have already been organized, and a fourth soon will be completed.
ANNAPOLIS, Md., Feb. 20. -- The Court of Appeals has handed down a decision in the case of Hyman against the State, sustaining the constitutionality of the "sweat shop" law.

Brokaw by 3 up and 2 to play. The play of both was brilliant throughout the match save on the fifteenth and sixteenth holes, where Brokaw's puts overreached.

Dawson, Treasurer of the New York Housesmiths' Union, was reported yesterday as missing from his home, 678 Marcy Avenue, Brooklyn, since Tuesday last, and yesterday Charles Maitland Beattie, counsel for the union, requested the police to send out a general alarm for him. Dawson is fifty-three years old, and has been married twice.

PRINCETON, N.J., Feb. 25. -- Fifty-one men from the freshman class responded to the call for baseball candidates this afternoon. The number of men who appeared exceeds that of last year by five. The men were given their first practice in the cage at the University Field House. They were divided into two squads, and given light work, consisting chiefly of fielding, under the direction of Capt. C.G. Stevens and Head Coach Hildebrand.

Recorder Goff yesterday decided that Charles W. Morse, the financier, under the subpoena first served on him, need not answer the questions put to him by the Grand Jury concerning his matrimonial tangle, holding that inasmuch as Charles F. Dodge already has been indicted, the Grand Jury is not now engaged in investigating a crime so far as the court knows.

Yesterday was a busy one for Lent. With Mrs. Vanderbilt's dinner, the meeting of the Thursday Evening Club at Mr. and Mrs. E.H. Harriman's, and of Miss Leary's Believue sewing class, besides smaller affairs, there was a great deal to do. Friday is not a brilliant day at any time, and the events for to-day are few and minor affairs.

PORT ARTHUR, Feb. 25. -- At about 1 o'clock yesterday morning the Japanese made a desperate attempt to block the entrance of the inner harbor and dock. With this object four merchant steamers, accompanied by torpedo vessels, were sent from two sides toward the entrance of the channel.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 25. -- The Committee on Medical Legislation of the American Medical Association has asked the President to appoint on the Panama Canal Commission a representative of the medical profession, and recommending Col. William C. Gorgas, a surgeon in the army, for the place.

President ORR of the Rapid Transit Commission said some time ago that the commission would welcome competition in the bidding for the contemplated extensions of the subway system. The soundness of this view will be borne in upon the mind of every patron of the city's transportation lines by the conditions of the plans and offers submitted to the commission yesterday by the Metropolitan Street Railway Company.

SANTO DOMINGO, Feb. 22. -- Government forces attacked San Pedro de Macoris last Saturday. They went in in small boats with the intention of landing, but were received with a fusillade from the insurgents which resulted in many being killed or wounded. The gunboat Presidente then bombarded the town and inflicted much damage.
LONDON, Feb. 26. -- The Times's Russian correspondents say that the Russian Government has recently been very active in arresting persons prominent in the Liberal movement.
Will you kindly give space to a few remarks in regard to a communication in this morning's issue, headed "Threaten to Whip Teachers"?

ALBANY, Feb. 25. -- Before Gov. Odell left here for New York to-day a definite legislative plan was arranged. The Legislature will not adjourn before the holding of the State Convention, and it is doubtful whether the members of the Legislature will be able to get away from Albany before the last week of April.

The Hon JOHN H. CLARKE of Cleveland, who was named by the Democrats of the Ohio Legislature as their candidate for the United States Senate against Senator HANNA last month, tells the New York correspondent of The Cleveland Plain Dealer that the Democrats of his State are waiting for some sign from New York.

HARRISBURG, Penn., Feb. 25. -- Against the earnest protest of Gov. Pennypacker, the Pennsylvania Commission to the St. Louis Exposition, by a vote of 16 to 3, to-day decided to request the municipal authorities of Philadelphia to adopt such measures as may be necessary to insure the exhibition of the liberty bell in the Pennsylvania State Building during the exposition.

CHICAGO, Feb. 25. -- Heavy purchases of wheat to-day on the probability of the Russo-Japanese war being of long duration sent the price of wheat for May delivery up to $1.09 a bushel. Compared with last night's close this figure showed a gain of 2 1/2c, and is a new high-record mark for that delivery.
WASHINGTON, Feb. 25. -- The House Committee on Judiciary resumed its hearings this morning on the Anti-Injunction bill.

ITHACA, N.Y., Feb. 25. -- The management of the Cornell crews has received word that it will be impossible for Georgetown to enter the Memorial Day second 'Varsity regatta arranged to be rowed on Cayuga Lake. Syracuse has not yet officially accepted the invitation, but it is understood that she will enter a crew.

Augustus C. Buell, in his new historical work, "William Penn as the Founder of Two Commonwealths," which is published this week, gives up much space to Penn's own account of the Colony of Pennsylvania and its Indians, which, Mr. Buell says, "is the only one of his historical writings that may be described as wholly free from a species of cant which his earlier theological career seems to have made second nature with him."

Dr. Lewis O. Brastow, in his new volume of biographical and critical essays on "Representative Modern Preachers," which the Macmillan Company is publishing, deals with Friedrich Daniel Ernst Schleiermacher, Frederick William Robertson, Henry Ward Beecher, Horace Bushnell, Phillips Brooks, John Henry Newman, James Bowling Mozley, Thomas Guthrie, and Charles Haddon Spurgeon.

MR. PETER ROBERTS presents in his volume, "Anthracite Communities," a long and extended history of the anthracite miners of Pennsylvania. The study includes the social, educational, and moral life of these workmen, and the data obtained are of exceptional interest.

Owing to the many strong points in favor of each of the two new rapid transit subway propositions now before the Rapid Transit Commission, the one presented by the Belmont syndicate and the other by the Metropolitan interests, it developed yesterday that the Commissioners may lay out a compromise route with the idea of having both the Belmont and the Metropolitan interests compete strongly for the contract to build and operate it.

ST. PETERSBURG, Feb. 26. -- A dispatch received here from Port Arthur, dated to-day, says:
Paul D. Mills of Philadelphia, Guardsman and member of many clubs, was elected a member of the Stock Exchange about a week ago. Yesterday he was "initiated."

WASHINGTON, Feb. 26. -- A sentence in a London dispatch published in the morning papers of Tuesday last, giving a synopsis of the decision of The Hague Tribunal in the Venezuela case, caused great surprise here, and has led to considerable comment relative to the supposed position in which the United States is placed regarding responsibility for carrying out the decision of the tribunal.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 26. -- The Panama Canal treaty was completed to-day by the exchange of ratifications and the issuance of a proclamation by the President making public the convention "to the end that the same and every article and clause thereof may be observed and fulfilled in good faith."

CHICAGO, Feb. 26. -- For the second time, to-day, Judge Jesse Holdom fined Franklin Union of Press Feeders $1,000 for a violation of an injunction of the court. The injunction was obtained by the Chicago Typothetae, which charged the Franklin Union with interference with non-union employes.

The "conversations" are after the fashion of newspaper "interviews," with Mr. Archer as the interviewer and a person of eminence in some particular field of thought or activity as his victim.

Alberto Santos-Dumont, the Brazilian aeronaut, has written all about his vessels, and the volume will be brought out in March by the Century Company under the title, "My Airships." M. Santos-Dumont writes scientifically about his many daring ascents into the clouds and his descents to earth.

The two-year-old stakes at Aqueduct have all been filled in a manner which is extremely gratifying to Secretary Rehberger. The Rose Stake, for fillies, closed with 78 nominations as against 50 last year; the Canarsie with 79, as against 57 last year; the Ozone with 86, as against 62; the Woodhaven with 78, as against 58.

John Lane will publish next week in his Crown Library a volume in which is given a picture of the Reign of Terror in the City of Lyons. France. This is the "Memoirs of Mademoiselle des Echerolles." It is translated by Miss Marie Balfour and contains an introduction by George Fortescue. The volume was first published in 1843 under the title "Quelques Annees de Marie," and later as "Une Famille Noble sous la Terreur."

Dodd, Mead Co. will publish next Saturday the "Memoirs of Anna Maria Wilhelmina Pickering," edited by her son, Spencer Pickering. In this volume are lively anecdotes about royalty and nobility, including such personages as Queen Victoria, the Duke of Wellington, and others. Mrs. Pickering, who died two years ago, at the age of seventy-seven, was the daughter of John Spencer Stanhope, a member of a well-known Nottinghamshire family.
TOKIO, Feb. 25. -- The steamship Korea has arrived at Yokohama with a large quantity of corned beef which was intended for Port Arthur.
