N.Y., Lawyers' Co-operative Publishing Company.) The book was compiled by order of the Legislature in 1885.

Frank, or, as he was better known, "Biff" Ellison, who was sentenced to Sing Sing in 1893 for an assault on William H. Henriques, a Wall Street operator, and who underwent imprisonment until he was pardoned six years later, died yesterday from pneumonia at his home, 130 West Thirty-fourth Street.

SCRANTON, Penn., Feb. 26. -- Fire to-day destroyed the business centre of the town of Nicholson, about twenty miles west of here. Seventeen frame buildings were burned, causing a loss estimated at $40,000. An overheated stove was the cause of the fire.

JUDGE WILLIAM O'CONNOR MORRIS of the Irish Country Bench has undertaken to write a volume on "Wellington" for the Heroes of the Nations Series, published in this country by G.P. Putnam's Sons.

So certain was the Governor last night that nothing could occur which would upset the programme he has laid out that he did not hesitate to forecast the committee's action with perfect assurance.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 26. -- After a spirited fight on the armor plate question, which was won by the advocates of the so-called trust, the House to-day passed the Naval Appropriation bill. It was a battle of corporations, in which the Democrats unitedly lined up under the banner of the Midvale Company, while the Republicans stood by what is called the Armor Plate Trust -- the Carnegie and Bethlehem Companies.

ROCHESTER, N.Y., Feb. 26. -- The most disastrous fire in the history of Rochester raged from 5 o'clock this morning until afternoon. Before the Fire Department, assisted by reinforcements from Syracuse and Buffalo, had checked the flames they had swept the retail clothing and dry goods district for a space of three blocks and had inflicted a loss which is now estimated by insurance experts at from $4,000,000 to $5,000,000.

The school building for the Society for Ethical Culture at the northwest corner of Eighth Avenue and Sixty-third Street is finished, and the scholars have taken possession of most of the classrooms. In the basement, which is a roomy structure two stories deep, with high ceilings and abundant light, the gymnasium is complete in all its parts; only the Summer garden on the roof awaits the Spring for its last touches.

William Michael Rossetti has brought together all of his sister's poetry, nearly a thousand pieces In all. The volume is being published by the Macmillan Company with the title, "The Poetical Works of Christina Georgina Rossetti." Mr. Rossetti has provided copious notes and an adequate memoir.

The annual report of the Pennsylvania Railroad for the year ended Dec. 31, 1903, was made public yesterday. The net earnings show a decrease of $237,818 on the main line to Pittsburg, of $696,119 on the New York Division, an increase of $741,998 on the Erie Division, and an increase of $433,043 on the Buffalo Division, making for all the lines directly operated an increase of $184,000.

The significant feature of yesterday's stock market was that all the active stocks declined, while many of the inactive ones advanced, some of them very sharply. The efforts made to support the list by marking up stocks that could be bulled on a few hundred shares had no beneficial effect on the stocks that supplied the bulk of the day's business.

DAPPLETON CO. have received the first part of the manuscript of the second volume of the memoirs of Madame Adam (Juliette Lamber), which will be entitled "My Literary Life." It will be published in June and will be uniform with Vol. I., dealing with "The Romance of My Childhood and Youth."

PATERSON, N.J., Feb. 26. -- Women forming a barrier between a crowd of infuriated men and a swiftly moving freight train alone saved Sedato Dejago, an Italian, from death by a novel form of lynching at the Erie station here to-night.

A posthumous volume by Sir Leslie Stephen is published to-day by G.P. Putnam's Sons. It is the last series of the Ford lectures delivered by him at Oxford, and treats of "English Literature and Society in the Eighteenth Century." The first address gives a history of the formative influences of society and literature in England leading up to the eighteenth century writers and their works.

The contestants in one canoe represented the "Babes in Toyland" company, while the other boat bore the name of the "Mother Goose" company.

Irwin's Georgie, which covered the fifteen-mile course in 44:49. Charles Burd's Torment was second in 48:01, Newton Doremus's Atalanta was third in 48:12, and Henry Grant's Tyro was fourth in 30:03.

CHICAGO, Feb. 26. -- A loss of over 2 cents a bushel in wheat prices caused wild excitement on the Board of Trade to-day. Wheat for May delivery, which closed last night at $1.07 1/2 a bushel, sold to-day at $1.05, and the July option was down 2 1/8 cents, selling at 96 cents. PORT ARTHUR, Feb. 28. -- Gen. Stoessel, Commandant of the garrison here, has issued a General Order directing the attention of the troops and inhabitants to the fact that the Japanese intend to land and seize the fortress.

The will of George Washington Egleston, a brother of the late Prof. Howard Egleston of Columbia University, and of William C. and David S. Egleston of this city, was filed for probate in the office of the Surrogate yesterday. In it the testator makes several peculiar bequests and directions, and it teems with interesting comments on affairs of the family and of the business world.

The architect to whom, by the general assent of his profession, was assigned the work of restoring the White House while enlarging and adapting it to modern needs, as to the fittest architect for that particular work, has probably not been much startled or disturbed by finding that there was a certain representation from Philistia in the United States Senate.

There was much enthusiasm and many evidences of friendly appreciation for the Kneisel Quartet at the last concert of their series, which was given last evening in Mendelssohn Hall. The audience was large, as all their audiences have been this year, and let no opportunity pass of manifesting its sentiments toward this organization, which sets sail to-morrow for a series of concerts in Europe.

More than 300 physicians, among whom were eminent practitioners and men connected with institutions of medical learning from almost every State east of the Mississippi and some from beyond, attended a dinner given at Delmonico's last night to honor Dr. D.B. St. John Roosa and to commemorate the twenty-first anniversary of the inauguration in this country of post-graduate medical instruction.

There were times last night at the New Amsterdam when it seemed that Richard Mansfield was increasing by one the meagre collection of modern masterpieces of acting. Never in recent memory has he been so free from mannerisms of voice and gesture, never has his virtuosity seemed more absolute, or his force of imagination more authentic and more pronounced.

Folsom Brothers have sold for the Ritter estate to Halprin, Lewin Diamondston 602 and 604 East Sixteenth Street, two two-story brick buildings, 50 by 103.3. The buyers will erect a six-story tenement.

Both the Port Chester and the Westchester companies renewed their applications for permits to cross streets in the Bronx in the construction of an electric railroad at the meeting of the Board of Aldermen yesterday.

Unable to face the stifling smoke that rolled up the stairway from a fire on the first floor of the two-story and attic brick house at 180 Forsyth Street, sandwiched between a small carpenter's shop and a big tenement, Mrs. Wolf Rosenbloom, who lived in the attic, took her helpless and crippled husband in her arms and jumped with him to the roof of the carpenter's shop, a few feet below.

ALBANY, March 1. -- Assistant Corporation Counsel Guy at the hearing on the McClellan gas bills, before the Assembly Cities Committee to-day, made an attack on Jastrow Alexander, State Inspector of Gas Meters, intimating that there was collusion between Mr. Alexander's office and the gas companies.

BURLINGTON, Vt., March 1. -- A decided change in sentiment on the license question was shown to-day at the annual local elections held throughout the State. Only forty-eight cities and towns, according to returns received at a late hour, voted in favor of liquor selling as compared with ninety-two last year, when the prohibition law of half a century was annulled.
PARIS, March 2. -- The Harbin correspondent of the Matin says that he was fortunate enough to meet the French explorer Chaffaujon and get from him information regarding the Trans-Siberian Railroad.

Elwyn A. Barron, once widely known as the dramatic critic of The Chicago Inter Ocean, who for nine years has dwelt in London and Paris, is now in New York conducting the rehearsals of his new play, "The Ruling Power,' to be produced at tile Garrick Theatre March 14.

ALBANY, March 1. -- The Republican legislative caucus to-night nominated ex-District Attorney Eugene A. Philbin and Edward Lauterbach of New York City to be Regents of the University in place of Carroll E. Smith of Syracuse and Bishop Thomas Hendrick, formerly of Rochester and recently transferred to the Philippines.
BERLIN, March 1. -- Prices on the Boerse to-day were firmer. Exchange on London, 20 marks 46 3/4 pfennigs for checks.

James A. Hart, President of the Chicago Baseball Club, was responsible for tying up the business of both the National and American Leagues schedule meeting yesterday. On his way to attend the session of his league, which was called for the Hotel Victoria at noon, he wired President Pulliam that he could get no further than Syracuse on account of snow.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., March 1. -- T.J. Cornwell, formerly President of the Bessemer Savings Bank, who, while under a charge of stealing $200,000 from that institution, fled to Honduras, arrived home to-day, having voluntarily returned to stand trial.
Recent portraits and a number of landscapes taken in France by Mr. Hubert Vos are shown at the Kraushaar Gallery, 260 Fifth Avenue, where they will remain for a fortnight.

ITHACA, N.Y., March 1. -- The passenger train over the Elmira and Cortland Division of the Lehigh Valley Railroad due here Monday morning from Canastota, is stalled near De Ruyter, and will not be able to reach Ithaca for another twenty-four hours.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- Whether the Beef Trust is violating the injunction resting against it will be made the subject of investigation by the Department of Commerce and Labor, if a resolution ordered reported favorably to-day passes the House.

About 200 motormen and conductors besieged the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street Station and demanded that Charles Farley, late of 153 East One Hundred and Seventeenth Street, who had obtained $2.35 apiece from them, be found forthwith. The men were very much excited, and it was some time before Capt. McNally was able to understand their story.

Another large and much interested audience gathered in Carnegie Hall yesterday afternoon to sit at the feet of Dr. Richard Strauss, to do honor to the composer, and to hear his music through his own interpretation and, upon this occasion, his wife's, Mme. Pauline Strauss-de Ahna. It was a song recital, in which Mme. Strauss-de Ahna sang and Dr. Strauss played the accompaniments.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- The case of Postmaster Van Cott engrosses a good share of the Administration's attention just now. According to report, the Inspectors who investigated the New York Post Office have recommended the dismissal of the Postmaster and twelve other officials, although it is said that the charges against Mr. Van Cott do not in any way involve his personal integrity.

ALBANY, March 1. -- Inquiry into the charges against Justice Warren B. Hooker in connection with the Fredonia and Dunkirk Post Office scandals was to-day taken up by the Grievance Committee of the State Bar Association. It was decided to refer the charges to a sub-committee of five, conslating of Chairman Huffcutt, Secretary Bascom, and three others to be appointed by the Chairman.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- A conference took, place to-day between Secretary Hay and Count Cassini, the Russian Ambassador, at which the growing ill-feeling in Russia against America and the continued attacks of certain American newspapers on Russia was the main subject discussed.

ST. PETERSBURG, March 1. -- A Russian correspondent of The Associated Press at Shanghai telegraphs that it is reported at Tien-Tsin that 4,000 additional Chinese soldiers have been posted in Northern China, and that the Chinese Government has recently placed large orders for guns and ammunition.

PALM BEACH, Fla., March 1. -- This has been a day of golf and water entertainment. There was widespread interest in the golf matches of Misses Mabel Higgins and Grace Ellis, and there were many sailing parties, especially evening parties. The chief of the evening parties was the moonlight sail given to their seventeen dinner guests by Mr. and Mrs. Newbold Leroy Edgar.

And we see no reason to suppose that this brutal challenge does not represent the dominant sentiment in the party, that is to say, a sentiment which the leaders can count on in the convention.

Our readers will recall the Peking dispatches of THE TIMES before the war was certain, recounting the elements of the military strength of Russia and fixing her actual force in Manchuria at not over 180,000.

ALBANY, March 1. -- Gov. Odell has been summoned to Washington by President Roosevelt. He will leave Albany Friday, and probably will remain at the National capital until Monday. The President did not tell the Governor the object of his summons, and Mr. Odell to-night was disinclined to speculate on the subject.

PHILADELPHIA, March 1. -- The Columbia basket ball team defeated the University of Pennsylvania five in an Intercollegiate League championship game, played in the First Regiment Armory before a large crowd to-night, by a score of 23 points to 12. The victory assures to Columbia the championship of the league, the team having a clean record of victories.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- The monthly comparative statement of the Government receipts and expenditures show that for the month of February, 1904, the total receipts were $45,805,406 and the expenditures $42,634,772, leaving a surplus for the month of $3,240,634. The receipts not only exceed those of February a year ago, but also those of January of this year by more than $4,000,000.

Charles W. Morse, the financier whose matrimonial tangle with the wife of Charles F. Dodge has resulted in court proceedings in many States, was chosen yesterday as one of the panel of forty-eight men from which twenty-three will be selected to act as Grand Jurors for the month of March.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- Like Lord Bacon, who some say would not own up to writing the plays of Shakespeare because it would ruin his reputation as a philosopher to be known as a poet, Senator Spooner has always studiously avoided gaining a reputation as a wit because he would rather be known as a lawyer.

The occurrence of a general conflagration in Rochester, recalling that of Baltimore and so closely following it, will doubtless give a powerful impetus to the movement to furnish New York an auxiliary salt water supply for fire protection, street washing, sewer flushing, snow melting, and other purposes requiring water in large quantities, and for which it is assumed that salt water would answer as well as fresh water at much less cost.

"A hold-up" is the vigorous and expressive and substantially accurate term by which the late WILLIAM H. VANDERBILT was used to describe the process of securing differential rates against New York in the transportation of freight on the trunk lines. The actual basis of the rule that compelled New York to pay higher rates was the simple fact that freight could be brought to this port at less cost than to the outports.

MOSCOW, March 2. -- Among thoughtful Russians there is a deepening apprehension of the prospect of Russia's having to encounter the combined opposition of the yellow races, despite the cunning Chinese and Korean declarations of neutrality.

WASHINGTON, March 1. -- The British Ambassador had a conference with Secretary Hay this afternoon, and it is believed that the question of what is contraband of war was the principal theme. It is probable the Governments of Great Britain and the United States will endeavor to formulate a declaration that will tend to remove points that are in dispute and others that are likely to arise.

ALBANY, March 1. -- The fiercest snowstorm of the season swept over the upper part of this State last night. High winds and heavy snowfalls are reported from all points, and the railroad service for several hours was practically paralyzed.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, March 1. -- The ballotting in the Senate and House to-day insures the formal election of Gen. Charles Dick at the joint session of the Legislature to-morrow to succeed the late Marcus A. Hanna as United States Senator from Ohio.

Prof. Toyokichi Iyenaga, a lecturer on Oriental political science in Chicago University, gave an address last night at the smoker of the Twenty-seventh Assembly District Republican Club, in the Sixth Avenue clubrooms, on "Japan, Old and New." He referred to the war during the lecture. When told about the universal Japanese habit of taking a bath every day, he said that in that respect his countrymen were in marked contrast to the Chinese.

The Easter egg for the children is being brought out in elaborate forms and there are even "Easter egg Christmas trees." These are gift trees, umbrella shaped, from which hang a number of fancy eggs each containing little presents of some kind.
PARIS, March 2. -- M. Hanotaux, ex-Minister of Foreign Affairs, has an article in the Petite Gironde on the Far Eastern policy of the United States.

NEW ORLEANS, March 1. -- The defeat of Floral King, a topheavy favorite in the third race to-day, was a blow to his owner's aspirations in the Crescent City Derby. The colt, always favorite in the betting, led for the greater part of the distance, but failed to respond in the final pinch.

GREENWICH, Conn., March 1. -- Before Judge Jeremiah Tierney, the Rev. A.M. Conway of Yonkers recovered judgment for $157 back salary against the First Baptist Church here. The Rev. Mr. Conway served the church from March, 1902, for a year. The church was struggling, and he accepted a salary of $35 to preach once a Sunday.

Serious difficulties have been encountered by several city departments owing to the incomplete state of the new Hall of Records, which will prevent the Finance Department, the Corporation Counsel's office, and the Register's office from being moved into the building for another year. All the departments in question expected to be housed in the building by the 1st of May, and lease troubles are the result.

Evidence that Senator Patrick H. McCarren will encounter some opposition in pledging the Kings County delegation to the support of Judge Parker as the candidate of the Democratic Party for the Presidency was given at the meeting of the General Committee held in the Jefferson Building, Brooklyn, last night.

LONDON, March 2. -- The Paris correspondent of The Times says a report is current that a syndicate of Paris banks, headed by a large and well-known concern, has opened a credit account of considerable importance to Russia, to be drawn in installments. The price of the issue is said to be 92, with 5 per cent. interest.

LONDON, March 1. -- Money was easy, in fair demand, and abundant in the market to-day, $18,750,000 in dividends having been distributed. Discounts were barely steady. A nervous feeling prevailed on the Stock Exchange as to the outcome of the Paris settlement, operators in all directions being unwilling to commit themselves.

Referring to the article in to-day's TIMES headed "Senators Score Mr. McKim," I am moved to observe that Mr. McKim need not be surprised that his labors in the reconstruction of the White House and the planning of a superb scheme for the development of Washington should be made the subject of attack by certain Senators.

Corporation Counsel Delany yesterday instituted replevin proceedings and took possession of sixty manuscript volumes of public records, comprising the original rough minutes of the Common Council, 1809 to 1831, and of the Board of Aldermen, 1831 to 1847. These old records have been missing for some time, and were recently offered for sale by a dealer in old books, who claimed that he could support his title to them by purchase through a junk dealer.

NEWARK, N.J., March 1. -- Ex-United States Senator James Smith, Jr., has purchased the patent and enamel leather establishment of T.P. Howell Co., located at New, Nuttman, and Wilsey Streets, this city. The deal, which has been pending for several weeks, was consummated last night. The exact terms are not made public.

The article signed "New Yorker," in the issue of the 22d inst., meets with the approval of a majority of the members of the New York Bar. It may not be amiss to state that Senator Elsberg has presented a bill in the Legislature to increase the salaries of the Municipal Court Justices from $6,000 to $7,500 per annum.

Years ago Albert G.E. Kribs, then a resident of Germany, took unto himself a wife, and, failing to achieve the bliss he had anticipated, cast about for a method of loosening himself from the ties which he had assumed. The wife, according to Kribs, was on record to the effect that if her husband was ever convicted of a crime she would secure a divorce from him.
The three-platoon police system with which Commissioner McAdoo would "triple rivet the lid" he is trying to keep down went into effect yesterday morning at 8 o'clock.

An original entertainment by amateurs was given last evening at the residence of Mr. and Mrs. John Henry Hammond, in East Ninety-first Street, for the benefit of the kindergarten of Hartley House, in West Forty-sixth Street. It was a late entertainment, beginning about 10 o'clock, and was completed about midnight, when refreshments were served.

An annual afternoon tea party began at the Masonic Temple, corner of Twenty-third Street and Sixth Avenue, yesterday afternoon, and the regular occupants of the building, recognizing the buzz of feminine voices, knew that the Dressmakers' Protective Association was again in session.

Five men returning from a party attempted to regulate the schedule of the Union Railway Company to suit themselves at an early hour yesterday, and, failing in their effort, inaugurated hostilities which raged at Westchester Avenue and Southern Boulevard until they assumed the proportions of a riot and necessitated the calling out of the police reserves.

Business on the Stock Exchange yesterday continued under the influence of the foreign situation. The Berlin settlement developed nothing unfavorable, and the Paris settlement nothing worse than the artificiality already noted as being strongest there where it has been expected least.

A number of Inspectors from the Health Department, accompanied by William H. Walker of the Bureau of Public Buildings, made a tour of inspection of the City Hall yesterday to see what it needs to place it upon a sanitary basis. They found the plumbing in very bad condition -- so bad, it is said, that if it were not the headquarters of the City Government certain portions of the building would be closed.

The declared purpose of the Board of Health rigorously to enforce, without further consideration for offenders, the ordinance which forbids spitting in vehicles and public places, will commend itself to all right-minded people who respect themselves and have a proper respect for others.

MINEOLA, L.I., March 2. -- Harry Payne Whitney, executor of the late William C. Whitney, yesterday filed with the Surrogate of Nassau County a provisional estimate of the value of the estate liable to taxation in this State.

The Greater New York Baseball Club will not be allowed to play Sunday games at Ridgewood Park. This will be the decision of Chairman August Herrmann of the National Commission, which will be officially announced at the meetings of the National and American Leagues to-day. Chairman Herrmann takes the stand that the playing of the Greater New Yorks at Ridgewood Park would do the Brooklyn Club a serious injury.

Nothing worth discussing happened upon the Stock Exchange yesterday, but why this was so is well worth consideration. Foreign markets and conditions lost much of their primacy in favor of domestic factors. We have begun to lose currency to the interior, and we are shipping gold to Argentina, but the call money market is a shade weaker, while first-class borrowers pay 5 per cent. on time money.

ALBANY, N.Y., March 2. -- Hill and McCarren will not take issue with Tammany Leader Murphy at the meeting of the State Committee Saturday upon the question of instructing for Judge Parker. Senator McCarren made this announcement to-day. He said he saw no good purpose to be served by a fight to commit the State Committee to Judge Parker's candidacy.

Authoritative information from Cleveland shows that city to be fighting a typhoid epidemic, already serious and daily gaining headway. It had attained the importance of 68 cases in one day on the first of the present month, and the official returns for February show 465 cases reported and 45 deaths.
LONDON, March 2. -- Orders were issued to-day to dispatch 2,000 troops to reinforce the British garrison at Malta.

Mme. Nordica, who is not singing in opera this season, has been moved to return to some of her favorite parts in Wagner's music dramas, so far as it is possible for her to do so upon the concert stage. She has arranged a series of what she calls "Wagner recitals" with the New York Symphony Orchestra, under Mr. Walter Damrosch's direction, the first of which she gave yesterday afternoon in Carnegie Hall.

HEMPSTEAD, L.I., March 2. -- William A. Wright, a prominent resident of Freeport, L.I., committed suicide by hanging last night. He was discovered when his housekeeper tried to call him this morning. He had tied a cord about his neck, fastened it to the hinge of the door, and thus strangled himself.

NEW ORLEANS, March 2. -- The Morris filly Viperine won her second stake at the meeting to-day, when she galloped home two lengths in front of her field in the Premier Stakes, worth $1,090 to the winner. Sweet Pepper was a strong favorite at evens, backed down from 3 to 2, while Viperine's price receded from twos to fours.

Conferences between Charles F. Murphy and several up-State Democratic leaders at the Waldorf-Astoria yesterday afternoon and last night resulted in at least five more State Committeemen coming into the Tammany Hall camp. All three committeemen from Erie County -- John J. Kennedy, W.H. Fitzpatrick, and Henry Burgard -- will be with Murphy at the meeting in Albany on Saturday, whereas only two had been counted on the day before.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., March 2. -- Two apparent attempts were made early, this morning to burn the Morristown School, on the Whippany Road, just outside the city limits, in Morris Township. During the excitement caused by the fires some one entered the office in the main building and stole from the cash drawer in the safe about $600 in money.

MONTE CARLO, March 2. -- The semifinal round of the international chess tournament was played in the Sporting Club today, when Marshall went down before Marco in the Jasnogrodsky variation. Swiderski played against Fleischmann, winning in fine style.

ALBANY, March 2. -- District Attorney Jerome let out more interesting gambling secrets at the hearing to-day before the Assembly Codes Committee on the bill prepared by him compelling witnesses to testify in gambling cases when assured of immunity from prosecution.

George Chittenden Smyth, a grandson of the late Gov. George Chittenden of Vermont, and a member of the firm of Cathrall Smyth of 395 Broadway, committed suicide some time Tuesday night by shooting himself in the head. Mr. Smyth's business, that of a selling agent for cotton woolen yarns, has not been paying of late, and this is believed to be the reason for his act.

R.C. Leonard of Central Valley, N.Y., won the fly-casting competition yesterday at the Sportsmen's Show in Madison Square Garden. The contest was with half-ounce bait for distance and accuracy, each contestant casting at two goals set respectively 60 and 80 feet from the casting mark. Leonard, who is the present champion, won with a total score in points of 175.5.

In Germany they deal with the reckless chauffeur afflicted with motormania in a very practical manner. In the Reichstag one day last week Prince SCHOENAICH-CAROLATH called upon the Government to introduce a bill placing automobilists under the provisions of the statute of 1871, fixing the terms of imprisonment for those committing assaults or manslaughter through carelessness on the public thoroughfares.

It is more than three years since Wall Street had as quiet a day in the stock market as yesterday was. Everywhere the chief topic of conversation in brokerage offices was the lifelessness of the market -- there was little else to discuss in offices where no business was being done, and these were in vast majority.

Why do these gentlemen always assume that whatever is peculiar in Russian life is necessarily wrong?
PARIS, March 2. -- Gil Bias publishes an article referring to the revision of the Dreyfus case, which begins to-morrow in the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation.

ALBANY, March 2. -- The condition of every fire and marine insurance company and Lloyd aggregation doing business in New York State on Feb. 23 that was affected by the Baltimore fire loss is shown in a series of tables given out by the State Insurance Department to-day. These figures were collected by the department on the request of State Superintendent Hendricks for a sworn statement from each company as to its Baltimore loss.

The proceedings to test the original Dodge divorce case will commence to-morrow at the offices of William G. Davies, the referee appointed Tuesday by Justice Truax. Both sides have expressed a willingness to have the testimony taken in public, but this will not be finally decided until to-day.

There was a stormy session of first mortgage bondholders of the Standard Rope and Twine Company yesterday afternoon in response to the call of the Manhattan Trust Company, trustee under the mortgage, to give the bondholders' protective committee, composed of William Alexander Smith, G.W. Montgomery, and G.T. Bonner, an opportunity to air their grievances.

MIDDLETOWN, N,Y., March 2. -- Two large real estate deals were consummated in Orange County this week, in which New York City people were the purchasers. Ex-Representative Henry Bacon, as referee, sold land in Cornwall and New Windsor, aggregating nearly 500 acres, to Franklin H. Head of New York City for $29,000.

FREEHOLD, N.J., March 2. -- Albert C. Twining and D.C. Cornell, President and Treasurer, respectively, of the defunct Monmouth Trust and Safe Deposit Company of Asbury Park, were convicted to-day. They were accused of having presented a false minute of a meeting of Directors on Feb. 9, in which the purchase, unauthorized the State claimed, of $30,000 of bonds, purported to have been sanctioned.

ALBANY, March 2. -- The Sub-Committee on Home Rule, of which Senator Elsberg is Chairman, met to-day and listened to a statement from Mr. Elsberg, who has been making an examination of the New York City charter with a view to ascertaining just what home rule New York now enjoys and what more it would be advisable for the Legislature to grant.

Goldman, Sachs Co. yesterday arranged for the shipment of $250,000 gold to Argentine, and other shipments, in addition to the $500,000 previously arranged for by Muller, Schall Co., were said to be likely. The $750,000 which it has already been decided to ship will go by next Monday's steamer, and it is possible that before the day of sailing the amount may be increased.

We hear from so many sources that Chinese troops are moving into Manchuria from the adjoining provinces that it is difficult to discredit the reports. That the reports are credited at Moscow and St. Petersburg is a fact of curious significance, even if the reports themselves should turn out to be untrue.

WASHINGTON, March 2. -- The end of the negotiations for the title to the Panama Canal property is in sight. Within thirty days, perhaps in shorter time, the United States will be in full possession of the property and the money consideration will have been paid to both the Republic of Panama and to the new Panama Canal Company.

Gibbs Kirby have sold for Boehm Coon 230 to 238 West Seventy-sixth Street, southwest corner of Broadway, a five-story apartment house, with four dwellings adjoining, on a plot fronting 77.4 feet on Broadway and 94.9 feet on the street. The property has been held at $250,000, and the present selling price is said to be close to that figure.

WASHINGTON, March 2. -- Pension Commissioner Ware, the poet laureate of the Administration, has written a poem for the celebration of Kansas's semi-centennial at Topeka on May 30. The Kansans expect that President Roosevelt and Secretary Taft will be present. Mr. Ware's poem is to be set to music and sung by the Topeka Choral Society at the ceremony.

ALBANY, March 2. -- Bills introduced in the interest of the Interurban Street Railway Company were denounced to-day at the hearing on them before the Assembly Railroads Committee as "grab" measures. Representatives of nearly fifty public organizations and Assistant Corporation Counsel Charles L. Guy, on behalf of New York City, appeared in opposition to the bills.

O.S. Eldridge of the Polytechnic Preparatory School won the one-mile Class A handicap skating race last night at the Clermont Avenue Rink, Brooklyn. Eldridge had 90 yards start on Phil Kearney of the New York Athletic Club, who was on scratch. Kearney fell after going 100 yards.

WASHINGTON, March 2. -- A row in the Democratic cloakroom to-day was prevented from ending in a fist fight by Representative Champ Clark of Missouri. He dragged Representative Charles F. Cochran of the same State out of the room.

LONDON, March 3. -- The Times's Russian correspondents say that Gen. Dragomiroff, ex-Governor General of Kieff and a well-known military authority, was summoned to St. Petersburg to take part in the deliberations in regard to the conduct of the war.

WASHINGTON, March 2. -- So far as the House is concerned, the present plan for a new Post Office in New York was blocked to-day in a sensational manner, after an unexpected scene in the room of the Committee on Appropriations. This result was effected by two members of the New York delegation, Messrs Douglas and Dunwell.

The giant steel skeleton of the Darlington Apartment Hotel, which since last Fall has been in process of erection on the north side of Forty-sixth Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues, collapsed at 1:30 o'clock yesterday afternoon without warning, carrying with it nearly every one of the workmen engaged on the ten stories that had been raised.

The plans for the merger of the Mechanics' National Bank and the Leather Manufacturers' National Bank are now practically complete, and will be mailed to stockholders within the next few days. It is understood that the combined bank will have a capital of $3,000,000, surplus of $3,000,000, and undivided profits of about $300,000.

WASHINGTON, March 2. -- The inquiry which is based on the effort to unseat Senator Smoot of Utah because of his connection with the Mormon Church opened in earnest to-day with Joseph F. Smith, the head of the Mormon Church, as the first witness. The room of the Senate Committee on Elections was not uncomfortably crowded, most of those present as spectators being witnesses from Utah.

The American Society of Civil Engineers last evening, by a vote of 1,139 to 662, decided not to become one of the constituent societies in the occupancy and control of the proposed Union Engineering Building, for the erection of which Andrew Carnegie has promised to give $1,500,000.

NEW HAVEN, Conn., March 2. -- Stockholders of both the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad and the Fairhaven and Westville Railroad Company, which controls all the trolley lines in New Haven, stated to-day that a deal by which the former company acquires the latter has been practically completed.
The statement of your correspondent "F.H." in last Friday's TIMES that "we all know Mme. Ternina's Brunnhilde" will assuredly not be endorsed by the great majority of the operagoers.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., March 7. -- The United Mine Workers in National convention, before adjourning to-day, voted to refer the final decision as to accepting the wage offer of the operators to the locals.

ALBANY, March 8. -- The Educational Unification bill was signed to-day by Gov. Odell.

McCarren against Charles F. Murphy was unanimously indorsed by the Executive Committee of the Democratic General Committee.

Schofield, commanding the Supply, from Guam for San Francisco, tells of the observance on Feb. 28 last of three meteors which he says appeared near the horizon and below the clouds, traveling in a group directly toward the Supply.

The Special Committee of Twenty named by the National Board of Fire Underwriters after the Baltimore and Rochester fires, has decided to levy a small assessment upon the companies in order to spend the greater part of the year in procuring such specific information as will enable local rating boards to establish uniform fire insurance rates in the larger cities of the United States.

WASHINGTON, March 17. -- Senatorial dignity received a shock to-day, when the spectacle of gray-haired members of the upper house wildly swinging rackets in their hands to illustrate how the game of jai-alai is played, was witnessed on the Senate floor. Protected by the closed doors of an executive session, the members of that august body amused themselves thus for more than an hour, and the liveliest interest was manifested in the sport.

His work in this department had not been unknown here before his coming, though it has not filled a large place in the programmes devoted to this kind of music.

Street-paving contracts let in the Borough of Brooklyn under the last administration caused some lively talk in the Board of Estimate yesterday. The outcome was the passage of a resolution calling upon the Commissioners of Accounts to investigate the matter. A communication from Borough President Littleton requested an issue of corporate stock to provide for the payment of these contracts, given out by Borough President Swanstrom.

ST. PETERSBURG, March 18. -- Concerning the loss of the armored cruiser Boyarin at Port Arthur, a private letter received here says that the vessel was struck by a floating mine dropped by the Japanese. Naval engineers are preparing to raise the Boyarin, though it is considered doubtful if she will be fit for fighting purposes.

March 28. It will bear the title "By the Fireside," and deals with family life and the relations of the members of the household.

The buyer is Daniel F. Lewis, as President of the New York and Long Island Realty Company.

It is to be entitled "Our Mountain." and is the narrative of several seasons spent by the eminent impresario and his wife at their Summer home, Felsengarten, near Bethlehem, N. H.

Mrs. John Van Vorst, joint author of "The Woman Who Tolls," has done well to call her new book "The Issues of Life." It is full of issues, and any one of them would give an ordinary novelist sufficient material for a book. There is subject matter in this one volume for at least five problem stories of American life and one French novel.

Benedict Peeke, the former Secret Service operator and special agent of the Department of Justice.

A collection of lectures which have been delivered by Dr. Brastow to divinity students at Yale, are published in book form in order to stimulate in the minds of young theologians and intelligent laymen a proper appreciation of good preaching and of its value to mankind.

Devereux of the New Jersey Democratic State Committee this afternoon issued a call for a meeting of the committee at the Jeffersonian Club in Newark on Thursday next, for the purpose of fixing the date for the New Jersey State Democratic Convention, which will name delegates to the National Convention, to be held in St. Louis.

Opinions have differed regarding the genuineness or artificiality of the improvement, but its existence is the chief characteristic of the week.

DETROIT, Mich., March 22. -- Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Wurzer to-day finished his opening argument in the trial of Edward E. Farley, the horseman, on the charge of "ringing" the mare Aimless as Sarah Black at the Grosse Point running meeting June 16 last.

ATLANTA, Ga., March 22. -- M.S. McDonough of Chicago, Southern representative for the American Hotel Supply Company, was arrested this afternoon for being drunk and disorderly. It is alleged that he beat his wife in a carriage while driving along Peachtree Street, Atlanta's fashionable thoroughfare.

At 12:20 o'clock this morning the Coroners' jury in the case of the Hotel Darlington collapse found that Eugene C. Allison and the contracting firm of Pole Schwandtner were grossly and criminally negligent.

Charles E. Ackron, who has been experiencing a run of troubles since he gave up the "Tivoli" resort in the Tenderloin and opened a road house and casino in East New York, was arrested yesterday in Brooklyn on complaint of Frederick Brandt of 209 West Broadway, Manhattan.

In discussing the New Jersey Child Labor bill in to-day's issue you make reference to a well-known fact that there are "manufacturers of one sort and another who are eager to get as many and as small children at work for as many hours a day and for as small wages as they can."

ALBANY, March 22. -- Frank M. Baker's nomination as Railroad Commissioner to succeed himself was sent to the Senate today by Gov. Odell. Senator Grady asked that the nomination be referred to the Committee on Railroads and that an opinion be requested from the Attorney General as to whether the rejection by the Senate of Mr. Baker's nomination last year did not preclude the Governor from again sending in Mr. Baker's name.

ALBANY, N.Y., March 22. -- The Hill Automobile bill is in such shape that it will probably pass the Legislature. What is expected to be a final draft of the measure was agreed upon to-night by Senator Allds, representing the sub-committee of the Senate Committee on Roads and Bridges, on the one side, and representatives of automobile clubs and of manufacturers on the other.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., March 22. -- Harry Le Moyne, Harvard's famous freshman athlete, will not be allowed to compete in the intercollegiate championship track games at Philadelphia this year because he unwittingly broke the intercollegiate rules while a student in Stone's School, Boston, last Winter, by participating in an open athletic meet in the Cambridgeport Young Men's Christian Association gymnasium.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., March 22. -- The feud which has existed for a long time past between "Jeffries" and "Corbett" is likely to end in the death of one or the other of them or of their owner, Robert Tweedy. "Jeffries" is an Indian game cock, vicious and wicked, while "Corbett" is a brindle bull terrier.

DALLAS, Texas, March 22. -- The Republican State Convention to-day indorsed President Roosevelt and selected Cecil A. Lyon and R.B. Hawley, white, and Charles M. Ferguson and M.M. Rogers, colored, as delegates-at-large to the National Convention.

The long-expected statement regarding the future of the Northern Securities Company was finally made public late yesterday afternoon. It is in the shape of a circular to stockholders, and is signed by James J. Hill as President, and Edward T. Nichols as Secretary.

TRENTON, N.J., March 22. -- A visit paid by ex-United States Senator James Smith to the Legislature at its reconvening for the last week of the session last night has revived the story that he is planning to make ex-President Grover Cleveland the Democratic candidate for Governor at the approaching State Convention.
ALBANY, March 22. -- Four Assembly District Conventions held to-day elected twelve delegates to the Democratic State Convention, all pledged to Parker. The delegates elected were:

CHICAGO, March 22. -- The features of the fiftieth convocation of the University of Chicago to-day were a letter from President Roosevelt, a message from Emperor William of Germany, and the conferring of the degree of Doctor of Laws upon the German Ambassador to the United States, Baron Speck von Sternburg, Ambassador Tower, and upon five professors of German universities.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., March 22. -- Owing to the very severe Winter many colonies of bees have been exterminated, with the result that honey will be scarce and high this Summer. Willis Andrew, who lives at Leamington, thought he would take a look at the colonies on Monday, and out of the twenty-four hives he found but five living bees.

WASHINGTON, March 22. -- President Roosevelt sent to the Panama Canal Commission to-day a letter in the nature of instructions that is regarded as an extraordinary document and in many particulars without precedent.

Gov. ODELL has kept his promise to the ear of Mr. PLATT by reappointing FRANK M. BAKER as a State Railroad Commissioner, but he has altogether broken it to the hope of Mr. PLATT by causing to be introduced by the hand of Assemblyman BEDELL a bill increasing the number of Railroad Commissioners from three to five, which would give him the control of the board.

CHICAGO, March 22. -- To search for the scarlet fever germ in a series of experiments on apes is the object of a trip to Europe about to be undertaken by Dr. Ludwig Hektoen, head of the McCormick Memorial Institute for Infectious Diseases. The institute was endowed by Mr. and Mrs. Harold F. McCormick, who lost a son through scarlet fever.

Not a single local union last evening had called off the strike of the bricklayers, which has tied up work throughout the city, and to all appearances yesterday it was likely to continue until the first open rupture in twenty years between the Mason Builders' Association and the bricklayers takes place.

Owing to the overwhelming importance of the trading in Union Pacific and other issues concerned in the movement in that stock, relatively little attention was given yesterday to the general list. Outside of the very active railroad properties, the transactions were relatively small, many of the issues appearing in the list of sales showing totals of less than a thousand shares.

When Daniel J. Sully stepped out of his office yesterday afternoon, leaving receivers in possession of all his property, his light jolly manner had disappeared and had given way to a feeling of bitterness, anger, and disappointment. The knowledge that those who had benefited from his advice had betrayed him he had been able to bear, but the belief that some of his friends had proved treacherous was too much for him.

Ethel Barrymore is coming back to the Hudson Theatre in "Cousin Kate" a week from next Monday. This is Miss Barrymore's third engagement in New York in this play of Hubert Henry Davies. It will last only two weeks, after which she will sail for London to make her appearance at the Duke of York Theatre.

Charles B. Van Valen has sold for J.V. and H.V.D. Black to the North River Insurance Company, 93, 95, and 97 William Street, a nine-story building, on plot 61 by 85. The buyers will make extensive alterations to the structure, and will ultimately occupy a considerable portion of it. This company sold its building at 84 William Street to the Queen Insurance Company a few days ago.

Worn and ill from anxiety for her husband, whom she believes to have been shanghaied a few hours before he was to sail for Honolulu as Chief Engineer on the American Line steamship California, from South Brooklyn, Mrs. Henry Shearer of 1,112 East One Hundred and Sixty-seventh Street again appeared at the Morrisania station last night to ask whether there was any news from him.

WASHINGTON, March 22. -- The House to-day added two amendments to the Post Office bill which are regarded as clearing the way for new Post Offices in New York City. One, offered by Mr. Moon of Tennessee, reduces the term of the lease with the New York Central from fifty to twenty-five years. The other, offered by Mr. Douglas of New York, authorized the Postmaster General to lease the Pennsylvania site.

ATLANTA, Ga., March 22. -- The New York American League baseball team defeated the Atlanta Southern League nine this afternoon by a score of 3 to 0. The game was the fastest played this season. It abounded in snappy plays, which delighted the large crowd of spectators. The work of Pitcher Griffith for the Americans was easily the feature.

The necessity of improving the Raymond Street Jail, in Brooklyn, was brought before the Board of Aldermen yesterday, when that body was asked to approve a resolution apropriating $20,000 for the jail improvements.

The remarkable rise in the Stock Exchange prices yesterday of Great Northern, Union Pacific, and Southern Pacific, and in the price of Northern Securities in the curb market, might lead to the inference that restraint of trade thrives on adverse decisions and prohibitory decrees of the courts.

BERLIN, March 22. -- A missionary in Southwest Africa has written to the Reichsbote defending the Hereros against the charges of massacring women, children, and men. Native Christians, the missionary adds, assisted a number of women and children to reach the military stations safely.

Both within and beyond the British Empire the decision of the British Government to authorize the importation of contract labor will be held to denote that the mysterious influence of "the Chartered Company" is as great now as it was when the trial of "Dr. JIM" became the rendezvous of fashionable London.

SEOUL, March 22. -- An interesting feature of the situation in Korea is the vigor with which the Japanese are working on the railway designed to join Soul and Wi-ju. The immediate object is the construction of a light military railway as far as Ping-Yang, which subsequently will be made permanent and extended to Wi-ju.

KANSAS CITY, March 22. -- Missouri Republicans, in State Convention here to-day, named delegates-at-large to the National Convention at Chicago and instructed them to vote for Theodore Roosevelt for President and Cyrus P. Wallbridge of St. Louis for Vice President.

NEW ORLEANS, March 22. -- To save the life of Benjamin Johnson, a barber who was shot last week in a quarrel, Dr. Stephen W. Stafford of the Charity Hospital removed a part of Johnson's spinal cord, performing the delicate operation after observation by the X-Rays.

The Trustees of the Cathedral of St. John the Divine adopted a new charter yesterday at the regular monthly meeting held in Mendelssohn Hall, in West Forty-fourth Street. It will become operative Dec. 27, St. John's Day. Meantime the present board will hold over.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., March 22. -- A bill for divorce which will cause a widespread sensation was filed here this afternoon by Mrs. Alice Fitts Hill Taylor against Robert L. Taylor, who has three times served Tennessee as Governor, and is now regarded as being sure to go to the United States Senate.
ST. PETERSBURG, March 22. -- A dispatch received from Ashkabad (the capital of the Russian Trans-Caspian territory,) says a rumor is current there that the Ameer of Afghanistan has been poisoned.

Prosperity is a hindrance to changes in National politics. There is a well-known and striking coincidence in the disappearance of mortgages in Nebraska and Kansas and that of Mr. BRYAN as a Presidential candidate. The price of the Southern staple, cotton, though not so intimately and obviously connected with the operation of the voters' minds -- which are influenced in that section by some other and powerful factors -- is still of considerable importance.

Booker T. Washington, President of the Tuskagee Normal and Industrial Institute at Tuskagee, Ala., addressed the Methodist Social Union of New York City last night at its meeting in the Hotel Savoy on "The Success of Negro Education." J. Edgar Leaycraft, President of the union, acted as Chairman.

PITTSBURG, March 22. -- The statement made last night by Walter Damrosch, that he had an offer of $15,000 a year from the Pittsburg Orchestra, has displeased the Or chestra Committee of the Art Society thoroughly. A long meeting was held this afternoon, which resulted in a statement being prepared for the papers.

Patrick H. Cunningham, known among his friends as "Harry," who lives at the Morton House, is missing. Several persons want to find him. The last heard of him he was in a lachrymose state, beseeching every one he met to find a policeman whom he had lost. The fact that the policeman had him under arrest did not make Cunningham any less sorry that he had lost him.
NEW ORLEANS, La., March 22. -- Baxter Martin, a young married white man of Augusta, Ga., compelled a negro to shoot him twelve miles from Berwick City, La., yesterday, to escape lynching.

ALBANY, March 22. -- District Attorney Jerome called on Supreme Court Justice Herrick to-day and, it is understood, asked him whether he would preside over a special Grand Jury called to consider the Shipbuilding Trust case. Mr. Jerome would neither admit nor deny that such was the purpose of his call, and Justice Herrick refused to discuss the matter.

Judge Henderson M. Somerville of the Board of United States General Appraisers, whose recent controversy with President Roosevelt on the negro question attracted National attention, issued a statement yesterday attacking Secretary Shaw for his attitude toward the Board of Appraisers and calling upon the Finance or Judiciary Committee of the Senate to make a thorough investigation of the whole subject.

BALTIMORE, March 22. -- The earthquake that shook New England early Monday morning was separate and distinct from the one that affected Baltimore. Dr. H.F. Reid to-day developed the film of the seismograph at Johns Hopkins University and found a record of a ten-minute shock that started in this vicinity at 2:30 Monday morning.

John Pope Hodnett, for years a familiar character to lawyers, politicians, and public men generally in Brooklyn, was taken yesterday afternoon to the Kings County Hospital for observation as to his mental condition. Hodnett appeared in the Adams Street Police Station and excitedly informed Capt. Harkins that a woman had tried to poison him.

There was an abrupt ending yesterday afternoon, in Trial Term, Part III., of the Supreme Court, of the suit which Samuel McFadden of Rutherford, N.J., brought against the Metropolitan Street Railway Company to recover $50,000 for alleged personal injuries. His action was non-suited, and Justice Bischoff directed that the plaintiff be arrested and indicted on a charge of perjury, in pursuance of what appears to have been a conspiracy to defraud.

Paul Schwandtner of Pole Schwandtner was arraigned before Coroner Scholer yesterday on a warrant issued after the jury at the inquest into the Darlington Hotel disaster had brought in a verdict holding Schwandtner, his partner, and Eugene C. Allison of the Allison Realty Company responsible for the catastrophe. Schwandtner was committed to the Tombs in default of $5,000 bail on a charge of homicide.

No statement of the assets and liabilities of the failed Sully firm was obtainable yesterday. It is known that a rough statement was submitted to the creditors at the first meeting which estimated the liabilities at $3,500,000, but this estimate is considered very liberal. It is probable that the liabilities will not exceed $3,100,000, and may be as low as $2,500,000.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- Ban B. Johnson, President of the American Baseball League, has sold the Washington Baseball Club to Thomas C. Noyes and William J. Dwyer, both of this city. Negotiations looking to this end have been in progress since last Fall. The new owners of the club have secured a lease of the grounds at Seventh Street and Florida Avenue, formerly occupied by the National League Club.

PHILADELPHIA, March 23. -- To-day's local market was the most active of the year, the sales aggregating 49,143 shares and $137,080 bonds. It was the arbitrage stocks, however, which made this record possible, as they furnished 39,975 shares of the day's total, leaving only 9,168 shares as the total for the purely active stocks.
TOKIO, March 23. -- The special session of the Diet to-day entered upon the business for which it was called.

Following the rout of the bears in Union Pacific Tuesday, there was heavy short covering yesterday in a number of stocks in no way directly connected with the Northern Securities group. The transactions considerably exceeded in volume those of the previous day and were, in fact, larger than on any day since early in 1903.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- Representative Weisse, the Democratic member from Wisconsin, is serving his first term in the House and has been congratulating himself that he had no record for getting salaries of Postmasters in his district increased or the rentals of Post Offices raised. To-day, however, the scent of scandal fastened itself on him with a vengeance.

LONDON, March 24. -- The Times publishes from a correspondent some observations on the Japanese campaign plans. The correspondent speaks of himself as one who had much experience of Japanese tactics in the war with China.

PROVIDENCE, R.I., March 23. -- In a speech which he delivered this evening before the Young Men's Republican Club, Leslie M. Shaw, Secretary of the Treasury, attacked the record of ex-President Cleveland on the subject of trusts.
The first authentic information of the death of Leonidas Hubbard, Jr., the magazine writer, who starved to death in the interior of Labrador in October last, was received in this city yesterday.

Seward.
ALBANY, March 23. -- The lobby which is working for the East River Gas Company bill followed up its victory in the Assembly yesterday by a victory in the Senate today.

Was he able, safe, conservative, and the master of his own mind and acts? What were his views upon public questions? These are some of the questions that have been asked by Democrats.

Daniel B. Freedman has bought, through E.H. Ludlow Co., from the Cromwell estate, the old Carlton House property, now a vacant plot, at 200, 202, and 204 William Street, and 18 and 20 Frankfort Street, 79 by 57. The property adjoins the Brooklyn Bridge along its northerly side and faces the open space formed by the junction of William, North William, and Frankfort Streets.

ALBANY, March 23. -- Some excitement was caused among members of the Assembly during the morning session by the actions of a young woman who made the threat within the hearing of several that she intended to shoot on sight Victor Shanley, who has been in Albany recently acting as a lobbyist to promote legislation in which New York City employes under the civil service are interested.

Dr. George R. Parkin, the representative of the Trustees of the Cecil Rhodes Scholarships, arrived here yesterday on the steamship Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse to make arrangements for the holding of preliminary examinations in the United States and Canada. The examinations will be held simultaneously in this country and in the Dominion on April 13 at places selected by the various committees in charge in this country, composed of the Presidents of universities and colleges.

In an opinion written by General Appraiser Lunt the Board of United States General Appraisers overruled a protest yesterday against the assessment of one-fourth of a cent a pound and 10 per cent. ad valorem on certain orris root "fingers" imported by McKesson Robbins of New York.
BOSTON, March 23. -- "It is probable that man gets nearer his lost paradise when he is dancing than at any other time."

In regard to the limitation of trade with the Philippines solely to American vessels, the policy suggested by Secretary TAFT in the hearings that have been held before him is wise and practical. It has already been agreed that the law making the inter-island trade coasting trade after July 1 cannot be applied because there is not American shipping enough to do the business and enough cannot possibly be supplied.

Gross earnings of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company for the year ended Dec. 31, 1903, were $16,545,632 and its net revenue $10,564,665, as compared with $7,835,272 for 1902. Dividends for the year amounted to $8,619,150, and there was carried to reserves $728,139 and to surplus $1,217,374.

NEW LONDON, Conn., March 23. -- Plans for the annual rowing races between Yale and Harvard, to be held on the Thames River June 30, were arranged to-day by Julian W. Curtiss, graduate manager of the Yale Navy; F.T. Dodge and W.S. Cross, also of Yale, and R.F. Manning and H.G. Dillingham of Harvard.

Florian Tobias lost his first game last night in the 14.2 billiard tournament for the championship of the Amateur Billiard Club, West Seventy-ninth Street and Columbus Avenue. He was beaten in an ordinarily played game by Dr. A.B. Miller by 230 points to 191. Tobias had formerly held a clean record of five games won.

Senator McCarren has carried the war into his enemy's camp with an earnestness that has surprised staid old Brooklyn. He did a thing last night heretofore unheard of in the political history of Kings County. For the first time since the days of John Y. McKane's downfall a political meeting was held in Coney Island by the opponent of those who carry the vote of that resort in their vest pocket.

Mourners for William R. Grace crowded St. Francis Xavier's Church, in West Sixteenth Street, to the doors at the funeral services yesterday morning. A feature of the attendance was people in humble life who numbered three-fourths of those who were present. Half of them were women, many of them nuns of various orders.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., March 23. -- Even with McGinnity, the "Iron Man," pitching the New York National League team narrowly averted defeat at the hands of the Birmingham team this afternoon. Both teams were on their mettle, and the fielding was of a high order.

Thirteen of the eighteen charges preferred against Justice Herman Bolte of the Second District Municipal Court, in the application of District Attorney Jerome for his removal from office are sustained by Referee William H. Willis in the report which he submitted to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court yesterday.

Beyerlein's "Zapfenstreich," the latest anti-military sensation from Germany, was given for the first time here last night at the Irving Place Theatre. It was greeted with enthusiasm that reached great heights at the end of an almost perfect third act, which afforded Bonn and Christians an admirable opportunity for individual effects and gave scope besides to one of the most perfect pieces of ensemble acting ever seen at this home of well-rounded art.

All overtures of peace had been rejected by the bricklayers when the Board of Governors of the Building Trades Employers' Association met last night at the Townsend Building. The board has now decided to take up the fight, and it is admitted by the National Fireproofing Company that it will continue its efforts to wrest from the mason builders a share at least of the installation of the material it manufactures.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- With cloudy threatening weather to-night and a heavy, holding track at Bennings there is some fear that the opening day of the Washington Jockey Club meeting may lose some of its attractiveness. It can hardly lose interest, for the city is already full of racing folk from both East and West, and never before in this particular did a meeting hold out more promise.

TRENTON, N.J., March 28. -- The wildest sort of excitement was occasioned at this evening's session of the Legislature by a manifesto issued by Republican Mayor Mark M. Fagan of Jersey City to Gov. Murphy, in which he severely arraigned the Legislature for, as he alleges, selling out to corporations, and calling on the Governor to take steps to blot out the disgrace to the State of New Jersey.

Baron Kentaro Kaneko, the Japanese statesman and peer, who has been at the Holland House since last Friday, when he arrived direct from his native country, announced last evening that he would leave this city at 4:23 o'clock this afternoon for a visit to Washington, from which he expects to return April 4.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- The Chinese Government has notified the United States that it does not desire the continuance of the exclusion treaty of 1894 beyond the time fixed, which is ten years from the date of the exchange of ratifications. This took place on Dec. 7, 1894, and in accordance with the requirements the Chinese Government denounces the treaty six months in advance of its expiration.

ALBANY, March 23. -- A four-track electrically equipped railroad for thirty-five miles between New York City and Croton; two tracks for fast trains and two for trains running practically without schedule, after the manner of long-distance trolley lines, is the plan behind a bill introduced to-day by Assemblyman Apgar at the behest of the New York Central Railroad.

At a meeting of the Contract Committee of the Rapid Transit Commission held yesterday afternoon, Samuel Rea, the Fourth Vice President of the Pennsylvania Railroad, pressed the application of the New York Connecting Railroad Company for permission to extend its tracks from the Bushwick section of Brooklyn for a distance of eight miles over land and water, to Mott Haven.

TRINIDAD, Col., March 23. -- The special train bearing 380 members of the National Guard arrived here to-day. The coming of the troops caused absolutely no excitement. Camp was established in this city, and detachments were sent out to various coal camps to relieve the mine guards employed by the coal companies, who have been drawing $5 a day each.

LONDON, March 24. -- The announcement from Salonika on March 3 that the Albanian revolt had been suppressed was, it appears, premature. It originated from Turkish sources, where it was believed that the acceptance of the offer of exemption from the cattle tax at Ipek would satisfy the Albanians.

LOUIS, March 23. -- Letters of complaint against the Rialto Grain and Securities Company received by the Post Office Department were identified by witnesses employed in the department when to-day's session of the trial of United States Senator J.R. Burton of Kansas, charged with having illegally accepted fees from the company, opened in the United States District Court.

LONDON, March 24. -- A series of messages dated between March 10 and March 17 sent by a correspondent of The Daily Mail at Chi-nam-pho describe the perfect organization and arrangements of the Japanese in Korea. The greatest difficulty is the commissariat, as, owing to the poor food supplies of Korea, it is only possible at present to maintain 90,000 men.
BERLIN, March 23. -- Most of the departments on the Boerse to-day were strong at the opening, but weakened slightly toward the close. American rails were higher.

ST. PETERSBURG, March 24 -- 6:15 A.M. -- Two belated press dispatches, dated Mukden, March 22, have been received. They refer briefly to the latest bombardment of Port Arthur, but shed no new light on the result of it.

PHILADELPHIA, March 23. -- In experimenting with a more powerful explosive flashlight powder than he had manufactured hitherto, Alexander Hemsley of 28 East Dudley Avenue, Lansdowne, dropped a spatula upon a marble mixing slab in his factory at 7321 Woodland Avenue to-day, causing a spark.

Natives of Saratoga County who have moved to New York met in the Manhattan Hotel last night, and Mirabeau L. Towns of Brooklyn gave them a description of the Saratogans of to-day as the Summer visitor sees them, and also an inside view of the Summer visitor himself.

Because Mrs. Emma Eames, mother of Mrs. Eames-Story, conducts a singing school in her apartments in the Inverness, at 200 West Fifty-seventh Street, from which issue daily, it is alleged, "prolonged, unseemly, discordant, loud, piercing, and penetrating noises," a mixed comedy of claim and counter-claim is expected in the Tenth Municipal Court to-day.

An investigation of the fire insurance business by the Department of Commerce and Labor was demanded in resolutions which were adopted at yesterday's meeting of the Board of Trade and Transportation. It was recited in the resolutions that the business as now conducted acts in many cases to the detriment of the public.
PARIS, March 23. -- Intrigues against M. Combes's Cabinet are still being actively carried on, and it is more than probable that sooner or later they will be successful.

PARIS, March 23. -- In the Chamber of Deputies to-day opposition by the Clerical Party practically stopped progress on the Religious Education bill, the Clericals resorting to every possible form of obstruction. Eventually the sitting was adjourned, owing to lack of a quorum.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- Senator and Mrs. Alger entertained at dinner this evening, having as guests Justice Brown, Justice and Mrs. McKenna, Justice and Mrs. Holmes, Senator and Mrs. Cullom, ex-Senator and Mrs. J.B. Henderson, Gen. and Mrs. Sternberg, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas F. Walsh, Senator Warren Mrs. Warder, Mrs. Frederick Alger, Mrs. William Bailey of Harrisburg, Col. Hecker, and Charles L. Freer of Detroit.

ATLANTA, Ga., March 23. -- After a riot which was quelled by policemen, the Republican State Convention this afternoon elected delegates to the Chicago Convention and instructed them for President Roosevelt.

ALBANY, March 23. -- Senator Dowling to-day succeeded in checkmating a move of Col. Michael J. Dady by which Col. Dady had hoped to have a Buffalo bill, designed to perfect the voting machines in that city, go through the Senate Judiciary Committee with a joker, under the provisions of which New York City could be compelled to invest $750,000 in voting machines without the city authorities having anything to say about the expenditure.

Nahaas, who is a Syrian, was being tried for assault in the first degree, but the jury that had listened to the testimony in the case brought in a verdict of not guilty.

A Stockholders' Protective Committee is regarded as not an improbable development.

The old-fashioned "children's party" given last night by Mrs. William Massena Benjamin at her residence, in East Seventy-second Street, was one of the few original entertainments that have marked the Lenten season. Baby parties, so called, are not a novelty in this or other cities, but a regulation old-time children's party for grown-ups is unique.

WASHINGTON, March 23. -- President Roosevelt soundly lectured a party of his callers to-day. They were Ogallala Sioux Indians, who, it is said, are more addicted to horse racing and gambling than they are to the pursuits of agriculture. The President endeavored to impress upon his visitors ideas of industry and thrift.

ALBANY, March 23. -- "To pass the Rapid Transit Commission's bills to amend the rapid transit law without the safeguards provided in the Elsberg bill would be to take 'the lid off,' so far as rapid transit is concerned in the City of New York," said ex-Senator John Ford to-day at the hearing before the Senate Committee on Cities.
BOSTON, March 23. -- Henry H. Rogers of New York was recalled as a witness at the opening of the gas trial to-day. This began the fifth day of Mr. Rogers's testimony.

My wife and I spent that night at The Inn, Newfoundland, N.J. Shortly after 1 o'clock she was awakened by a trembling of the house, rattling of the windows, and shaking of a pitcher in the washbowl on the bureau.

NEWARK, N.J., March 24. -- Walter J. Roe of Augusta, N.J., has a Holstein cow that now holds the world's record for producing milk. He appeared before the creditors' committee at a meeting held in the offices of one member of the committee in the Cotton Exchange Building, and told them the history of his last disastrous pool.

Nisard, the Ambassador of France at the Vatican, to the Papal Secretary of State, Cardinal Merry del Val.

William McNeight, a junk dealer, seventy-four years old, lay for 108 hours on the floor of his cabin, the victim of three masked burglars, who had tried to force him to disclose the hiding place of his savings.

The ex-Senator is to sail for Europe April 22, and the State Convention for the selection of delegates to the St. Louis Convention was fixed for a date early in April so that he might attend it before sailing.

Theodore H. Price, formerly of the firm of Price, McCormick Co., which failed in 1900, it was learned yesterday, has paid additional sums to certain of his creditors. Knowledge of this action on the part of Mr. Price leaked out on the Cotton Exchange and caused a good deal of discussion.

Urging the installation of a combined fresh and salt water high pressure fire service in the business districts of both Manhattan and Brooklyn, not only as a desirability, but as an absolute necessity, the Board of Engineers named by the Board of Estimate and Apportionment made its report to Mayor McClellan yesterday.

He was arrested by Detectives Cosgrove and Carroll on a warrant charging him with being responsible for the death of Patrick Farrell, a bartender in the saloon at 242 Myrtle Avenue, that borough.

At a conference held last night at the Building Trades Club at 1,123 Broadway, at which seventeen members of the Greater New York Executive Committee of the Bricklayers' Union and the Executive Committee of the Laborers' Protective Union, the members of which are now on strike, an unsuccessful attempt was made to come to some understanding so that work might be resumed on buildings in course of construction throughout the city.
TOKIO, March 29. -- The special Diet concluded its labors to-day, finally passing the series of war tax and financial measures proposed by the Government.
WASHINGTON, March 30. -- The Hearst movement seems to have had the effect of solidifying the Democratic members of Congress for Judge Parker.

Miss Maud Ingersoll, a middle-aged woman, said to be a relative of the late Robert G. Ingersoll, was temporarily in Bellevue Hospital yesterday for observation regarding her sanity. She has been living recently with Miss Helen Tinkham of 304 West One Hundred and Twelfth Street. About 10 o'clock yesterday morning Miss Tinkham called in Bicycle Policeman Ennis and asked him to take charge of her guest, who she seemed to fear had become irresponsible.

TOKIO, March 30. -- Vice Admiral Togo reports that at 3:30 o'clock on the morning of March 27 four steamships, escorted by eleven destroyers and six torpedo boats, approached Port Arthur and were successful in getting within two miles before they were discovered. Then they were met by a fierce cannonade from the forts on both sides and the enemy's destroyers on guard.

BERLIN, March 30. -- A giant three-cylinder locomotive which it is the intention to exhibit at the St. Louis Exposition, was tested on the military railroad to-day in the presence of a large company of civil and military personages.

Detective Garrick of Hoboken and Court Officer William Wagner of the West Side Court late Tuesday night arrested Patrick H. Cunningham, the son of James Cunningham and executor of the large estate bequeathed by his father. The young man was charged with being a fugitive from justice.

Consternation was general in the Police Department yesterday when it became known that Commissioner McAdoo had re-instituted the system of detailing Roundsmen to act as "shoo-flies" in watching policemen in precincts other than their own. The men detailed were Roundsmen McCullough, Londregan, Schmidt, Maher, Scanlan, and Herrigan.

In the Democratic State Convention which meets at Albany on April 18 more than two-thirds of the 450 delegates will favor the nomination of Judge PARKER. His friends and supporters will have it in their power to pass a resolution of instructions to the New York delegates, and that power they will undoubtedly exercise.

LONDON, March 31. -- The Daily Telegraph says the Japanese authorities have refused to allow to correspondents the use of the field telegraph lines, and that all dispatches must be sent to Tokio by mail. The paper further says that there is no sign that any foreigners will be permitted to go to the front, though the native newspaper men will be allowed to do so.

ALBANY, March 30. -- As a result of the primaries held yesterday, and from his knowledge of the conditions which prevail in the sections in which primaries are still to be held, ex-Senator David B. Hill estimates that 309 of the 450 delegates to the Democratic State Convention will vote to instruct the delegates to the St. Louis Convention to cast their ballot for the nomination of Judge Alton B. Parker for President.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 30. -- But for Ames's effort to get the kinks out of his high-priced pitching arm in to-day's exhibition between the New York National Leaguers and the local Southern League team, there would not have been much to say about the game. The visitors had a walk-over up to the seventh inning, when Ames relieved McGinnity, and proved to be so bad that he was soon forcing runners over the plate.

At sunset last evening the Jewish people throughout the world began the celebration of the festival of "Pesach," or the Passover. This festival was instituted to celebrate the deliverance of the children of Israel from their long bondage in the land of Egypt, and, lasting for eight days, is a season of peculiar observances.

GAETA, Italy, March 30. -- Emperor William, on board the imperial yacht Hohenzollern, left here to-day for Messina, Sicily, escorted by the German cruiser Prinz Friedrich Karl.

Mrs. Botkin is charged with the murder, by poisoned candy sent through the mail, of Mrs. John P. Dunning of Wilmington, Del.
