MONTGOMERY, Ala., April 5. -- While the Montgomery team of the Southern League made a good showing against the New York Nationals for a few innings to-day, McGraw's men batted lively in the sixth inning, and after that victory for the New Yorkers was no longer in doubt. The latter played a perfect game in the field, but, like yesterday, they found the Montgomery team the fastest pacemakers they have met on their Southern tour.

ALBANY, April 5. -- The Court of Appeals to-day handed down a decision in favor of the Medical College Laboratory of New York City in its contest with New York University over the ownership of real estate which the former institution occupies in that city.
SEOUL, April 1, via Shanghai, April 5. -- The Japanese First Army, consisting of 45,000 men, which had been concentrated at An-ju, is moving on Wi-ju by three routes.
There were sales on the Stock Exchange yesterday of 150 shares of Bank of Commerce, in small lots, at 202 1/2@203.

There was a tempest in a teapot in the Board of Aldermen yesterday over the inadvertent granting by the board of the $370,000 appropriation to Commissioner Woodbury of the Department of Street Cleaning for his "chateau" or stable and administration building in Brooklyn. In the printed calendar for the meeting yesterday appeared the resolution of the Board of Estimate making this appropriation.

Aided by Republican votes, the Tammany members of the Board of Aldermen, together with the three Doyle Democratic members from Brooklyn, yesterday defeated the McCarren candidate for the vacancy caused by the death of Alderman Arthur Guthrie, and elected William C. Boerner by a vote of 44 to 9.

ALBANY, April 5. -- Senator Elsberg to-day presented to the home rule conference a report concerning the little amount of home rule which the Republican leaders have concluded it is advisable to grant.

CHICAGO, April 5. -- In the municipal election to-day the Republicans elected eighteen Aldermen and the Democrats sixteen. One independent Republican who repudiated the "machine" in the Sixth Ward, was chosen a member of the Council.

TRENTON, N.J., April 5. -- Henry Tatnall, receiver of the Asphalt Company of America and of the National Asphalt Company, filed his last report to-day, and in it declared that he could not see his way to enforcing the $40 call on each $100 of stock from the shareholders who transferred stock in the Asphalt Company of America to the National Asphalt Company.

After months of secret preparation, involving the bringing together of all street railway employes of Greater New York into one mammoth organization, plans are now being perfected for a big strike which, if carried into effect, is destined to tie up not only every surface and elevated line in the Borough of Brooklyn, but which may even extend to the elevated system in the Boroughs of Manhattan and the Bronx.

ALBANY, April 5. -- At the instigation of New York associations, Senator Burton in the Senate to-day made a fight for an amendment to the Forest, Fish and Game Commission's bill making appropriations for continuing the acquisition of lands in the Adirondacks and Catskills.

A somewhat difficult task confronts the reviewer who would do justice to everybody concerned when considering such a production as that of "The Shepherd King," presented at the Knickerbocker Theatre last night. It was obvious at the outset that a very large sum of money had been spent and that those who made the venture did so in confidence, staking much on the result.

NEWPORT NEWS, Va., April 5. -- With bands playing "The Star-Spangled Banner" and "Dixie," and 30,000 people cheering her godspeed, the battleship Virginia left the ways at the yard of the Newport News Shipbuilding Company to-day. The launching was without a hitch. Miss Mathilda Gay Montague, daughter of Gov. Montague, was sponsor for the ship.

FALL RIVER, Mass., April 5. -- Twenty of the corporations in this city engaged in the manufacture of print cloths, controlling sixty-five mills, have entered into an agreement to curtail production by shutting down two days a week. The action is due to unsettled conditions in the cotton and cloth markets.

WASHINGTON, April 5. -- Representative Wade of Iowa made a Democratic speech in the House to-day. He wanted to know why Attorney General Knox, after successfully prosecuting one trust, refrained from prosecuting any more, and announced that he would not "run amuck."

WASHINGTON, April 5. -- The extortions of the Paper Trust were the subject of a hearing given to-day by the House Judiciary Committee on a resolution introduced by Representative Lilley of Connecticut. This resolution provides for all investigation of the Paper Trust by the Department of Commerce.

WINSTED, Conn., April 5. -- Burton H. Mattoon, formerly State Senator and ex-Treasurer of the Watertown Savings Bank, pleaded guilty in the Superior Court this afternoon to four charges of making false entries in the books of the savings bank. He will be sentenced next Tuesday.

The special organ of the protected interests takes exception to the opinion recently expressed in our columns by Mr. MOSELY of London that the question of protection is a closed one in the United States. Its view is that so long as there are active opponents of special legislation for private interests among the leaders of the Democratic Party, like Mr. WILLIAMS of Mississippi, the question must remain open.

WASHINGTON, April 5. -- The card was an ordinary one at Benning to-day. St. Juvenal was the only favorite to win, the remaining events going to four second choices and to an outsider. Mrs. Frank Foster, always a popular entry at Washington, won her first race of the season. City Bank, that is entered for some of the big handicaps in the East, showed considerable improvement over his previous running here.

ALBANY, April 5. -- By a vote of 25 to 13 the Senate to-night refused to strike out the enacting clause of the Thompson bill extending the corporate existence and increasing the powers of the Niagara, Lockport and Ontario Power Company. The principal fight on the bill will be made when the measure comes up on the order of final passage.

A man came to New York to spend a few days. He had pecuniary experiences as follows: A railroad cabman wanted 85 cents for bringing him to his hotel; proper charge, 35 cents. The hotel newsstand wanted 10 cents for a newspaper; proper charge, 3 cents. Fee to waiter for dinner, 15 cents; waiter grumbled and was reported.

NEWPORT, April 6. -- Charles Astor Bristed is here to arrange for the opening of his villa on Wickham Road, and will arrive the latter part of the month with his family to occupy the place for the Summer. Mr. Bristed purchased the villa a year ago, but did not occupy it last Summer.

WASHINGTON, April 6. -- The Navy Department to-day received a cablegram from Commander Mason of the Cincinnati, at Shanghai, announcing the arrival there this morning of the gunboat Helena from Niu-Chwang.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., April 6. -- Senator Joseph R. A further step in the policy of retrenchment inaugurated by President Ismay of the International Mercantile Marine on his return to this country was taken yesterday, when the private telegraph service of the American and Red Star Lines between their respective offices and piers here and in Philadelphia was discontinued and the employes discharged.

ALBANY, April 6. -- District Attorney Jerome's Anti-Gambling bill, the object of which is to compel Reginald Vanderbilt and Jesse Lewisohn to testify in proceedings to be begun against Richard A. Canfield, was passed in the Assembly to-day after a debate of over four and a half hours by a vote of 93 to 47. The bill now goes to the Governor.

Charles E. Sand and Joshua Crane, Jr., were the victors yesterday in the two matches that were played in the Racquet and Tennis Club, West Forty-third Street, in the National indoor court tennis championship tournament. The semi-finals will be completed to-day, but the results are not expected to make any difference in the opponents who are regarded as sure to be competitors in the final match on Saturday.

Poisoned candy rabbits and candy tops, it was discovered yesterday, caused the death of two children and made another so ill that he may die. The dead children Were Peter Farrel five years old, of 533 West Thirty-fifth Street, and William Haugh, two and a half years old, of 137 East One Hundred and Nineteenth Street.

Agnes Pemberton, a chambermaid, committed suicide yesterday afternoon by jumping from a tenth-story window of the Hotel Willard, at 252 West Seventy-sixth Street. She landed on a dome over the office at the second floor and was almost instantly killed. A porter was cleaning the stained-glass windows of the dome when the body fell at his side and stunned him.

Hoadley of seizing all the assets -- more than $1,000,000 worth -- that Cyrus Field Judson retained after the sensational collapse in 1902 of the famous "International Power pool," counsel for Judson's creditors argued yesterday before Supreme Court Justice Davis against the motion of Hoadley's lawyers to Set aside the order which had been issued commanding Hoadley to open his books for inspection.
BERLIN, April 6. -- Prices on the Boerse to-day in most departments were weaker, but iron and coal shares were higher.
ST. PETERSBURG, April 6. -- The scheme for retrenchments in expenditure in consequence of the war was gazetted to-day.

HUNTINGTON, West Va., April 6. -- John McFarland, Chief of Police of North Fork, and J.A. Ballard, merchant, capitalist, and lumberman, are dead as the result of a pistol duel, which followed the Republican District Convention there last evening. The convention was for the purpose of selecting delegates to the McDowell County Convention, held at Welch to-day.

The dispatch we published yesterday morning regarding the efforts of King EDWARD to promote a settlement of the war in the East shows the feeling on this subject in the capitals of Europe. It was a telegram from Berlin to the Soir of Brussels, a paper having the reputation of being unusually well informed as to matters of high importance in European politics.

PHILADELPHIA, April 6. -- It was fortunate local houses had the arbitrage shares to fall back on to-day, otherwise the trading here would have been dull indeed. Cambria Steel improved fractionally in sympathy with the rise in United States Steel issues. Electric Storage Battery was up 1/4 and Huntington and Broadtop preferred 1/2. These were the extreme changes.

Active stocks did not show a single decline exceeding a fraction, and but few of them, while among fifty advances there were a dozen of a point or more. The volume of business was but a trifle smaller than on Tuesday, and the distribution continued to show improvement, many into the ten-thousand-share class.
BERLIN, April 6.--Fabulous swarms of locusts have devastated the Valley of the Usumbara, in German East Africa. They were first noticed coming from Wombo on Feb. 22.

Heretofore all the Mayors who joined the league have been in favor of continuing the fight for equal taxation until a victory is achieved or defeat assured.

The joint arbitration board of the Mason Builders' Association and the bricklayers' unions will meet to-day to settle the disputed points.
LONDON, April 6. -- Major Seely (Independent) was re-elected without opposition yesterday to represent the Isle of Wight Division of Hampshire in the House of Commons.

OSWEGO, N.Y., April 6. -- Urged on by over a thousand citizens, the Superintendent of Streets and a gang of men, headed by Mayor Mansfield and several city officials, to-night tore up the Delaware, Lackawanna, and Western tracks from the Water Street crossing, regarded as the most dangerous in the city.

LONDON, April 6. -- There was a plethora of money in the market to-day, but there was a moderate demand, owing to the consols settlement, while heavy repayments were made to the Bank of England. The issue of u2,000,000 of new Treasury bills on April 11 will, it is expected, reduce supplies and have a steadying effect on discounts.

Pennypacker, James Elverson of Philadelphia, O.D. Bleakley of Franklin, and Francis L. Robbins of Pittsburg were elected delegates at large to the National Convention, and instructed to vote for the nomination of President Roosevelt.
BINGHAMTON, N.Y., April 6. -- Alderman Joseph Gilbert, who was known throughout Northern Pennsylvania as the "marrying Alderman," died at his residence in this city this afternoon from pneumonia.
ALBANY, April 6. -- Frank M. Baker's nomination as Railroad Commissioner was to-day confirmed by the Senate by a vote of 30 to 18.

With Bishop Edward G. Andrews presiding, the New York Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church opened its one hundred and fifth session yesterday morning at St. Paul's Methodist Episcopal Church, West End Avenue and Eighty-sixth Street. W.F. Brush was elected Secretary, A.A. Walker Statistical Secretary, Arthur Thompson Treasurer, and R.L. Ross Postmaster.
ASBURY PARK, N.J., April 6. -- Charles Murphy, William Brace, and Edward Wright, according to reports in Bradley Beach and the vicinity of Shark River, were drowned in that river Monday morning.

Miss Crosby has instructed her attorneys to bring suit against Carleton to force him to make an accounting to her of the sale of a certain book called "Fannie Crosby, Her Life Work," also to bring an injunction to restrain him from continuing its publication.

While attempting to save a woman from being killed in the Melrose yards of the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad yesterday afternoon John Haverly, a brakeman, twenty-four years old, of 653 Courtlandt Avenue, had his left leg cut off clean, close to the hip and also sustained serious internal injuries.

RICHMOND, Va., April 6. -- The New York American League team played an errorless game to-day, and defeated the Montreal team by 4 to 0. Chesbro and Hughes, who pitched in four and five innings each, were batted for four singles each. Ganzel made the only two-base hit of the game, in the third inning, when two of New York's four runs were made.

WASHINGTON, April 6. -- A curious occurrence at the White House which happened ten days ago came to light to-day. It has been kept dark for some reason by everybody concerned, and was revealed to-day by Representative Baker of Brooklyn.

ITHACA, N.Y., April 6. -- The Cornell 'Varsity crew and the two junior 'Varsity eights rowed to-night for the first time this year on Cayuga Lake. Coach Courtney followed the men in the launch, and made them pull to Crowbar Point and back, a distance of twelve miles. The oarsmen have been rowing on the inlet for nearly two weeks, and stood the hard practice well, although all were tired when they reached the boathouse.

Antonio Ferratti of 118 Mulberry Street, better known as "The Passionate Antonio," on account of the fervor with which he grinds "Hiawatha" and "Bedelia" from his street piano, has met with a sad misfortune. His sole means of livelihood -- the piano -- has been ruined forever by the eccentricity of a horse which he purchased to drag the instrument through the streets. The horse is dead too, and that augments Antonio's grief.

WASHINGTON, April 6. -- The expectation that there might be, based on the recent decision of the United States Supreme Court in the case of South Dakota vs. North Carolina, an effort to enforce the payment of a large amount of Southern State and Confederate bonds which for many years have been considered worthless, does not receive much encouragement iron lawyers here who are conversant with the facts in the case in question.

WASHINGTON, April 6. -- Bishop Spalding of Peoria, a member of the Anthracite Coal Strike Commission, to-day urged the plan of arbitration contained in the Foss bill before the House Committee on Labor. The bill provides for a permanent Board of Arbitration, to which shall be referred disputes between labor and capital.

Further details which came to light yesterday regarding the large purchases of real estate at Rector Street and Trinity Place disclosed the plans of the United States Express Company to erect a large office building on the site, which will be occupied jointly by that corporation and the Interborough Rapid Transit Company.

Mrs. Anna Roberts of Eighth Avenue and One Hundred and Eleventh Street was the victim of a bold highway robbery on the One Hundred and Twenty-fifth Street station of the west side elevated roads at 1:30 o'clock this morning.

That is to say, although there was some loss of buoyancy, except in restricted cases, there was an increase of activity, and, although there were a few more fractional declines and limitation in the number and extent of the advances of a point or more, nevertheless maintained strength was the day's characteristic, and was all the more remarkable because occurring on four consecutive days.
WASHINGTON, April 7. -- A representative and distinguished company attended the dinner of the Periodical Publishers' Association of America given at the New Willard Hotel to-night.

These have been very much in evidence at the meetings held to protest against the increase. CHICAGO, April 7. -- A special car containing sixty-three Indians belonging to Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show was smashed in a collision between the Oregon Express and a fast mail train on the Chicago and Northwestern Railway near Maywood, Ill., to-day during a fog. Both trains were east-bound.

While testifying in his own behalf, during his trial on the charge of perjury in connection with an alleged fraudulent bail bond before Recorder Goff and a jury in the Court of General Sessions yesterday, Herman Froelich of 1,877 Third Avenue, a professional bondsman, by his own admission, declared that he had divided the fees for his services with four Police Sergeants.

DEDHAM, Mass., April 7. -- The divorce libel of Mrs. Augusta Partridge against the noted sculptor, William Ordway Partridge, was heard before Judge Wait in Norfolk County Superior Court to-day. There was nothing sensational brought out and no contest. Mr. Partridge was present with his counsel, but took no part in the proceedings.

ALBANY, April 7. -- The plans of Dr. Andrew S. Draper, the new Commissioner of Education, for the unification and organization of the State Educational Departments, were submitted by him to-day to the Regents of the university in their first meeting as recreated under the unification law, and were unanimously approved.

BOSTON, April 7. -- A dispatch from Providence says that Addison's disease has caused the death there of Miss Violetta M. Potter, a beautiful young society woman, who lived with her parents at 746 North Main Street.

Bridge Commissioner Best has altered his plans for a Brooklyn Bridge terminal and forwarded a communication to that effect yesterday to the Board of Estimate and Apportionment, where the matter will be taken up to-day. The Commissioner now advocates the cutting down of the bridge terminal so that it will extend north only to Duane Street, instead of to Worth Street, as first planned.

WASHINGTON, April 7. -- The Senate to-day listened to eulogies of the late Senator Hanna by Messrs. Foraker, Scott, Cockrell, Platt of Connecticut, Cullom, Blackburn, Elkins, Fairbanks, Daniel, Perkins, Depew, Beveridge, Dolliver, Kearns, and Dick.
NATCHEZ, Miss., April 7. -- A violent storm, which in some districts reached the proportions of a tornado, swept over parts of Mississippi and Texas to-day.

ALBANY, April 7. -- This was a field day for the so-called "grab" bills. Several of the most favored of the measures were passed and several more were advanced. The principal "grabs," passed by either one body or the other, were the Niagara Power bill, the Merritt Water Storage bill, and the Ramapo Water bill.

With only a single dissenting vote the Chamber of Commerce at its regular monthly meeting yesterday adopted resolutions requesting Commissioner McAdoo to establish in the Police Department a Bureau of Street Traffic for the particular purpose of regulating the matter of sidewalk obstruction by merchants through an ordinance proposed by the Chamber.

WASHINGTON, April 7. -- It is no uncommon thing for a member of the House to be a prominent Presidential possibility, but it is a very unusual thing for a Congressman to be thus vividly in the limelight and yet for so little to be known about his work in Congress as is the case with William Randolph Hearst.

ALBANY, April 7. -- The Hill Automobile bill passed the Assembly to-day without discussion. It regulates in detail the registration and identification of motor vehicles and the use of the public highways by such vehicles. Display of registration numbers on aluminum seals affixed to the vehicle and chauffeurs' licenses and registration are prescribed in detail.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., April 7. -- After all, it appears that the beautiful place at Morristown, N.J., known as Erin Farm is not the property of Hubert M. Hartigan, who was coachman for Granville W. Garth and who has been the reputed owner. A deed was placed on file with the County Clerk to-day conveying the property from Hartigan to Mr. Garth's widow.

WASHINGTON, D.C., April 7. -- Three favorites again finished in front at the Benning track to-day, but May Holladay, a 20 to 1 outsider, produced consternation in the ranks of the talent by defeating City Bank in the third race, at six furlongs, John Madden's colt showed a complete reversal of form.

WASHINGTON, April 7. -- The Census Bureau to-day issued a bulletin which gives the estimated population of the United States for 1903, exclusive of Alaska and the insular possessions of the United States, as 79,900,389. This is an increase of 3,905,814 since the census of 1900.

PHILADELPHIA, April 7. -- Detective James Tate, Jr., and William Laycock, a jeweler of this city, left here to-day for Washington to bring Back George J. Engleman, the diamond thief who was arrested there last night and is wanted here for robbing Mr. Laycock of $2,500 worth of diamonds.

He has lain there since 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and to-night no one knows whether he is alive or dead.

Mr. O'Connor's article in review of the Autobiography of Herbert Spencer, which we publish this week, points out clearly its inevitable defects (from the literary point of view,) as well its many merits. It is not, as the reviewer expresses it, "good literature"; in all its pages "no person or event is quickened into a reality." As a revelation of self, even, the work is "vague and abstract."

IT is not strange that the author of the article entitled "A Limited Philosopher" should condemn Spencer's judgments on poetry and art. Influenced by distinctly literary ideas, as Spencer is by those distinctively scientific, his critic is naturally precluded from comprehending sympathetically, or even tolerantly, the "anfractuosities" of the philosopher's intellect.

Detectives charge that stolen property has been recovered from the home of young Creider, and that the son's wife has made confessions implicating both her husband and father-in-law.

AUBURN, N.Y., April 23. -- The disclosures following the death of Albert G. Burtis of the town of Fleming, Cayuga County, a year ago, which were brought out by the contest over the probate of his alleged last will and testament are of general interest, not alone because of their peculiar nature, but on account of the important legal questions involved.

WASHINGTON, April 23. -- The Gridiron Club gave a dinner to-night at the Arlington Hotel which closed the club's series of entertainments for the season. It was a "Spring" dinner, and in recognition of that fact the color scheme was green. The guests numbered 125, and for a dinner so late in the season the list was notable in number and quality.

A Shan-Tung terrier invariably regards any other canine not of his own strain with supercilious contempt.

Allen on the courts of the New York Lawn Tennis Club. One Hundred and Twenty-third Street and St. Nicholas Avenue. The final score was 6 -- 4, 6 -- 2, 3 -- 6, 8 -- 10, 7 -- 5.

BOSTON, April 23. -- An operation which took place yesterday at the Eye and Ear Infirmary in this city seems to indicate that the color of the human eye can be changed by the use of needles.

Dunstan, Director of the Imperial Institute. The Greater New Yorks were unable to play their last contest with Washington, but at the Polo Grounds McGraw's men failed to keep up their recent powerful hitting, and had to succumb to the Brooklyns.

I am a frequent visitor to your city, and have dropped into various churches, as I happened to be near them. I have heard many sermons in these churches, good, bad, and indifferent.

In a decision written by General Appraiser Eugene G. Hay the Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday reversed itself and sustained a protest by Henry Pfaltz of New York against the assessment of a duty of 15 cents a pound and 20 per cent., as gelatin, on merchandise known as gelatin sheets. The importer claimed that it was dutiable at 35 per cent. as a manufacture of gelatin.

It was Miss Jennie A. Rogers of Brooklyn who brought about the nearest approach to discord in the third convention of the New York City Federation of Women's Clubs, which was held yesterday in the Clinton Avenue Congregational Church, Brooklyn. Miss Rogers is a gentle-looking little woman, but she was determined that the Federation should go on record against the Remsen Gas bill, and she made her point, despite all opposition.

Citizens of King's Bridge to the numberf of thirty-one, of whom nine were women, held a "mass" meeting in the Marble Hill Hose Company's hall last evening and drafted a petition that is to be submitted to Gov. Odell asking him to veto Senator Plunkitt's Spuyten Duyvil bill.

POUGHKEEPSIE, N.Y., April 26. -- As a sequel to the burning of the Van Alen country place at New Hamburg in February, 1903, Ellis B. Southworth, a New York lawyer of 68 William Street, was arrested by Deputy Sheriff Baumbush at his office this afternoon on a bench warrant charging him with arson in the first degree.

A Tammany Alderman returning from travels in the West reports that Judge PARKER "will not get a solid delegation from Indiana." It appears that the Judge has "lost ground there on account of the action of the Democratic State Convention of this State." It is "the conduct of DAVID B. HILL" that offends the Tammany Democrats.
PARIS, April 26. -- An important meeting of Colombian bondholders, convened by the Foreign Bondholders' Committee, is to be held in London to-morrow, according to private information received here.

BOSTON, April 26. -- As a result of an alleged indignity to Mrs. Montaigue and her sister of Washington, intimate friends of President Roosevelt and Secretary Shaw, by Special Employe Martin of this port, Martin has been arraigned by Collector Lyman, who is preparing an account of the treatment of Mrs. Montaigue for Washington officials.

Conditions widely different from those of the opening day confronted the race-going crowd at the Jamaica track yesterday, the attendance falling off to about one-half of what it was on Monday, and the races being run on a wet and heavy course, while a chilling breeze from the ocean searched through every nook and corner of grand and field stands.
INDIANAPOLIS, April 26. -- The Indiana Republican Convention organized to-day, and will complete its work to-morrow after having nominated a State ticket and adopted a platform.

ST. PETERSBURG, April 26. -- While King Edward's move to restore peace between Russia and Japan has failed, it is nevertheless regarded as highly significant in diplomatic circles. It is the first tangible evidence of a change in the relations between Russia and Great Britain.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- The Senate to-day passed the Military Appropriation bill, the last of the supply measures. The amendments suggested by the Committee on Military Affairs for a reorganization of the Medical and Ordnance Departments of the army and for the establishment of a number of camp sites were thrown out on points of order.

The Republicans did not dare to press the ship subsidy scheme to a vote at the present session of Congress. Probably it would have been defeated by the votes of the Northwest, where neither the farmers nor the manufacturers are enamored of the idea of paying money from taxation to hire American vessels to carry freight as cheaply as it is now carried in open competition for all the world.
LIAO-YANG, April 26. -- Between last night and this morning the Japanese forced a passage of the Yalu, two companies crossing between Tchangjiou and Siaopoussikhe.
MADRID, April 26. -- Premier Maura, who arrived here this morning, was shot at, but was not wounded, while on his way here from the Balearic Islands.

Startled by the death cry of her little son Theodore, two and a half years old, Mrs. Joseph Ginsberg, looking from window of her home at 181 Christopher Street, East New York, saw the little fellow knocked down by a team of horses and the wheels of a heavily laden lime truck pass over his body.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- Admiral Dewey placed himself on record in favor of the general board plan of Secretary Moody before the House Committee on Naval Affairs to-day. The present Naval Board, the Admiral said, was too large. Its sessions were like "town meetings."

Knowing you to be on the side of honesty and fair play, may I call your attention to the number of "skin game" agencies in this city. I mean those for the class of workers other than domestics. The unfortunate girl or woman in the vain hunt for work sees the tempting advertisements of these places in the "help wanted" columns of the newspapers.

Death laid a sudden hand on Charles Kelly, engineer of the East River ferryboat America, as she was crossing the crowded stream from Grand Street, Manhattan, to Broadway, Williamsburg, at 7 o'clock last evening, bearing more than 300 passengers, and many horses and wagons. No one was near Kelly, and none suspected that anything was wrong until the pilot gave the customary two bells to slow as the old sidewheeler forged toward her Brooklyn slip.

David B. Hill came down from Albany yesterday, and during the course of the afternoon he conferred with August Belmont and William F. Sheehan at their down-town offices, had a curbstone confab with James J. Martin, the Tammany leader of the Twenty-seventh District, and was closeted for over an hour with Senator Patrick H. McCarren at the Hoffman House. He had a second conference last night with Mr. Sheehan at Mr. Sheehan's residence.

Lord CHOMER in Egypt has had troubles such as our own officers in the Philippines have encountered through the inability of the native mind to grasp the ideas and methods of the Western mind. This is shown in the tendency to observe minutely the letter of orders and regulations, no matter what the circumstances may require.

The main significance of the Russian attack upon Gen-san is in the fact that the Russian Vladivostok squadron is "out" and must henceforth be reckoned with by the Japanese as part of the Russian effective. It has broken out once before, and done rather more damage than it did on this later occasion.

The Executive Committee of the Trust Company Section of the American Bankers' Association met yesterday afternoon in the offices of the United States Mortgage and Trust Company preparatory to the meeting of the Executive Council of the association to-day and to-morrow. Several questions came before the committee for discussion, upon which report will be made when the annual meeting of the section is held in connection with that of the American Bankers' Association next Fall.

Contrary to the expectations of the cynics that the National Arts Theatre Society's year of existence had ended with mere theories, as it began, there came to light at its annual dinner last night the fact that at least one very rich man was ready to put down $50,000 toward the scheme for building a temple of dramatic art in this city.

My interest has been aroused by the publication of the latest ideas of Prof. Patten of the University of Pennsylvania upon the solution of the labor questions. He gives us to understand that a solution of these questions will be produced if the wives of men who earn less than $20 per week will also become wageworkers.

We have had quite enough about the revolting effects of Mermonism upon the tastes and habits of the Mormons, in the testimony of the witness CANNON, who deposed that he married two sisters on the same day, and in the testimony of other witnesses. We have also had ample evidence of the extent to which the Mormon Church interests itself in politics, insomuch that the State of Utah is only another name for it.

The discussion in the United States Senate on Monday, started by Senator HALE in his comments on the conference report on the Naval Appropriations bill, was extremely significant. It warranted the conclusion that if the matter of the appropriation for new battleships had not been agreed to by both houses and thus placed beyond the jurisdiction of the conference committee its recommendation would be to strike out the provision for battleships.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- Senator Quarles to-day bade the President good-bye preparatory to an immediate return to Wisconsin to "fix his fences," as he expressed it. Next January the Wisconsin Legislature will choose a successor to Senator Quarles, whose term expires in March, 1905.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- The climax to the Cockran-Dalzell affair came in the House to-day, and but for the Speaker's personal participation in the proceedings, in violation of all custom, Cockran might have stampeded the whole body, Republicans as well as Democrats.

HUDSON, N.Y., April 26. -- After an entire day spent at Bell Place investigating the depredations of the vandals who disturbed the old Gen. Livingston tomb, Chief of Police Lane of this city and Deputy Sheriff Drumm of Columbia County declare to-night that robbery of jewels believed to have been buried with "Widow Mary" Livingston was the real motive for the crime.

Four alarms were turned in for a fire in the big plant of the John Stanley Soap Works, at the foot of West Thirtieth Street about 1:30 o'clock this morning. The building has a frontage of 100 feet on West Thirtieth Street. In the rear on Twenty-ninth Street, is the plant of the Dunbar Lumber Company, and to the East is the Philadelphia Schuylkill Coal Company.

The officials of the Philadelphia National League Club, alarmed at the many reverses sustained by the team since the championship season began, closed two deals yesterday which will materially strengthen the nine. First Baseman Jack Doyle has been secured from the Brooklyn Club, and the New Yorks have released "Billy" Lauder, last year's third baseman.

Further contraction in business accompanied a slight advance in a number of stocks in yesterday's market, but the improvement in prices as a favorable factor was offset by the smaller volume of business. United States Steel was again the most active stock, supplying about 40,000 shares out of the total of 197,000 shares.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- The last Cabinet dinner of the season took place this evening, when the Secretary of Commerce and Labor and Mrs. Cortelyou were the hosts of the President and Mrs. Roosevelt and all the Cabinet officers now in the city.

That Edward Theodore Chalmes is blessed with the "cool cheek" that women are prone to admire is evident from the picturesque tale of love and deception which came out in Jefferson Market Court yesterday when Chalmes, who is a valet, was arraigned on a charge of grand larceny. His pretty wife, who is known on the stage as Hazel Hughes, is the tearful heroine of what appears to be a tragic comedy.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- When the Smoot investigation before the Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections was opened to-day. Moses Thatcher was again called to the stand, and Lawyer Van Cott interrogated Mr. Thatcher in regard to his views on Church interference in politics.
ST. PETERSBURG, April 26. -- It is officially admitted here that the Japanese are crossing the Yalu River.

WASHINGTON, April 26. -- Notwithstanding inauspicious weather, the Countess Cassini held her fair for the Russian Red Cross this afternoon in the grounds of Belmont, the home of Mr. and Mrs. A.L. Barber, at Fourteenth and Clifton Streets, where a semi-circle of booths and a huge vaudeville tent, which later served as a dining hall, afforded shelter from the frequent showers.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., April 26. -- Members of the Conference for Education in the South poured into this city to-day in large numbers. The Robert C. Ogden party arrived early this afternoon. The hospitable people of the city took to their homes many of Mr. Ogden's guests. The others were quartered at the Hotel Hillman.

ALBANY, N.Y., April 26. -- The Court of Appeals to-day sustained District Attorney Jerome in the method used to secure evidence in the prosecution of Lawyer George E. Mills and Dr. Richard C. Flower. The court's decision denies the appeal of Mills from a judgment of conviction of grand larceny in the second degree, and of an attempt to unlawfully remove from the custody of the courts certain indictments.

When the volume of human pathos is finally published, a page will be filled by the story of the life and love of Bila Szabo, a disinherited son of Count Bila Szabo, physician to the Austrian Emperor Franz Josef, and of his wife, Rosa, for whom he threw away wealth and title, and in whose arms he died on Monday, at their home, 260 West Forty-third Street.

The small boys of the west side, in view of the growing scarcity of buffaloes, think it great sport lassoing dogs. Whenever the automobile of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals appears the official dog hunters are reinforced by an army of youthful rangers, who help to lasso the stray animals and yank them to the wagon.

The work and the vigilance of the Board of Health Department are evidence of great progress made in civil government and the results are eminently gratifying. From time to time its responsibilities are increased by the detection of things constituting a menace to the health of the public.

Some 300 depositors in the Grand Street branch of the wrecked Federal Bank held a meeting last night at Odd Fellows' Hall, in Forsyth Street, to denounce ex-Alderman Minsky, who, as a solicitor for the bank, had induced many of them to part with their money. They accomplished their purpose in the most thorough manner, and altogether the meeting was one of the stormiest the east side has seen in many a day.

After the poolroom matter had been disposed of at the City Club's annual meeting several of the Citizens' Union men in the club gave President Peckham an unpleasant ten minutes over the Remsen Gas bill, which last week was approved by Mayor McClellan and now is before Gov. Odell for action.

LOUISVILLE, April 27. -- The Smith family, not specifically but generally, will assemble in Louisville this Fall, if the plan of John Cabell Smith, a wealthy Kentuckian, is concurred in by the Smiths at large.

In future women teachers may marry without opposition from the Board of Education. Yesterday afternoon the board not only canceled its by-law prohibiting such marriages, but also reinstated Mrs. Vandewater, the only one who has been dismissed on this ground, all other offenders having resigned as soon as charges had been preferred against them.

A gang of eight desperate burglars armed with the most modern housebreaking tools was arrested yesterday afternoon at 145 and 147 Eldridge Street, and with their booty, $7,000 worth of tailor's supplies, were locked up in the Eldridge Street Station. The prisoners, say the police, broke into the store of Bauer Doctor, tailors at 247 Bowery, on the corner of Stanton Street, early yesterday morning and carried away everything valuable in the place.

Polo and saddle races under saddle were the big features that aroused the enthusiasm of the crowd last night in Madison Square Garden. It was the closing night of the horse fair, which, while a novelty in many respects, has been more successful for its initial attempt than the promoters of the enterprise had looked for.

WASHINGTON, April 27. -- Prof. Wrightson of the University of West Virginia had some friends, mostly musicians, at the new Willard on Monday night to meet Richard Strauss, the composer. The party was jolly and informal, and as the story telling moment arrived Strauss, under the influence of the cozy and comfortable atmosphere of the occasion, removed his coat and hung it on the back of his chair.

The precipitate ending of the strike of the employes of the State railroads in Hungary is instructive. It was effected by the simple and perfectly natural expedient of the Government in ordering all the employee of the roads who are members of the reserve or liable to military duty to join their respective regiments.
WASHINGTON, April 27. -- Attorney General Knox to-day transmitted to the House replies to the two resolutions of inquiry introduced by Mr. Williams (Miss.) relative to trusts.

In a decision written by Judge Henderson M. Somerville the Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday dismissed a protest by the Central Vermont Railway Company, consignees for R.F. Downing Co., against the action of the Collector at Burlington, Vt., on the ground that it had no jurisdiction.

Brokers on the floor of the Stock Exchange yesterday did not have much to occupy their attention, and to while away a dull hour an automobile was "raffled off." The machine was said to be a $5,000. sixteen-horse power machine, the property of some one in Philadelphia. The chances ran from 1 cent to $10 apiece.

In some respects the twenty-sixth has been one of the most successful of the exhibitions held by the Society of American Artists. This is the last week, the time when the doubters and waverers among buyers are apt to decide to purchase. So far the sales have passed the $5,000 mark, and by Sunday they are likely to reach $7000.

WADING RIVER, L.I., April 27. -- In the possession of Isaac Valentine, notary public, is a packet which every inhabitant with a bump of curiosity would like to see opened. The little bundle is loaded down with seals, which will not be broken except in the presence of several parties having more than a curious interest in the contents.

Placing the blame for the maintenance of poolrooms at the door of the Western Union Telegraph Company, Capt. F. Norton Goddard, as Chairman of a sub-committee of the City Club, read a report at the club meeting last evening in which he detailed arrangements made by three men working in his interests to get information as to how officials of the telegraph company work with supposed poolroom men.
NEWPORT, R.I., April 27. -- Mrs. Vanderbilt arrived here this afternoon and is the guest of Mr. and Mrs. Reginald C. Vanderbilt at Sandy Point Farm.

TORONTO, April 27. -- A dispatch to The Globe from St. Johns, N.F., says a bill has passed the Legislative Assembly of the island providing for the granting of assistance to a United States company, which proposes to go into the cold-storage business on a large scale.

PRINCETON, N.J., April 27. -- It became public to-day that the Faculty has made an important change in Princeton eligibility rules. Hereafter a student having one condition will be allowed to compete in athletics provided he has not had two chances to remove it, otherwise he will be debarred.

CHICAGO, April 27. -- William Preston Harrison wants $750,000 from William Randolph Hearst, his employes, and his newspapers. He filed five suits to-day, in which the damages are placed at $150,000 each. The cause of action is libel, based on recent publications in the Hearst newspapers.

Horace S. Ely, President of the corporation of Horace S. Ely Co., and one of the best-known real estate men in the city, died yesterday morning at his residence, 19 East Fifty-fifth Street. Mr. Ely's death, resulting from heart disease, was very sudden. He had been at his office as recently as last Saturday, and his indisposition during the last two or three days had been looked upon as only temporary.

ATLANTIC CITY, N.J., April 27. -- The British steamship Craigneuk, sugar laden, from Matanzas for Sandy Hook, thence to Philadelphia, is ashore three miles below the South Brigantine Life Saving Station. Capt. Calvin of the stranded steamship says that his vessel went ashore early to-day during the severe northeast storm.

Additional gold to the amount of $2,000,000 was engaged for export yesterday, making the total to go by to-day's steamer $2,500,000, and the total for the week thus far $9,100,000. Besides the $500,000 being shipped by Ladenburg, Thalmann Co., Lazard Freres are shipping $1,500,000, and Heidelbach, Ickelheimer Co. $500,000.

CHICAGO, April 27. -- The tenth annual meeting of the National Municipal League began in this city to-day, with delegates present from every large city in the United States. President Charles J. Bonaparte of Baltimore called the assemblage to order. Clinton Rogers Woodruff of Philadelphia spoke on "A Year's Disclosure and Development."

ALBANY, April 27. -- Gov. Odell to-day signed nearly 100 bills. One of them is the New York Home Rule bill, which confers upon the Board of Aldermen and the Board of Estimate and Apportionment the power to provide for a municipal ferry service, to establish a telegraph service in connection with the Police and Fire Departments, and provide for the extension of any public building.

NEW ORLEANS, April 27. -- Wildly cheering every reference to the recent overwhelming defeat of the Lily White ticket in the State election, the regular Republicans met here to-day, strongly indorsing President Roosevelt and his Administration, and sent a mixed delegation -- two negroes and two whites -- to the National Convention.

Summer had been far too long in coming to suit twelve-year-old Carl Christoffer and his sister Lena, two years younger, who live in the tenement 309 East Ninety-seventh Street. So they decided to go and look for it at Katonah, N.Y.

BERLIN, April 27. -- Capt. Dannhauer, the Lokal Anzieger's correspondent with Major von Glasenapp's column in Southwest Africa, has sent a dispatch by heliograph via Windhoek, announcing that the losses of the column through deaths, wounds, and sickness since March 13 have been, officers 63 per cent., and privates, 35 per cent Forty-four men are now sick with typhus, besides those sent to Windhoek.

Dullness and strength characterized yesterday's market, and of the two characteristics the dullness was the more significant. A market which loses activity when prices are bid up does not encourage further operations of the same sort. It looks too much as though buyers were "landed" with the stock which they would be unable to pass along to other buyers.

John E. McDonald of 216 West Seventy-seventh Street has brought suit in the Supreme Court, through Bowers Sands, against Charles W. Morse, ex-President of the American Ice Company, to recover $2000,000, out of which he says Mr. Morse defrauded him in 1900 on a deal in the stock of the company.

James H. Ottley has bought from the various owners 232, 236, 238, 240, 242, and 246 West Thirty-seventh Street and 241 and 243 West Thirty-sixth Street. Mr. Ottley is President of the McCall Company, publishers of McCall's Magazine and Patterns, and will begin at once the erection of an eight-story building on this plot, which he will lease to the McCall Company for a term of years.

Collector Jessup, winner of the Columbus Stakes Selling, at the Jamaica track yesterday, was bid up after the race by J.L. Maginnis, owner of Monet, the second horse, who bought him for $3,200. As Collector Jessup was entered to sell for $1,600, Maginnis, who was entitled to half of the surplus over the entered price, secured the horse for an actual cost of $2,400.

Through the "Returns of Trade for 1903," published by the Maritime Customs Department of China, and just received in this country, it is possible to trace distinctly the relative shares of the foreign trade of China belonging to Russia and Japan, now engaged in war on Chinese territory, and to Great Britain and the United States, the two nations most directly and largely interested.

ST. LOUIS, April 27. -- Cass Gilbert of New York, one of the architects of the World's Fair buildings, has resigned his position and brought suit in the United States Circuit Court against the Exposition Company for $47,113.96 salary alleged to be due him.

President ROOSEVELT is a very determined man. Opposition seems only to increase the tenacity with which he sticks to his purposes. More than a year ago he sent to the Senate the name of WILLIAM D. CRUM, a negro, to be Collector of Customs at Charleston, S.C. The Senate had not confirmed the nomination when the day of adjournment was reached.

ALBANY, April 27. -- In arguing before Gov. Odell to-day for the veto of the J.T. Smith Dutchess County Water bill, representatives of the McClellan administration and of the Merchants' Association informed the Governor that in affixing his signature to the bill he would leave the City of New York no alternative but to go to the Ramapo Water Company for its needed supply or face a water famine.
In order to show the plan drawings for its new clubhouse, the Woman's Club of New York, gave a reception at its present home, 9 East Forty-sixth Street, yesterday, from 4 to 10 o'clock.

"It is a case of persecution, pure and simple," said Frederick A. Southworth yesterday, referring to the arrest of his brother, Ellis B. Southworth, a lawyer of this city, on the charge of arson in connection with the burning of the Van Alen homestead at New Hamburg in February, 1903. Both the Southworths have their law office at 68 William Street. Ellis B. was arrested in Poughkeepsie on Tuesday.

WASHINGTON, April 27. -- The conferrees on the Panama Canal bill to-night averted the prolongation of the session, which seemed likely, by reaching an agreement on the government of the Panama Canal zone. The first section of the Senate bill providing for the payment of $10,000,000 to Panama, and the House provision placing the canal zone under the control of the President, are accepted.
ST. PETERSBURG, April 28. -- Disappointment prevails in St. Petersburg that no official dispatches giving details of the operations on the Yalu River have yet been made public.

Heinrich Conried, impresario, sat at his desk shortly after the noon hour yesterday ruminating upon the successes and the failures of his grand opera season. He was feeling drowsy, as people do after luncheon, and happy -- for was not the last of the operas sung last Monday?

PARIS, April 27. -- The wedding of Capt. Algernon Sartoris, grandson of the late Gen. Grant, and Mlle. Germaine Cecile Noufflard, a niece of Charles E. Halle, Director of the New Gallery, London, occurred this afternoon at the Church of St. Honore d'Eylau.

-- Practically everything that can be said in defense of menageries, public or private, was presented, and well presented, in the letter from "H.A.C." printed on this page yesterday. We have considered our correspondent's arguments carefully, and recognize the weight of some of them, but they leave us unconvinced that menageries are useful enough to justify the amount of suffering and cruelty their maintenance involves.

PATERSON, N.J., April 27. -- A fast train on the New York, Susquehanna and Westtern at 8:30 o'clock to-night struck a trolley car at the Vreeland Avenue crossing. The trolley car was lifted from the rails and hurled into the ditch, beside the tracks of the railroad. The collision threw the pony trucks of the locomotive from the rails.

Eleven members of the Panama Canal Commission arrived here yesterday on the steamship Yucatan. They were preceded by Commission William Barclay Parsons, who came here a week ago. Rear Admiral Walker, the President, had prepared a written statement about the work done on the week's tours along the canal, but after landing he suddenly remembered that he had locked it in his trunk, which already had started on its way to Washington.

LIAO-YANG, April 27. -- The Japanese troops which crossed the Yalu north of Euit-ju (Cheng-ju) charged, during the night of April 26-27, the Russian position near Lizavena, a village on the Manchurian bank of the Yalu.
WASHINGTON, April 27. -- The beginning of the end of the House session, a day which began two hours before the usual hour for opening and continued until late at night, was a stirring one.

From the fact that during the noon hour of yesterday's session of the stock market the trading amounted to only 10,000 shares can be judged the size of the day's market. The conditions which prevailed are perhaps still more clearly shown by the amusing diversions to which the brokers on the floor gave a considerable part of the day.

Robert Grau, who brought Mme. Patti to this country for her late disastrous tour, was up in supplementary proceedings in the City Court yesterday in connection with the judgment for $95.72, secured against him some weeks ago. The cause was a printing bill contracted while he was managing one of Loie Fuller's American tours.
PHILADELPHIA, April 27. -- Owen Wister, the novelist, is in the Pennsylvania Hospital here in a serious condition, after an operation for appendicitis.
WASHINGTON, April 27. -- Representative Morgan C. Fitzpatrick of Tennessee was taken ill to-night in the House.

NEWARK, N.J., April 27. -- Vice Chancellor Stevens to-day granted an injunction restraining David Greenhill Bruce Gardyne of London, England, and Lafayette Hoyt De Friese and Benoni Lockwood, Jr., of New York, as trustees, from declaring dividends upon or from voting or disposing of in any way 6,640 shares of stock of the Guayaquil and Quito Railway Company, pending final hearing in the case.

Col. MARCHAND of Fashoda fame -- or obloquy -- has resigned his commission in the French Army. His resignation has been "reluctantly" accepted. He retires, he says, for "motives of a diplomatic and military order." He does not specify. Neither does Gen. ANDRE. The word "reluctantly" may stand for an eloquent, anguishing sense of loss or it may not. No one knows.

At a meeting of the Directors of the Metropolitan Opera Company yesterday Heinrich Conried reported that the total receipts for the entire grand opera season, including the tour, amounted to $1,500,000. In addition to the regular dividend of 6 per cent. an extra dividend was declared on the capital stock of the corporation.
PARIS, April 28. -- A dispatch published in Paris to-day says Viceroy Alexieff's report to the Czar on the affair at Gen-san contained details which were not made public.

NEWARK, N.J., April 28. -- The Public Service Corporation of New Jersey proposes within the next four weeks to sell tickets from Jersey City to Philadelphia. The route will be from Jersey City to Newark, thence to Elizabeth, Cranford, Westfield, Plainfield, Dunellen, Bound Brook, New Brunswick, and Trenton.

ALPENA, Mich., April 28. -- H. Irving Andrews, alias E.H. Witherout, was arrested this afternoon on an indictment found against him by a Grand Jury in Brooklyn. N.Y., for grand larceny in the first degree, the specific charge being raising drafts and thereby fraudulently recovering nearly $19, 000 on Dec. 31.

Quotations from "Mary's Little Lamb," other statements equally non-committal in their tendency, and complete silence were forthcoming yesterday from officials and Directors of the Western Union Telegraph Company when they were asked about the charges made by Capt. F. Norton Goddard to the City Club on Wednesday night. The Captain accused the company of deliberately aiding and abetting poolrooms of this city in violating the criminal laws of the State.

Louis Minsky, ex-Alderman and President of the Minsky Realty Company, Bowery and Grand Street, was arrested yesterday afternoon on a charge of grand larceny in connection with the Federal Bank case. The arrest was made by Detective Sergeant Clark at Minsky's real estate offices. He will be arraigned to-day before Justice Wyatt in Special Sessions.
The racing stable of John E. Madden and the horses trained by W.P. Burch arrived from Washington yesterday and went into quarters at the Morris Park course.

Until Sunday inclusive a very fetching little exhibition of paintings by two Japanese artists will be visible in the gallery of the Century Club, West Forty-third Street. The artists are Messrs. Taikan Yokoyama and Shiunzo Hishida, members of an art movement in Japan led by Mr. Kakuzo Okakura, who belong to an art league called the Bijitsuin, or Hall of Fine Arts.

The case is of considerable interest, inasmuch as Mlle. Sylviac is the champion of the long-suffering public, and although it is improbable that she will win her case, her Joan of Arc attitude excites general sympathy and admiration.

The Justice had been called to act as a juror in an inquest. He went to the Coroners' office and modestly told the clerk in charge that he thought he should be excused from jury duty.

They adopted a non-committal attitude on the subject in Congress.

Two boys, thirteen and fourteen years old, who had tried to get a free ride on a New York Central train coming into this city late Saturday night, were found on top of a tall refrigerator car early yesterday morning, both seriously hurt and one dying. They had struck a low bridge while seated on top of the car.
GALVESTON, Texas, May 15. -- Paul Clarkson, who poses as a prize fighter, was operated on in the jail this morning, and a diamond, valued at $250, was taken from his stomach.

Business in fine cloaks and suits, which has been very poor throughout the Spring, has shown a decided improvement during the last week, and the retailers have begun to place substantial orders for lightweight garments for Summer wear.

BOSTON, May 15. -- Lilian Whiting, who wrote "World Beautiful," "The Spiritual Significance," "The Life Radiant," and other well-known works, has been charged in an affidavit filed in Greeley Colo., with conspiring with Ralph C. Meeker, a New York newspaper man, to defraud his sister, Rose E. Meeker.

On account of the rain and fog of the early morning, which made it difficult and dangerous for the crews from the Hudson River and Long Island rowing clubs to get around to the Harlem, the oarsmen's opening day parade, whch was to take place on the Harlem River yesterday afternoon, was postponed until next Sunday afternoon, when it will be held if the weather is favorable.

NEWARK, N.J., May 15. -- It is not often that Frank Kramer, the National champion cycle racer, is caught in a spill on the track, but the unexpected happened to-day at the weekly cycling meet at the Vailsburg track, and both Kramerer and his team mate, Fenn, were put out of the five-mile professional handicap in consequence of the mishap.
JACKSON, Ky., May 15. -- News reached here to-night of the assassination of Riley Coldiron, in Perry County.

It is to be regretted that the encouraging predictions of an abatement in the typhoid death rate of Philadelphia have not been vindicated by official statistics. During last week 297 new cases were reported and 38 deaths. Until quite recently the occurrence of the disease was largely confined to West Philadelphia.

ANNAPOLIS, Md., May 15. -- As the result of rash daring, Midshipman Philip Brittingham, the nineteen-year-old son of the Rev. Joseph Brittingham of Wheeling, W.Va., was drowned two miles off the Naval Academy this afternoon. Brittingham sank only after several heroic attempts to rescue him had been made by his classmates.

Anatole Leroy Beaulieu, author of "Israel Among the Nations," who has recently completed a course of lectures at Harvard University, was entertained at a reception given in his honor by the Judeans last night at the Tuxedo, Madison Avenue and Fifty-ninth Street. The gathering comprised the leaders of numerous Jewish organizations in this city, as well as a large number of New Yorkers interested in educational work.

Ten weeks ago Judge Fitzsimons of the City Court died, and up to the present time no appointment to fill the vacancy has been made. Why Gov. Odell (the Governor-Chairman) has not made the appointment no one knows.
AN-TUNG, May 5. -- Operations which resulted in the crossing of the Yalu by the Japanese culminated on May 1 in the occupation of Kiu-lien-Cheng, on the north bank of the river, opposite Wi-Ju.

In the poolroom controversy both sides are "sparring for points." No poolrooms will be closed until the Western Union Telegraph Company exhibits a higher degree of morality or the District Attorney and the Commissioner of Police more sense and judgment.

How Sir Thomas Lipton's attempts to obtain from the New York Yacht Club a statement as to whether that organization would consider a challenge for the America's Cup under its new measurement rules, were baffled by the refusal of the New York Yacht Club to commit itself in the matter, was told for the first time by the publication yesterday of the correspondence between the Irish yachtsman and the local club on the subject.

A petition in bankruptcy has been filed against T. Hill Leary and James A. May, who compose the firm of T.H. Leary Co., stock brokers, at 41 and 43 Wall Street, with branches at Kingston, Rondout, and Poughkeepsie. They were expelled from the Consolidated Stock and Petroleum Exchange on May 5.

LONDON, May 17. -- "Cynthia," in which Ethel Barrymore appeared at Wyndham's Theatre last night, is regarded by the critics as inferior to the previous efforts of Henry Hubert Davies, and as hardly giving Miss Barrymore a good chance.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 16. -- Sir Charles Hardinge, the new British Ambassador to Russia, arrived in St. Petersburg this afternoon. As soon as the Emperor returns to St. Petersburg Sir Charles will present his credentials, and at the same time deliver a speech which it is expected will reveal, guardedly of course, the object of his mission, which is generally known to be the establishment of better relations between Russia and Great Britain.

Eighty families in the line of five-story brick tenements at 203, 205, 207, and 209 East One Hundredth Street are on strike against what they declare to be an unjustifiable and unreasonable advance in their rents. The women by day and the men by night are picketing the houses and, mounting guard on the stoops, are warning away possible renters.

Ex-Senator David B. Hill came to Manhattan from Albany yesterday afternoon. His presence was explained by some of his friends thus: "Law business." Nevertheless, Senator McCarren, Controller Grout, and exLieut. Gov. Sheehan conferred with him about dinner time, and as a result there was a general understanding last night that Mr. Hill stood committed to the candidacy of Edward M. Grout of Kings for the Democratic nomination for Governor this year.

Signalizing her last appearance as an independent star, before her happy conjunction next season with E.H. Sothern in a Shakespearean repertory, Miss Julia Marlowe appeared last night at the Empire in Frederick Halm's impossibly romantic, deliciously sentimental piece of old- fashioned theatrics, "Ingomar," the play in which she made her first prominent appeal to recognition some years ago.

M. Anatole Leroy-Beaulied was the guest of honor at a dinner held last night at Delmonico's, where a silver loving cup was presented to him on behalf of his friends in New York. Oscar S. Straus, as Chairman of the Dinner Committee, delivered the address of welcome and Nathan Bijur the remarks incident to the presentation of the cup.

MUKDEN, May 15. -- (Delayed.) -Lieut. Col. Schuyler, United States Army, military observer with the Russian Army, arrived here to-day, and after an interview with Viceroy Alexieff left for Liao-Yang in the afternoon.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 16. -- The Chinese Minister here has given Foreign Minister Lamsdorff fresh assurances of the purpose of his Government not to violate its neutrality and to preserve tranquillity throughout the empire.

Within a short period the public have been shocked by the death of a little girl while at play on the roof of her house. The slaughter of a boy by an automobile while engaged in a game of ball on the streets was chronicled by the press only a few weeks earlier. It is full time that such tragedies should receive the attention of other officials of the city than the Coroners.

Jesse Lewisohn, reputed possessor of certain secrets about Canfield's gambling house, which the District Attorney seeks to hear, twice refused yesterday to answer questions propounded him by Mr. Jerome, and was saved from prison only by a stay of proceedings granted on application of his lawyer, Alfred Lauterbach, by Justice Dugro of the Supreme Court.

CHAMBERLAIN, S.D., May 16. -- The notorious desperado Jack Sully, who for many years has been the terror of the Rosebud country, was killed in a running fight with officers on the Rosebud Reservation this morning.

Shortly after 1 o'clock yesterday afternoon a diminutive messenger boy, carrying big suit case, discovered that the cover of the fire hydrant at the southeast corner of Fifth Avenue and Fourteenth Street was open. The wrench with which to turn the faucet inside was lying on the sidewalk, where a street clearer had left it.
New styles in carpets were shown and new prices announced for the Fall season yesterday. The carpet opening occurs every six months, and is an event in the trade.

It is more agreeable to dwell upon yesterday's later prices than those made earlier and reflecting appreciation of the bank statement and gold engagements, reinforced by failures in the South and worse crop reports. Probably neither of the two latter factors should count for very much.

TOKIO, May 16. -- The Japanese dispatch boat Miyako has been destroyed by striking a submerged mine while assisting in the operations of clearing the Russian mines from Kerr Bay, northeast of Talienwan Bay, on which Port Dalny is situated. There were twenty-four casualties.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 16. -- The Japanese evidently are determined that there shall not be any further rail communication between Gen. Kuropatkin and Port Arthur. Official advices received to-day by the General Staff say the Japanese have destroyed fifty miles of the railroad north of KinChow.
ON THE YALU, May 8. -- To-day I examined the trophies captured from the Russians. The field guns number 21. All are of the latest patterns, dated 1901 and 1902.

PITTSBURG, Penn., May 16. -- Through a balk called on Mathewson in the fifth inning to-day when two men were out and New York five runs ahead, Pittsburg was enabled to get a foothold in the first game of the series here. In the next inning Mathewson was batted almost off the rubber by the Pittsburgs, who managed to get six runs all told.

There is reason to believe that Edward K. Sills, fifty-six years old, of 146 West Eighty-seventh Street, a retired member of the wholesale grocery firm of Sills Co., at 750 Eighth Avenue, was the man who leaped into Lake Erie from the steamboat City of Erie last Thursday night, when the vessel was about three hours out from Cleveland.

PITTSBURG, May 16. -- The Bostonians produced "The Queen of Laughter" at the Nixon Theatre tonight. Henry Clay Barnabee is not in the piece, and W.H. McDonald is the star with Gertrude Zimmer. The latter received eight curtain calls in the first act.

WASHINGTON, May 16. -- The range of gossip about the prospective Chairman of the Republican National Committee has reached Secretary Cortelyou and he has been slated in current conjecture for the place.

SANTA CRUZ, Cal., May 16. -- At the opening to-day of the California Democratic Convention to choose delegates to the National Convention, William R. Hearst failed to gain control of the assemblage, by a vote of 367 to 345.

The English yachting season has just opened and news is awaited on this side with considerable interest of the schooner Ingomar's first showing in those waters. The Ingomar arrived abroad about a week ago and went at once into dock to be overhauled and fitted with her racing spars, so she ought to be, if she is not already, in commission during the current week.
SAYVILLE, L.I., May 16. -- Robert B. Roosevelt, the venerable, but still youthful, uncle of the President, has arrived at his country home, Lotos Lake, for the Summer season.

WASHINGTON, May 16. -- In an opinion written by Chief Justice Fuller, the United States Supreme Court to-day sustained the action of the immigration authorities at the Port of New York in ordering the deportation of the Englishman Turner, alleged to be an Anarchist.

ST. JOHN'S, N.F. May 16. -- The sealing steamer Aurora, which has been landing machinery for the whale factory at Cape Charles, Labrador, returned to Wesleyville, 100 miles north of here, this morning, bringing the body of Leonidas Hubbard, Jr., assistant editor of Outing, who perished in the interior of Labrador last October while on an exploring expedition.

Much remains to be explained concerning the manner in which Letitia O'Neil, the sixteen-year-old nurse girl employed by William Smylie, the wealthy licorice manufacturer of Brooklyn, received the bullet wound from which she died on Saturday night. Her mother, Mrs. O'Neil Kerrigan, of 349 Herkimer street, is firm in her belief that her daughter was murdered.

WASHINGTON, May 16. -- The Supreme Court of the United States to-day dismissed for want of jurisdiction the case of Ferdinand Holzendorf, an action to compel Secretary Hay to "prosecute with great vigor" a claim for $500,000 against the Emperor of Germany.

After four straight defeats at Boston the Dtroit team came to town yesterday to play four games with the Greater New York. With the prestige of thre victories over the powerful batting aggregation from Cleveland, went into the contest decided favorites, but after the fourth inning the visitors had everything their own way, and won by a score of 11 to 6.

CHICAGO, May 16. -- When Pitcher Weimet was not giving the Brooklyn players bases on balls to-day he was either striking them out or preventing them from hitting safely. The Chicagos scored ten singles to Brooklyn's five, but this advantage would not have operated against the visitors but for their poor fielding. At that the finish was close, the Brooklyns coming within a run of tying the game in the ninth inning.

Where novelty was lacking at Morris Park yesterday the returns from strict adherence to public form made ample recompense to the betting crowd, and when Oarsman, with one pound off, beat Major Daingerfield, with three pounds on, as against the last meeting of the two, when positions were reversed, the "regulars," who made up the greater part of the attendance became as warmly enthusiastic as their kind can become.

Clarence Whitman, the President of the Merchants' Association, wrote to Mayor McClellan yesterday making further charges against the Aqueduct Commission, and informing the Mayor that the association had laid the matter before the District Attorney.

Bernard Smyth Sons have sold for the New York County Realty Company to Lowenfeld Prager 738 and 740 Ninth Avenue, southeast corner of Fiftieth Street, a plot 44 by 80, now covered by a frame building with stores.

The exercises in connection with the annual commencement of the General Theological Seminary were begun with the delivery of the baccalaureate sermon by Bishop Doane of Albany yesterday afternoon in the Chapel of the Good Shepherd, in Chelsea Square. Not all of the class of 1904 will receive degrees, but those to whom will be granted degrees or diplomas, including some not able to be present, will number between thirty and forty.

MEMPHIS, Tenn., May 16. -- Hair was pulled and more serious trouble was narrowly averted between prominent State politicians this morning in the lobby of the Tulane Hotel. Ex-Gov. McMillin and W.R. Romaine, the latter editor of The Pulaski Citizen, met for the first time since editorial comments on Gov. McMillin's position on the whisky interests of Tennessee appeared in The Citizen.

WASHINGTON, May 10. -- The Moros who attacked the American troops on May 8 and killed two officers and a number of men may be severely punished, by Major Gen. Leonard Wood, who is marching on the band with a force of 450 officers and men. Major Gen. Ainsworth, military secretary, to-day received a cablegram from Gen. Wade in reply to a message asking particulars concerning the movement against the Moros in Mindanao.

ATHENS, May 16. -- In view of the manifestations of Greek sympathy for Russia, the Russian Legation here, by the express desire of the Czar, issues daily reports of the progress of the war in the Far East.
Controller Grout and Alderman McCall, Chairman of the Finance Committee in the board, had another clash in the meeting of the Sinking Fund Commissioners yesterday over the Staten Island Ferry matter.

Serious embarrassment to the City Government has been caused through the action of Gov. Odell in vetoing the bill increasing from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 the limit to which the city may go in authorizing issues of special revenue bonds. Owing to this veto, Mayor McClellan was compelled yesterday to call a special meeting of the Board of Estimate for to-morrow at 10:30 o'clock.

As the steamship Minneapolis, from London, steamed up the bay yesterday morning, six lean, sad-looking men were seen huddled together alongside the rail well forward, looking with longing eyes toward the city before them. All of them were good types of the coster boy of the London music hall. One very short fellow, whose face was almost as red as a grenadier's coat, turned to his companions and said in a weepy voice:
Will you please tell me where to make a complaint for carelessness in the inspection or repairs of elevators?

In a notice addressed to owners and trainers of horses at Morris Park, the Stewards of the Westchester Racing Association made announcement of action that is a trifle unusual, in an order that withdraws from the programme three overnight races for the latter part of the week, for which other races will be substituted later.

The Inter-State Commerce Commission will begin a hearing on the question of the differentials in freight rates between New York and Atlantic Coast seaports and interior points on Wednesday at the United States Court Room in the Post Office Building. A large number of the commercial organizations of the city will be represented at the hearing, of which the Produce Exchange and the Merchants' Association have taken the most active part in the present movement.

The extremely interesting war news which we printed yesterday makes it fairly clear that the immediate objective of the Japanese is the capture of Port Arthur. But we say "immediate" advisedly. The capture of the place would be a great moral victory for the Japanese and a great moral defeat for the Russians.

PARIS, May 17. -- The Matin is publishing the history of an alleged treasonable incident of a seasational nature. It declares its London correspondent obtained from one "Fragola Pietro," a London hotel employe, nearly 100 plans of the French naval defenses.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., May 16. -Attempts to use Federal influence to break the dead-lock in the Illinois Republican State Convention gave a new turn to the bitter political fight today. After the twenty-ninth ballot the convention took a recess until tomorrow, and to-night conferences are being held to prevent the operation of such an interference.

LONDON, May 16. -- Notwithstanding the highly flattering reception of "The Prince of Pilsen" Saturday by the firstnight audience, the London papers, from The Times downward, are practically unanimous in condemnation of the production.

BALTIMORE, Md., May 16. -- An insurance policy, on which the premiums amount to $75,000, for the protection of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition from claims on account of accidents on the Fair Grounds at St. Louis resulting from its own acts or those of employes has been issued by the Maryland Casualty Company.

For one week only Mr. Charles Hawtrey is in vaudeville at Proctor's. His vehicle is "Time is Money," a "comedietta" by Mrs. Hugh Bell and Mr. Arthur Cecil, in which, as the programme avers, Mr. Hawtrey has appeared in London "with marked success."

NEW ORLEANS, May 16. -- J.H. Maury, a noted cotton bull leader and member of the New Orleans Cotton Exchange, and George Courtenay, a liveryman of Pass Christian, Miss., had a shotgun duel yesterday over a horse deal.

MUKDEN, May 17. -- It was announced here to-day that the main body of the Japanese forces is advancing on HaiCheng (about ten miles southeast of Niu-Chwang) and Kai-Ping, (about thirty-five miles south of Niu-Chwang.) and that a smaller force is marching in the direction of Liao-Yang.

Messrs. Hornblower, Nicoll, and Joline, the committee of three appointed by Chairman Cord Meyer of the Democratic State Committee to investigate the eligibility of James T. Woodward, Harry Payne Whitney, and Isidor Straus, National Bank Directors, as candidates for Electors on the Democratic National ticket, have finished their report.

After a long and tedious row in the Board of Aldermen over the Port Chester Railroad franchise again yesterday, and after the majority of the board repeatedly had voted adversely on all attempts to compel action on the railroad application, Chairman Haggerty of the Railroad Committee announced that a public hearing would be held on the entire Port Chester matter on Monday afternoon next at 3 o'clock.
