The letter of President VREELAND of the Metropolitan system to the President of the Board of Rapid Transit Commissioners, suggesting certain changes in the plans for subway extension, is in the main wise and well-considered. The most important of these is that a cross-town loop under Chambers Street be provided, to furnish a connection between the east and west side lines.

WASHINGTON, May 17. -- The full story of the killing of the American missionary, Dr. Labaree, near Mount Ararat, as a re-result of a bitter religious hatred, is told in a report just received at the State Department from Richmond Pearson, United States Minister to Persia, under date of Teheran, April 18, 1904.

Gen. Samuel Pearson of Scranton. Penn., who served in the Boer war, and Cornelius W. Van Der Hoogt, a foreign correspondent, of Baltimore and Washington, who are stopping at the Everett House, were arrested yesterday on the complaint of ex-Assistant Secretary of the Interior Webster Davis, who served under the McKinley Administration.

WASHINGTON, May 17. -- Ex-Postmaster General Charles Emory Smith testified to-day, in the Tyner-Barrett postal conspiracy case, as to the custom in the department in relation to the issuance of fraud orders.

It's a fight to the finish between the union musicians of New York and the theatrical managers, and each side is prepared to stick to its demands to the last ditch. Heinrich Conried, who left for Europe yesterday, has been most active in urging drastic action against the Musical Mutual Protective Union, but he has behind him all the members of the Association of Theatrical Managers.

QUINCY, Mass., May 17.--The battleship Rhode Island was launched to-day after a delay of more than two weeks caused by a strike of the mechanics at the works because of trouble over the hours of labor. No announcement was made in advance of the day on which the launching was to take place.

CHICAGO, May 17. -- Although the Brooklyns outplayed the local National League team to-day both in batting and fielding. Selee's men were enabled to win by a lucky streak of batting in the first and sixth innings. In the first inning Wicker's base on balls and Kling's hit to the clubhouse, which resulted in the first home run of the season on the home grounds, netted two runs.

TRENTON, N.J., May 17. -- Argument was begun to-day before Vice Chancellor Stevenson in the suit brought by Alfred F. Stevens to compel the United States Steel Corporation to pay dividends on its common stock. The case was before the court on a demurrer filed by the corporation.

It is extremely unfortunate that the Governor has vetoed the bill authorizing the city to issue $2,000,000 of revenue bonds in each year in place of $1,000,000 as allowed by the law at present. The special purposes for which the bonds were needed were the maintenance of the night schools, the Summer schools, the recreation grounds of the Board of Education, and the removal of ashes from the big buildings by the Street Cleaning Department.

William Nelson Cromwell, counsel for the Panama Canal Company, with Charles W. Russell and William A. Day, who represented the United States Government at the transfer of the property and papers of the company in Paris, returned to this country yesterday on the steamship Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse.
DENVER, Col., May 17. -- At 9:30 P.M. Chairman Hodges of the Republican City Committee claims the election of Springer, Republican, for Mayor by 7,500 to 10,000 plurality over Speer, (Dem.)

While crossing Broadway at Sixty-second Street shortly after 6 o'clock last night the four-horse coach "Good Times," which had taken a party from the Morris Park races to the Waldorf-Astoria, collided with a south-bound Broadway car, which was crowded with passengers. There were no passengers in the coach, which was on its way to the Mineola stables with the driver and grooms.

I notice that Mother Eddy, in her order forbidding Christian Scientists to join single sex societies, makes an exception of the Masons. It was not necessary to make this exception. For the Eddyites cannot join the Masons, nor remain members of the Knights Templars in good standing. Freemasonry is founded upon the Scriptural truth of a living, personal God, and the Knights Templars base their existence and work upon the Apostles' and Nicene creeds.

CONCORD, N.H., May 17. -- Without friction or delay in the Republican State Convention, which met here to-day, delegates at large and alternates at large to the Chicago National Convention were elected.

A statement so delightful simply must be accepted as true, and we would not for the world suggest that perhaps the professors are with the army not as professors, but as patriotic Japanese, like the rest of the staff.

The dispute over the estate of Arthur Beckwith, the artist, who was not heard of after his escape from a Flushing insane asylum, was settled yesterday by Surrogate Thomas's acceptance of Referee James Yerrance's report that Beckwith died on April 24, 1901. The creditors of the artist's brother, Leonard, will be prevented from claiming any portion of the estate, but Leonard's children will get about $250,000.

Your editorial about the officer and soldier in Germany in THE NEW YORK TIMES of May 12 has not surprised me. It only shows again your well-known and often-before manifested animosity toward everything German, and especially toward the German army officer.

According to a too familiar formula the market has recently shown activity only at the expense of values. Yesterday's market reversed this experience, prices improving at the expense of activity. In other words, the market was firmer but duller. This is not mere phrasemaking; it corresponds to significance in the observed phenomena.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., May 17. -- With the dead-lock still unbroken, although nine more ballots were taken to-day, the Republican State Convention took a recess to-night until to-morrow morning.

In the midst of the excitement caused by yesterday's announcement that the President of the Western Union Telegraph Company had cut off all racing information from the poolrooms, Police Commissioner McAdoo sent Inspector McLaughlin and twenty detectives to raid what they called a "poolroom exchange" in East Forty-second Street, between Third and Lexington Avenues.

SYRACUSE, N.Y., May 17. -- In one of the most exciting ball games played in Syracuse this Spring Manhattan defeated Syracuse University by a score of 8 to 4. After the visitors had been held down for six innings to one hit, the bombardment began in the seventh, when Capt. Duffy sent out a three-bagger and tied the score.

In a decision written by General Appraiser Howell, the Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday sustained protests against the assessments of $3 a pound on certain fabrics imported by the American Whalebone Company. They are described as "woven fabrics in the piece, of silk and cotton, weighing between 1 1-3 and S ounces a square yard, yarn dyed, colors, silk under 30 per-cent."

WASHINGTON, May 17. -- There is as little known to-night as there was twenty-four hours ago in regard to the accession of Secretary Cortelyou to the National Chairmanship of the Republican Campaign Committee. The general view of the matter is that the suggestion has been made in a tentative way to see how it would strike the party and the country.

The National commission charged with the duty of erecting a monument to the memory of WILLIAM McKINLEY held a meeting in this city last week. It is announced that there will be a second competition for designs. The monument will be erected at Canton, Ohio, at a cost of $400,000.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., May 17, (World's Fair Grounds.) -- When the second day's session of the National Editorial Association was called to order Col. John Lyman of Louisiana read a paper by Joseph Pulitzer of New York entitled "Institute of Journalists." This was followed by a brief address from Sir Hugh Gilzean-Reid of London, President of the World's Press Parliament, chief founder and ex-President of the British Institute of Journalists.

PARIS, May 17. -- A dispatch to the Temps from Vienna says information received there shows that the conflict between Viceroy Alexieff and Gen. Kuropatkin is acute. The latter attributes the Russian defeat on the Yalu River to Viceroy Alexieff's orders countermanding his previously given instructions.

The discontinuance of horse-race reports to "subscribers" is not the same thing as depriving the poolrooms of the news they need. We presume President CLOWRY of the Western Union is well aware of that fact. The public, which upon the first reading of President CLOWRY'S order, jumped to the conclusion that the Western Union Company had cut off the poolroom service became aware of it a little later.

Ex-Senator David B. Hill spent the greater part of yesterday down town. Several of his friends met him in the financial district, but to all of them he would give no inkling as to his status in the McCarren-Murphy fight.

CAMBRIDGE SPRINGS, Penn., May 17. -- This morning Janowski and Marshall continued play in their adjourned game from the eleventh round of the international chessmasters' tournament. Twelve moves were made, bringing the total number to 76, when Janowski resigned. Marshall now leads the Parisian with 1 1/2 points and Lasker with 2 1/2 points.

The examination of Daniel J. Sully in the proceedings in bankruptcy against Daniel J. Sully Co. was continued yesterday before Macgrane Coxe, the referee in bankruptcy. Mr. Sully was questioned about the account of Frederick Zerega Co. of Liverpool, which appears in the Sully Co. books.

Arrangements for the annual Irvington-Millburn bicycle road race on Memorial Day are being completed by the Bay View Wheelmen of Newark, and at a recent meeting of the committees in charge of the historic event it was stated that there will probably be over fifty place prizes in addition to the team and time prizes.
The United States Steel Corporation has made application to the Stock Exchange to list $17,098,000 of its 5 per cent. bonds, the remainder of the $170,000,000 outstanding.

The result is that poolrooms are run in San Salito, just across the Bay. The Western Union is serving these poolrooms with Morris Park results as usual to-day, having received no orders to cut them off.

The old adage that all whisky is good, but some is better, was attacked yesterday before the Food Standards Committee at the Hotel Wolcott by Col. W.M. Thomas of Kentucky, who declared that much of the whisky sold in the United States was unfit for human consumption.

We should like to know how Mayor McCLELLAN and Controller GROUT reconcile with a decent standard of public service the methods employed in the fight between Mr. MURPHY on the one hand and Mr. McCARREN on the other.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, May 17. -- New York was well represented at the Fasig-Tipton blue ribbon sale in Glenville to-day. Prices were very low, only three horses bringing over $1,000. The highest price paid was $2,000, which C.K.G. Billings gave for the pacer Prince Direct, 2:07. Baron De Shay, 2:08 1/2, consigned by M.E. Sturgis of New York, was purchased for $1,300 by Joseph Hubinger of Hartford, Conn.

NIU-CHWANG, May 16, (delayed.) -- The Russian evacuation of this city has been completed. Nothing remains but the destruction of the gunboat Sivouch, which it is expected will take place early in the morning.

" Regulars" had a day of their own at the Morris Park race course yesterday, and for practically the first time this season went about racing as a business undisturbed by the jostling of a large crowd, though quite a number was on hand for all that.

Apparently, for no better reason than that prices had been going down for a number of days, the stock market yesterday showed a more or less rally in prices confined for the most part, however, to fractions. And yet the poolrooms continued to do business, with scarcely noticeable interruption.

Parent wrenched his leg through a collision with Lush at second base, and was forced to retire. He was succeeded by O'Neill. Turner played a brilliant fielding game for Cleveland. Attendance, 5,474.

Woodend said he expected to resume business before a great while. Nothing further was done in the way of forcing him to disclose the names of the New York Stock Exchange firms with whom he had arrangements to place orders.

LOS ANGELES, Cal., May 17. -- At the afternoon session of the Methodist General Conference to-day the Episcopacy Committee recommended the election of eight new Bishops, this recommendation being adopted by the General Conference. The election will be held to-morrow morning.

Only one home player reached third base, and but two reached second in the game. In the meantime McGraw's men took kindly to the pitching of Phillippe at times and scored seven runs.

Pepper of the Bay State Gas Company of Delaware, in his action for the nullification of the sale of the Boston Gas Companies in connection with a plan to merge them into a new combination.

Ely, a Williams College graduate, won the University Club golf tournament yesterday in the thirty-six hole handicap tournament, held as usual on the links of the St. Andrews Golf Club, near Chauncey, Westchester. Berry, editor of The Epworth Herald -- who received more than two-thirds of the entire vote cast on the first ballot. Lenney, attorney for the partners, on the basis of 10 per cent in cash and the remainder in notes running from one to twenty-eight months.

WASHINGTON, May 18. -- Lieut. de Faramond of the French Embassy went to New York to-day to meet his uncle and aunt, the Marquis and Marquise de Feizen, who arrive to-morrow from France to attend the marriage of their nephew and Miss Ivy Langham next Tuesday. Mile. Yvonne de Feizen, who accompanies her parents, will act as a bridesmaid at the wedding.

Hay. It involved the duty on 72,930 okes of Syrian wool at the rate of either 7 or 4 cents a pound.

LEXINGTON, Ky., May 20. -- Information has been received here that Boundless, winner of the $50,000 American Derby of 1893, has fallen and broken his neck on a farm eight miles from here. Boundless was by Harry O'Fallon-Endless, and it is said made a fortune for his owner, J.E. Cushing of Minneapolis, when he won the American Derby. He had not raced since the Chicago World's Fair.

Frank Wolf, who has won local fame as the "worst boy in Jersey City," was arraigned before Judge Blair, in the Quarter Sessions Court yesterday, on a charge of grand larceny. His head reached only a little above the table in front of the Judge's desk and Assistant Prosecutor Vickers was obliged to move him to a place where the Judge could see him.

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court yesterday handed down a decision reversing an order of the Special Term and ordering the release of Joseph A. Farley, who was recently committed for the action of the Grand Jury by Magistrate Leroy B. Crane on the charge of grand larceny.

BOSTON, May 20. -- The suicide of Miss Kate Greene in New York to-day was due, so her relatives here say, to grief over the death of her sister Fannie several months ago. When Robert B. Greene, a retired New Bedford oil merchant, died, he left his large estate, including the house at 345 Beacon Street, to two of his three daughters. The third daughter, Mary, lives abroad.

WAS it a pessimist who wrote that the Balkan States were "a heap of refuse, always subject to spontaneous combustion"? There are some persons who, very deep in the politics of the fag-end of Europe, insist that the Balkan States really are quite innocent of all the charges brought against them, and that the constant strife is entirely due to the machinations of Russia mad Austria.

The almost limitless Northland of Canada is the subject of Mr. David T. Hanbury's volume, and the country is almost a terra incognita. To the sportsman, the naturalist, and the ethnologist, there may be found in these arctic wilds much that is interesting. The explorer, however, must be willing to face the rigors of the climate and the privations of hunger.

IN a thousand pages, with innumerable photographs to illumine the text, Capt. Otto Sverdrup has set down a very detailed and homely narrative of his expedition into the north of Greenland begun on St. Hans's day, June 24, 1898, and concluded Sept. 19, 1902.

A GHOST STORY fit to rank with the best of those recently recalled by the readers of THE BOOK REVIEW is "The Lady's Maid's Bell," one of nine admirable tales in Edith Wharton's newly published volume of collected short stories called "The Descent of Man," and the only one of them that deals with the supernatural. In truth, Mrs. Wharton's short stories are generally concerned with the very practical affairs of contemporary social life.

Police Commissioner McAdoo dealt yesterday afternoon what he hopes will prove a deathblow to the poolrooms of New York. At his direction and under his supervision simultaneous raids were made at 4 o'clock upon 7 poolroom exchanges and 15 poolrooms, 70 prisoners being taken and 152 telephone and 15 telegraph instruments confiscated.

It is obviously a serious situation which compels so loyal a Republican and so strenuous a partisan as Senator SPOONER to head a bolting delegation from his State to the National Convention. We do not mean to say that Mr. SPOONER has the narrow mind and the indifferent conscience which ordinarily go with partisanship.

LOUIS, Mo., May 20. -- At to-day's session of the seventh biennial convention of the General Federation of Woman's Clubs a storm of objection was raised when, after the presentation of a resolution providing for the use of ballot boxes at federation elections, a substitute was offered which provided for an oral vote by States, the ballot of each delegation being announced from the floor by the State Federation Presidents.

Gov. Odell, Chairman of the Republican State Committee, is to sail for Europe Tuesday morning, in company with his son Herbert, on the North German Lloyd liner Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse. He will return to America in time to be present at the Republican National Convention, to be held in Chicago June 21.

There are eight stories included in this volume. Undoubtedly they are good stories of their kind, the kind with which the author has familiarized us in "The Call of the Wild." They are all about the Klondike, and that fact involves monotony. There is not much to be said in favor of that country as a field for fiction, except that it is a field which has not been worked.

Those godfathers and godmothers who gave to Anna's sister the name of Annabel made almost as much trouble for the heroine of Mr. Oppenheim's latest novel as did Annabel herself -- and that was not a little. For the sisters so closely resembled one another in looks that the similarity of names simply made confusion worse confounded.

RUPERT HUGHES has written a novel entitled "The Real New York," in which he describes the different sections of our city. A group of persons from various parts of the country -- Chicago, Terre Haute, San Francisco, and other cities -meet on a railway train entering New York.

In connection with two important and necessarily costly public improvements now in hand or about to be undertaken, Mayor McCLELLAN has at once an opportunity and a responsibility which he should not permit himself to forget. He may add to the credit of his administration the initiation of pipe galleries in New York or he may win the "reversed prestige" of failure to see what was obvious to every intelligent student of municipal development.

Another story by Mr. S.R. Crockett dealing with love, adventure, intrigue, and final reward and retribution is that of the career of "Strong Mac," a comely youth, bold and handsome, much in love with Adora Gracie, the daughter of the village dominie. And no wonder, for Adora was certainly adorable, and smart and self-reliant as well.

One purpose of "The Religion of the Universe," the new book by J. Allanson Picton, M.A., author of "New Theories and the Old Faith," "The Mystery of Matter," "The Religion of Jesus," , is to show that the issues between religion and science have no definite finality, as set forth by Herbert Spencer in his "First Principles."

LONDON, May 20. -- A new and cheaper edition of Herbert Spencer's works will be issued by Messrs. Williams Norgate. The first volume will be "The First Principles" and will sell for about $1.87, or less than half the cost of the present edition.

ELIZABETH ROBINS is certainly a woman of some extraordinary gifts. Perhaps if she had never been an actress she might have gained larger and more enduring fame as a writer. The chief quality of the best of her histrionic efforts has been intelligence -- which often counts for less in the actor's art than some other qualities.

SAN FRANCISCO, May 20. -- In the United States District Court to-day George W. Rumble was convicted of using the mail for fraudulent purposes. The case will be appealed and Rumble will be given his liberty on a bond of $10,000.

LAST Saturday, a fortnight before the date of publication, it was necessary to send a new large edition of "A Texas Matchmaker" to press, and this before the news companies have begun to send in their orders. Careful study of the advance sheets leaves one chiefly impressed by the absence of extravagance in the behavior of the cattlemen.

An agreeable change in the weather, a fast track, and an interesting programme were circumstances that added much to the enjoyment of about 10,000 visitors to the Morris Park race course yesterday, but more than these things, the fact that four post favorites passed the winning poet first, while well-backed horses won in the two remaining events, filled the crowd with satisfaction and left little to be desired.

Though yesterday's total in the stock market was the smallest of the week the tone of the market was somewhat improved, and with very few exceptions the closing prices were at advances over those of the previous day. The early recovery in Union Pacific from 82 to 83 1/2 helped sentiment a good deal, and traders became more willing to work for an advance.

Two new volumes have been added to "The Builder" Student's Series, which is issued in this country by the Macmillan Company. They are "Roads; Their Construction and Maintenance, with Special Reference to Road Materials," by Allan Greenwell and J.V. Elsden; and "Stresses and Strains; Their Calculation and that of Their Resistances, by Formulae and Graphic Methods," by Frederic Richard Farrow.

While mentally unbalanced as the result of acute nervous prostration, Miss Kate Greene, forty years old, of 345 Beacon Street, Boston, dropped from a sixth story window of the Hotel Endicott, at Columbus Avenue and Eighty-first Street, yesterday morning, receiving injuries from which she died shortly afterward in the Roosevelt Hospital.

Just now, when the building of a new home is being considered, the special issue of The Architectural Review will be of interest to architects and owners. The number contains articles on American country and suburban houses. The opening article, by Robert D. Andrews, deals with "The Changing Styles of Country Houses."

Hyben -- a name not found in encyclopedia or atlas -- is "a straggling green island" on the Hampshire coast. The "tyrants" of its northern end are two blacksmiths, not dependent upon the forge for a livelihood, men of landed property, who work at the smithy simply because their trade has come to them as an inheritance.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., May 21. -- The Brooklyns fared no better to-day against the local team than they did yesterday, and in a close finish were beaten by a score of three to two. The St. Louis men played a perfect fielding game and outbatted the visitors, but with the exception of the sixth inning, Jones kept the hits well apart.

The long contemplated combine of the broom manufacturers of the country now appears to stand a fair chance of becoming a reality. Representatives of many of the largest factories are now in Chicago to talk over the situation and come to some definite understanding with the Western and New York capitalists who have agreed to put up the money.

WHILE Guilford clams are not in the market because the Connecticut beds were almost ruined by the severe Winter, there is an ample supply of the delicacy from Lone Island. The bivalves are not as large as Guilfords -- the diameter of the golden belly about that of a silver dollar, but plump and succulent.

NEW HAVEN, Conn., May 21. -- A colored man who gave his name as Samuel Blackson was arrested by the police of the Grand Avenue Station shortly before midnight to-night. He was found on Orange Street, in the neighborhood of Humphrey Street, where last Thursday evening the daughter of a Yale professor, whose name the detective department has refused to divulge, was beaten and robbed.

OWING to a mistake in "feeding" sheets into a printing press there appeared in South Africa one sheet of five-shilling stamps on which King Edward's head is reversed. Some of the stamps got into circulation before the error was discovered, and collectors are now willing to pay about 500 times the face value of the bit of paper to secure specimens.

For the purpose of determining just how he stands in the Democratic fight in Brooklyn, Senator McCarren last night arranged to meet a score of district leaders and other influential men in the local organization in private conference this evening.

The one in charge of Motorman "Abe" Bishop was standing in front of 184 Park Row discharging some passengers when Car 1,579 of the same line, in charge of Motorman George Edwards, crashed into the rear of it.

Dean swindle, because unaccompanied by police raids, appears to be more far-reaching in its consequences, and therefore likely to produce a more lasting effect for good.

Jones that she was holding Mr. O'Connell's baby as security pending the return of $85 alleged to have been stolen by the other woman's husband.

The dinner of the Arctic Club, that is given about this time each year in honor of the "Field Workers," and which was held in the Aldine Association at 111 Fifth Avenue last evening, was made notable by the announcing of a startling theory as to the best and quickest way to discover that mysterious point of land that is situated somewhere beyond Franz Josef Land and is known as the north pole.
TIFFIN, Ohio, May 21. -- Daniel Crum, a wealthy farmer, and his hired man, Albert Rice, were shot and fatally wounded to-day by Adam Reinman, a neighbor, while at work plowing in a field.

It was announced last week at the Appraisers' Stores that the Finance Committee of the Senate had appointed a sub-committee to investigate the alleged necessity of changes in the Customs Administrative act, which formed the basis of the Payne bill introduced at the last session of Congress.

Play was continued yesterday in the championship lawn tennis tournament of the New York Lawn Tennis Club. Two matches in the doubles and one in the singles were decided, and were productive of excellent sport and drew a numerous gallery of spectators to the courts at One Hundred and Twenty-third Street and St. Nicholas Avenue.

The threat of Thomas Healey, walking delegate of the freight handlers' organization, to call out the freight handlers of the New York, New Haven and Hartford system along the east side river front was carried out yesterday. The orders were given early in the day, though Healey went to Fall River in the morning to extend the strike to the other piers.

The action taken is the selection of a committee to advocate one particular site.

ATLANTIC CITY, N.J., May 21. -- The past week was a gay one at the Hotel Rudolf, and the amusements included the season's third german, led by Miss Lotta Cummings of New York City. She had as her partner S. Freeman Kirkland of Baltimore.

NEW YORK is soon to have three more free public baths, one of which will be opened this month and the others somewhat later in the season. The first to be completed is at 347 and 349 West Forty-first Street.

The announcement last week that the entire stock of Sweetser, Pembrook Co. would be sold at auction this week and that the firm, which is one of the oldest in its line in the city, would finally go out of business, marked another step in what many believe to be the gradual extinction of the jobbing trade in this city.

LOS ANGELES, Cal., May 21. -- Dr. J.R. Day, the Chancellor of Syracuse University, was to-day chosen to be Bishop of the Methodist Church. He was the eighth choice of the General Conference, and was elected on the fourteenth ballot, completing the list of Bishops.

The order of Judge Holt directing Edward S. Hatch of the suspended Stock Exchange firm of Hatch Hurlburt to "execute a request" upon the Exchange to sell his seat, transfers the controversy over the disposition of that highly valuable asset of the respondent from between Mr. Hatch and his creditors into the hands of the Stock Exchange and the United States Court.

Poor Master Hewitt of Jersey City reports an unprecedented flight of tramps from this part of the country to St. Louis. He says that his office is besieged, as never before, by nomads seeking passes on the railroads to points in that direction.

The usual Saturday surprise was of an agreeable nature for a novelty. The market opened as it closed, stolid rather than strong, and immovable above all. But this changed in the twinkling of an eye upon the appearance of the bank statement. The reduction of cash was somewhat larger than had been expected, but there was an unexpected and large reduction of loans.

It was a basket of La France roses with a card bearing the words: "From the youngest Baroness to the oldest Baroness."

The scheme of the United States Realty and Construction Company for erecting gigantic twin skyscrapers, covering the old sites of the Trinity and Boreel Buildings and the small block at the rear of the latter structure, promises to be the most noteworthy building operation ever undertaken in this city.
BERLIN, May 21. -- I am informed from an excellent source that the oft-repeated rumors that the days of Count von Buelow as Chancellor are numbered are about to be confirmed.

Senator Elsberg of the Fifteenth Senate District, which comprises the Twenty-fifth, Twenty-seventh, and Twenty-ninth Assembly Districts, will have a difficult fight for renomination, if the combination just effected between the Twenty-fifth District organization, of which ex-Alderman Herbert Parsons is the head, and the Partridge- Morris-Ware-Schwartzler followers in the Twenty-ninth District, succeeds in putting the blocks in his path it is expected to.

With their hats tilted and loose strands of hair blowing over their faces, two young women alighted from a trolley car at the foot of East Thirty-fourth Street and made their way to one of the ferryboats of the Long Island Railroad.

DEAR to the heart of the old-time Southerner was the faithful "mammy" nurse, with her scarlet bandanna, snowy apron, and weird collection of ghost stories and "spook" songs. The children loved her and their parents prized her above all the servants on the plantation. Benignant and patient to a fault, the old nurse never wearied of following her restless charges through the gardens and orchards.

WASHINGTON, May 21. -- Naval officers here are talking about the recent heavy losses of naval vessels through the explosion of mines near Port Arthur, and it is suggested that the subject of regulating the use of such mines by international agreement will come up at the next meeting of the Naval General Board for consideration.

Awards of fifty-six scholarships for the academic year 1904-5 have just been announced by the University Council of Columbia University. One of those to receive a scholarship is Samuel Lucas Joshi, a high caste Brahmin of Madras, India. He was graduated from the University of Madras in 1896, and is now pursuing studies in political economy and finance at Columbia.

FROM present indications the Spring floods this year will be unusually severe. To the average reader the report in a newspaper of a great flood comes as first news, yet to hundreds of thousands of people the coming of the catastrophe has been known for days, sometimes weeks, in advance.

TUXEDO PARK, N.Y., May 2. -- Ideal Spring weather favored the colonists at Tuxedo during the week's end, and in consequence a large gathering assembled at the clubhouses and among the cottagers. Nearly all the season's arrivals are now here, and each cottager is entertaining guests over Sunday.

CLEVELAND, May 21. -- The Twenty-first district Democrat convention to-day nominated Edmund G. Vail for Congress. Mayor Tom L. Johnson and John H. Clarke were selected as delegates to the National Convention. They were not instructed.
The Atlanta-Birmingham Fire Insurance Company has been licensed to do business in the State of Minnesota.

Conventions for the election of delegates to the Democratic National Convention were held in the week just ended in Wisconsin, Montana, California, South Carolina, Ohio, and Minnesota. In the two latter only district conventions were held.

The United States Government is making investigations and has already issued a bulletin upon the subject of rubber gathering in the Philippines. It is known that in some of the southern islands the Hevea or Para rubber tree grows as perfectly as it does upon the Amazon and its tributaries, and in all of the islands the Castilloa or Mexican rubber tree can be made to grow.

An investigation is being made by the domestic manufacturers of underwear as to the exceedingly low price at which much foreign underwear is being sold in this market. Special complaint has been made about certain lines of Swiss ribbed goods, and it is said that certain firms of importers are able to sell the goods here at less than it costs other importers to land them in this country.

WHILE Uncle Sam and the Insular Government officials of Porto Rico have been worrying a great deal over the ravages of the disease known as tropical anemia, or blood impoverishment, which is prevalent throughout the island, they have not reckoned at all apparently on the havoc caused by that other great foe to health and happiness -- nostalgia.

A NEW BOOK PLATE has just been designed for the Mayflower Society of this State to use in the books now being secured for its library. It is the first bookplate issued by any of the purely patriotic societies, and was designed by a direct descendant of the little band of men and women who made themselves and their ship famous years ago.

The contracts for the construction of the two mammoth turbine transatlantic liners that the Cunard Company is going to operate between Liverpool and New York have been signed. These great ships, which the Cunards insist must be the fastest vessels that ever plied the Atlantic, will be built by John Brown Co. and Swan, Hunter Wigham, Richardson.

Chicago's leadership in the National League was of short duration, for with McGinnity pitching, the New Yorks turned the tables on their conquerors of the previous day and did not allow them to score a run. Twenty thousand persons witnessed the contest, which was an unusually large crowd for a week day at Chicago.

Bridge Commissioner Best met representatives of the New York City Railway, the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company, and the Coney Island and Brooklyn yesterday, and the contract providing for the running of cars over the Williamsburg Bridge was signed. The contract itself literally is between the Bridge Company and the city, the Bridge Company being owned by the three street railroad systems.

CURIOSITY as to the personality of Tom Browne, the English artist, has been aroused among our readers by his remarkable series of impressions, drawn expressly for THE NEW YORK TIMES, and now in course of publication. ORANGE, N.J., May 21. -- Six Newark school teachers -- Miss Lou K. Beardsley, Miss Jane Schaeffer, Miss Elsie Johnson, Miss S. Mailison, Miss Mary North, and Miss E.N. Davis -- journeyed to the South Mountain Park this afternoon on a botanizing expedition. Botanizing is not allowed in the park, and Policeman O'Brien says he told the visitors they must not do it.

The American liner St. Louis came up the bay yesterday afternoon on her arrival from Southampton with her flags at half-mast for Joseph Humphreys, Charles Frohman's general stage director, who died on board at 9:30 o'clock yesterday morning shortly after the vessel had passed Nantucket.

LONDON, May 21. -- The approach of the Whitsuntide holidays had the usual effect of restricting business on the Stock Exchange this week, dealings being influenced by a desire on the part of the brokers to leave their affairs as snug as possible on Friday night, when the house closed for three days.

THE Fourth of July is not a distinctly American institution. To be sure, it happens to be Independence Day for the United States, and more than a century and a quarter of observances of that great event have brought it about that the signing of the charter of American liberties in the old State House in Philadelphia on that date overshadows all else when the holiday arrives.

With the general improvement shown in bonds within the past month or two the gains made in the Jersey issues traded in on the curb have attracted as much attention as any. Some of the issues in question are regularly quoted, but very seldom have transactions in them been reported up to the beginning of April.

WASHINGTON, May 21. -- The young men who have been eating poisons under the direction of the Agricultural Department and the immediate administration of Prof. Wiley, since January last, have been graduated, so to speak, and to-day resumed the diet of the ordinary person.

LONG BRANCH, May 21. -- The cottages here are rapidly filling up for the season, and the activity of Long Branch has begun. The town is now governed by the Coult Charter act, which was adopted last Tuesday.

LAKEWOOD, N.J., May 21. -- The many reasons that combine to make Lakewood an ideal Spring resort have induced several of the cottagers to plan to linger here through June. The Laurel House has a good patronage, and the Rhinelanders, de Peysters, and other well-known New Yorkers who have season apartments at that hotel will remain until the close.

That the man chiefly responsible for the looting of the Federal Bank should be convicted of the vulgar crime of grand larceny is in a way satisfactory. It stamps him with the infamy he justly earned in the transaction for which he was tried and puts him personally a little below the level of the footpad who faces the risk of being resisted and hurt in his operations.
NEW ORLEANS, May 21. -- A verdict for $28,390 was given in favor of the Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans against the National Contracting Company in the United States District Court to-day.

NEWARK, May 21. -- Argument on the application of E.H. Harriman to restrain the Northern Securities Company and the Equitable Trust Company from distributing the Northern Pacific stock on the proposed plan was continued here to-day. Former Secretary of War Elihu Root, for the defendants, resumed his argument. Mr. Root contended that the differences in the price of the Northern Pacific stock prompted the present suit.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 21. -- The Government to-day received news confirmatory of the rumors in circulation here that Gen. Stoessel has made a successful sortie from Port Arthur, resulting in the defeat of the Japanese, with the loss of over 1,000 killed or wounded. The Russian losses were 116 killed or wounded.

ROME, May 21. -- France has practically broken off diplomatic relations with the Holy See. M. Nisard, her Ambassador to the Vatican, acting under instructions from Paris, left Rome to-night on an unlimited vacation.

A TINY mite of five years attracted more attention and more applause at the recent military tournament on the afternoon of his appearance than any one or anything else. He was drum major of a drum corps formed of nineteen other midgets, none over six, but none of whom, however, was quite as diminutive as himself.
MORRISTOWN, N.J., May 21. -- John Newcomb of Dover, a shoemaker at Sussex and Clinton Streets, occasionally sends Nero, his big Newfoundland dog, to fetch his luncheon from home.

H.C. Schradeick of the Brooklyn Boys' High School, in the dual athletic meet held between Polytechnic Preparatory School and the Brooklyn Boys' High School yesterday, at Grand Street Park, Brooklyn, won the half-mile and one-mile runs.
ANNAPOLIS, Md., May 21. -- In their last boat race of the season here this afternoon the midshipmen defeated both the first and second crews from Georgetown University in record-breaking time.

MORRISTOWN, N.J., May 21. -- Mr. and Mrs. Thomas W. Cauldwell will leave Morristown about June 15 and go to the Adirondacks, where they will spend the Summer. Their house on Elm Street will not be closed, as it has been leased to New York parties for three months.

CHICAGO, May 21. -- Rumors are current in railroad circles that a new deal between Hill and Harriman is contemplated whereby the Northern Pacific will practically become a part of the Harriman system.

Despite much early doubt in Wall Street about the possibility of successfully floating a foreign loan in this market, the principal difficulty encountered by the syndicate that had charge of floating half of the $50,000,000 Japanese loan in New York was in giving banking houses enough share in the syndicate to satisfy them.

Once again Conductor Duss will give nightly concerts in the large building, and the gondolas will make their leisurely way around the Grand Canal. To-night Venice's New York season opens with a flourish.

ALBANY, May 21. -- Oneida County, comprising the Thirty-fourth Senatorial District, promises to be again this Fall the arena of a lively political fight. It has been the field of many a battle royal from before the times of Horatio Seymour and Roscoe Conkling.

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J., May 21. -- Mrs. Cordova, wife of the Rev. J.R. Cordova, pastor of the South River Methodist Church, who disappeared after conducting a prayer meeting with his pretty choir singer, Miss Julia Bowne, has sworn out a warrant for the arrest of her husband on a charge of desertion.

Although there is no precedent for the action of President ROOSEVELT in confiscating the films for a representation by kinematograph of a scene on the Capitol grounds in Washington, one cannot but sympathize with his desire to stop the burlesque. Strictly speaking, it was a high-handed proceeding which might establish a precedent.

LOS ANGELES, Cal., May 21. -- The announcement is made that the California. Fruit Agency, the big merger company in control of the packing and shipping of a large part of the orange crop of Southern California, will go out of business next September.

Staten Island formally acknowledged, declared, and gloried yesterday afternoon that she was an integral part of the Greater New York on the occasion of the laying of the cornerstone of the Richmond Borough Hall at St. George. The ceremonies attendant on the laying of the cornerstone were elaborate.

The day was perfect for coaching and every one was in fine spirits when the coach left the Metropolitan at 10 o'clock in the morning, exactly on schedule time.

They grow used to it in time, however, and finally, with continued experience, do not notice it at all. The Mayor announced to-day that he would start on his trip to St. Louis on Tuesday morning, although his big racing auto has not arrived.

Within a fortnight many of those who sailed in the Lenten time will have returned. Newport cottagers also are overhauling their houses, ready for an early and a brisk season.

Moharib, winner of the Kansas City Derby, was third. The mile and a quarter was covered in 2:06, a fraction of a second slower than English Lad took in his try-out over the same distance a few days ago.

LONDON, May 11. -- Mme. Melba made her first appearance for the season at the Covent Garden Opera House last night to a house crowded with fashionable Londoners in their most gorgeous costumes and jewels. The Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales occupied the royal box, and in all the big opera house there was not a box or a stall vacant after 10 o'clock, and upstairs the crowd was standing two deep.

BERLIN, May 14. -- Germany will send teams to St. Louis to take part in swimming, turning, lawn tennis, wrestling, and rowing contests. The last-named sport, owing to the initiation of the Kaiser, in recent years has been especially developed in Germany. This above all is true of Berlin, as is shown by the large number of fine rowing clubhouses found on the Spree.

NORFOLK, Va., May 21. -- In the United States Court to-day Mrs. Naomi K. Sheridan of New York entered suit for $15,000 against the Standard Oil Company for injuries she alleges she sustained in a recent collision between the yacht Diana, owned by Mr. Sheridan, and the yacht Petrolia, owned by the Standard Oil Company.

WILL Castlegould, the largest and most wonderful residence yet conceived by an American, ever be completed? This is a question that architects all over this land, and other persons familiar with the scope of Howard Gould's mammoth undertaking, have been trying to answer for more than three years.

The United States battleship Kentucky, which for the past three years has been the flagship of the China squadron, arrived here yesterday flying the flag of Rear Admiral Robley D. Evans. She is now at anchor off Tompkinsville, after making a warship record by her run from Hong Kong, covering the distance of 12,699 miles at an average speed of 12.7 knots, following a 9,000 mile run from the China station to Honolulu and back.

The letter this new-comer has written about the inscription has given a decided turn to the controversy that has raged over it.

SAN JUAN, Porto Rico, May 9. -- The Americanization of Porto Rico is a thing of years. There is much to be done before the majority of the people here, uneducated and simple as they are, can be made successful American citizens. But there is no doubt that these particular descendants of the Latins and Indians have some peculiar attributes which we in our zeal to reform should neither make over nor endeavor to better.
CHEYENNE, Wyo., May 21. -- Four bodies of persons drowned during last night's floods have been recovered. A number of persons are still missing.

Mr. Wakeman is the wheelhorse of the American Protective Tariff League, the citadel of the "stand-patters." He believes that the tariff is the principal issue at this time and that it will be the thing in the approaching campaign.

He has found the weak point in their system. Poolrooms are a device for extending far beyond the limits of the race track the area within which betting on horse races is possible.

In 1870 there were 2,001,293 farms in the United States. According to the last census there were 5,739,000 in 1900. The advance in the value of farm products was from a fraction less than $2,000,000,000 in 1870 to $3,764,000,000 in 1900. In 1870 there were 5,888,987 persons engaged in farming, while in 1900 the number had grown to 10,483,000.

The lives of more than a hundred passengers on a suburban train of the New York, New Haven and Hartford were imperilled in a peculiar accident that occurred at One Hundred and Thirty-first Street and Brook Avenue yesterday afternoon. A fire that did considerable damage to the telegraph and electric light wires of the Edison Company occurred in the subway at the southwest corner of Broadway and Fulton Street yesterday morning, its exact location being the same as that of the fire that paralyzed telegraphic and telephone service in the down-town district on April 6.

HACKENSACK, N.J., May 22. -- Out of a party of five thrown from a carriage in a runaway accident here to-day only Mrs. Helen Herring, who is past eighty-five, and her greatniece, who is just five, escaped injury. Mrs. Henry Banta, a niece of Mrs. Herring, was the most seriously hurt. Her right leg was broken in four places and her face was cut.

The marine firemen and oilers on the lines controlled by the New York, New Haven and Hartford Company who quit work originally in sympathy with the freight handlers at the Fall River piers at the foot of Warren Street have now changed their attitude into a general demand for an increase in wages from $40 to $45 a month. According to the strikers this demand will be made on all the coastwise steamship lines.

The $35,000,000 5 per cent. bonds of the Republic of Cuba, due 1944, which recently were purchased by Speyer Co., have been privately sold to a considerable amount. The loan has a practically unique interest in that it is the first loan issued after the acceptance by the Cuban Republic of the so-called Platt amendment.

Pacers furnished the best of the Sunday morning sport on the Harlem River Speedway yesterday. The footing was ideal for fast work when the contests opened with a half-mile tilt between Don Derby, (2:04 1/2,) winner of the 1903 Speedway pacing championship, driven by John Kelly, and Nathan Straus, (2:05 1/4,) driven by his owner, Joseph Meyer of Newark, N.J.

Voronetz and deputations of the military, naval, and municipal authorities, as well as by an enthusiastic crowd, and bread and salt were given him.

Nevertheless, it is unusual for the Governor of the State of New York, or for that matter of any other State, to go beyond the seas during his term of office.

BUFFALO, May 22. -- The proposed union of the Cumberland and the Northern Church continues to be the absorbing topic among the Commissioners to the one hundred and sixteenth General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in session here. The supportters and opponents of union are lining up for the contest next Thursday.

Martin had first attempted to shoot Vastel's father, and had fired one shot when the boy wrested a revolver from his father's hand and sent three bullets into Martin's body, and Martin died soon after at the hospital.

GYANG-TSE, May 22. -- A small force from our garrison, Chung-lo, moved out yesterday under Col. Brander to clear the line to the south.

PARIS, May 23 -- The Ministry of the Interior authorizes a denial of the statement that M. de Navonne, First Secretary of the French Embassy to the Vatican, will act as Charge d'Affaires at the embassy, stating that the Government considers that his selection would attenuate the importance of the action taken in the recall of Ambassador Nisard.

WASHINGTON, May 22. -- One of the questions with which the Panama Canal Commission will have to deal is whether the eight-hour law applies to the construction of the Panama Canal. The application of either the present law or the pending bill, if enacted, would extend the time of construction at least two years, and increase its cost by many millions of dollars.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, May 22. -- The Democratic State Convention will be held here next Tuesday and Wednesday. All who are opposed to Hearst are classed as conservatives and as they have a majority of the uncontested delegates, they will no doubt decide the contests against Hearst contestants and control the convention.

DES MOINES, Iowa, May 22. -- When the funeral of E.L. Dubois, a prominent Des Moines clubman, began to-day, three women advanced, each demanding recognition as his wife. One was Mary E. Dubois of Denver, another was Grace A. Dubois of New Orleans, and the third was the Mrs. Dubois with whom he has lived here.

That Senator McCarren still holds a firm grip on the leadership of the Kings County Democratic organization, despite the combined efforts of Charles F. Murphy and Willoughby Street to depose him, was demonstrated last night to the complete satisfaction of his friends, when fifteen of the Executive Committeemen, gathered together at his call, unqualifiedly pledged him their support to the end in the fight.

DUBOIS, Penn., May 22. -- Mrs. Frank Paul, wife of a well-known resident of Cardiff, a village near here, sacrificed her life for her husband's hat to-day. An Italian, with whom her husband had quarreled, shot her down in cold blood as she was trying to recover the hat.

Jerome D. Gedney, a lawyer living at East Orange, N.J., was a prisoner before Magistrate Mott in the Jefferson Market Court yesterday morning charged with assault. The complainant, was S. Carl Gerstle, a coffee merchant, who also lives in East Orange.

A record-breaking crowd sunned itself in Central Park yesterday, and half a dozen collisions, runaways, and other accidents marked the celebration of the finest Sunday so far this year. With the big crowd, however, there were, aside from the principals in the accidents, but two arrests all day, one of a man who was annoying the animals, and the other a suspected pickpocket.

VINELAND, N.J., May 22. -- That Alfred Morgan, an aged recluse and a relative of J. Pierpont Morgan, was murdered early this morning and the little frame house in which he lived set afire in order to hide the crime is the belief of the Vineland police. His death makes a mystery such as Vineland has never had before.

JOHANNESBURG, Transvaal Colony, South Africa, May 22. -- Persistent rumors of unrest among the native tribes have been rife for some time. "Unrest" is perhaps too strong a word to use at present. The natives have been talking a good deal and feel themselves dissatisfied, but only in a vague manner.

WASHINGTON, May 22. -- The effect of the split in the Republican Party in Wisconsin on the election of members of the next House of Representatives is arousing apprehension. There is fear that in the sharp combat between the two factions several seats may be lost by the Republicans.

LONDON, May 23. -- Lord Inverclyde has a letter in The Times this morning in deply to the letter of Herr Ballin published May 16. In that letter the Director General of the Hamburg-American Line said he never knew why the Cunard Line retired from the agreement entered into between British and Continental lines, under which the latter renounced the Anglo-Scandinavian emigrant traffic.

H. Christoffers of the St. George Athletic Club won the half-mile run, which was a feature of the annual celebration of the Kerrymen's Association at Celtic Park, Long Island, yesterday. Christoffers received an eighteen-yard handicap, and by using excellent judgment won by several feet. W.G. Frank of the Greater New York Irish Athletic Association, with ninety-five yards handicap, captured the one mile and a half run easily.

Ward, General Manager of the carriage firm of Ward Johnson, spent a considerable part of to-day in vain striving to reach that spot between his shoulder blades where there still clung remnants of a porous plaster, stuck there by a thief who got away with Mr. Ward's two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar diamond stud, his watch and chain, and $50.

The enterprising managers of the "greatest shows on earth" at Coney Island were smiling and happy yesterday. With clear skies overhead, gentle breezes, and a temperature more suggestive of July than May, the amusement places were all thronged with people bent on seeing the new wonders of the island.

There are now 124,062 Odd Fellows in Pennsylvania, 12,721 having been initiated into the order last year. In the last thirty-six years the lodges in the State have distributed $16,398,948 for relief and the prevention of distress and actual want. The order has four orphans' homes in the State.

Enough activity and strength were shown in the first hour of trading yesterday to give the impression that the upward movement with which the market closed on Saturday marked a radical change in the character of the market, as it certainly had marked to some extent change in market sentiment.

CHE-FOO, May 23. -- The Captain of a Russian merchantman, who left Port Arthur on May 20, and is among the recent arrivals from Dalny, says that on the 20th the Russians succeeded in sinking a small Japanese gunboat and two torpedo boats. All the damaged warships, except the Czarewitch and the Retvizan, are ready to rejoin the fleet.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 23. -- A message from Hazard, Perry County, reports the reopening of the French-Eversole feud, John Eversole assassinating William Smith to-day.

Lee Ridley, winner of the selling steeplechase yesterday at Morris Park in the colors of Thomas Hitchcock, Jr., is one of four horses bought by his owner at Washington for $500. LONDON, May 24. -- The Times's Russian correspondents say the war has already begun to produce a serious effect on the economic life of Russia, and a writer in the Viedomosti presents reports which go to show that commerce and industry throughout the country are passing through a severe crisis.

Griggs, who is an expert golf player, has been elected Captain of the golf team of the North Jersey Country Club, which has an excellent eighteen-hole course at this place. THOMPSONVILLE, Conn., May 29. -- Assistant District Attorney Frank P. Garvan of New York was one of a party of automobilists arrested this afternoon by Town Constables on the charge of speeding their machine beyond the limit allowed by law. With him at the time were Mr. and Mrs. Frank Black and Mrs. Nicholl, all of New York.

Nathan Straus, the bay pacing gelding with a record of 2:03 1/2 who will make an attempt to capture the world's pacing record in the Grand Circuit this season, scored a notable victory on the Harlem River Speedway yesterday morning, when he defeated the 1903 Speedway champion Don Derby, 2:04 1/2 two heats out of three.

Another large dock fire, the fifth in four years to spread destruction on the New Jersey shore, raged yesterday afternoon and last night, making a spectacle that in grandeur was second only to the catastrophe of June, 1900, when the piers and three of the great liners of the North German Lloyd Steamship Company were destroyed.

PITTSBURG, May 29. -- Senator Quay last Friday signed his will, having previously destroyed one he wrote while at Morganza. The estate is valued at about $800,000, according to the calculation of William Montgomery, cashier of the Allegheny National Bank.
EAST ORANGE, May 29. -- Capt. Demorin Libby, known to old New Yorkers as "The Original Libby," will celebrate his ninetieth birthday on June 7, at the home of his son, in East Orange.

Your editorial about the officers and soldiers in Germany in THE NEW YORK TIMES of May 12 is entirely justified. It shows again how well you are informed as to the shameful ill-treatment of the German soldier by his superiors.

LONDON, May 20. -- British naval officers generally doubt very much whether their Government will consent to be concerned in a remonstrance directed to Russia or to Russia and Japan against such use of floating mines as tends to endanger neutral shipping on the open seas.

PHILADELPHIA, May 29. -- An attempt to assassinate the Rev. Antonio Isoleri, rector of the Church of St. Mary Magdale di Pazzi, was foiled by the police to-day during a pageant in honor of the church's patron saint. A band of Anarchists rushed to the priest's carriage, the leader leveling a revolver.

Of a total attendance of 1,547,873 visitors to the New York Aquarium in 1903, the daily average for July, August, and September was 6,255 -- or about 2,000 more per diem than attended during the Winter months. It is fair to assume that the present Summer will see an increase in the number of visitors.

CHESTER, Penn., May 29. -- The naphtha launch White Seal left here to-day for Wilmington with a party of pleasure seekers. Before going five miles the launch had rescued the crews of two sailing yachts which capsized in the Delaware River, and saved the lives of fourteen persons. One person was drowned.

CHIHUAHUA, Mexico, May 29. -- According to the statement of Henry B. Welschen, a well-known mining man, who has arrived here from Jiminez, Dr. R.C. Flower of New York passed through that place two days ago on his way to Parral, this State. Welschen says that he knew Dr. Flower in Arizona several years ago.

WASHINGTON, May 29. -- Secretary Moody has issued a general order containing certain extracts from the report of the Missouri court of inquiry regarding the conduct of the officers and men at the time of the accident on board of that vessel, April 13, and letters from the President to the Navy Department regarding the bravery of the officers and men of the Missouri.

Two arrests were made by the Jersey City police yesterday, both of which were supposed at the time to be in connection with the murder of Dominic Sokotoski, the non-union freight handler who was beaten to death on Saturday night as he was returning from work at the Fall River Line pier.

They fear him so much, however, that whenever the Commissioner appears among them with his red automobile and warlike demeanor they say nothing, but simply stand and quake.

The origin of the blaze has not been ascertained, but it spread so rapidly upward and so dense was the smoke that poured up the stairway that exit by that way was cut off.

CHICAGO, May 29. -- After pitching fine ball for seven innings Hess showed weakness in the eighth, when three bases on balls, a double, a single, and a passed ball scored all of Chicago's runs. Both teams put up a fast fielding game, Holmes carrying off the honors.

WASHINGTON, May 29. -- Exports of manufactures in the fiscal year which ends with next month seem likely to exceed those of any preceding year, according to ten months figures just presented by the Department of Commerce and Labor through its Bureau of Statistics.

TRENTON, May 30. -- Nathan Sibbett, the fourteen-year-old boy who was arrested here late last night after his mother was found dead in her home, at Jacobs Creek, was held to-day for the Coroner's inquest.

J. Flanagan of the Greater New York Irish Athletic Association won both the sixteen and fifty-six pound weight-throwing contests in the games held at Celtic Park yesterday. Flanagan also finished second to John Sheridan in the discus-throwing event. Harry Hillman of the New York Athletic Club won the 120-yard low-hurdle race from S.C. Northridge by several yards. George Bonhag was defeated by H. Cohn in the one-and-one-half-mile invitation race.

Memorial Day was observed with more of the real spirit of the occasion yesterday than for many years. There were greater throngs in the streets to cheer the veterans and greater crowds at the centres of interest.

PHILADELPHIA, May 30. -- The New Yorks did not have the slightest trouble in defeating the Philadelphia team this morning, and up to the eighth inning in the afternoon game they were in an excellent position to score another victory. Taylor, however, weakened in that inning, and by good, hard hitting the Philadelphias put together three runs, which proved to be one more than enough to win the game.

One of the waiters at the Cafe Francis, 53 West Thirty-fifth Street, on going into the cellar yesterday evening, was confronted by a volume of smoke that quickly filled the halls, kitchen, and dining room. The kitchen servants hurried to the street, as did also a number of the guests, who were on the lower floor.

With a field of thirty-two competitors, many of them the college experts in singles, the annual tournament of the New York Lawn Tennis Club was begun yesterday on their courts at One Hundred and Twenty-third Street and St. Nicholas Avenue. Three of the competitions in the opening round brought out some fine tennis and held a large gallery about the grounds the entire day.

The long-mark men received most of the prizes at the annual games of the Brooklyn Athletic Club, held yesterday at Grand Street Park. B. TRENTON, May 30. -- Elmer Gilbert stood on a wharf at Saugers Creek this evening and decided that life was not worth living. The overcast sky was in accord with his gloomy spirits, and the metallic lustre of the coal oil spread on the waters of the creek to kill mosquitos reminded him that an avenue to death was at hand.
LONDON, May 30. -- Money was in good month-end demand in the market to-day. Discounts were easy, in anticipation of easier money at the month-turn.

A thunderstorm, after threatening all the afternoon, burst over the city early last evening, menacing lives and causing much inconvenience to belated holiday makers. A crowded music hall was struck by lightning, causing a panic; the thousands along the Speedway were drenched, and an eight-oared shell competing in the Harlem Regatta was swamped, and Bellevue Hospital was left in darkness by the lightning's pranks.

NEGAUNEE, Mich., May 30. -- All hope of finding Mayor Hudson alive has been abandoned. He is believed to have perished in the woods. The mines here have shut down, and since Saturday morning 1,500 men have scoured the woods, but no trace has been found of him except some papers belonging to him which were found Saturday afternoon.

NEWARK, N.J., May 30. -- When the members of the Celtic Club of this city visited the graves of their departed members to-day the final resting place of Thomas Dunn English, for years an honorary member, was found to be neglected.

RALEIGH, N.C., May 30. -- News has reached here from Wilkesborough of the reception accorded James E. Boyd, Judge of the United States Court for the Western District of this State, on his arrival there. When Congress authorized the court at Wilkesborough Judge Boyd was bitterly hostile to the move.

WASHINGTON, May 30. -- President Roosevelt and party returned to Washington from Gettysburg at 8:20 o'clock to-night. On arriving at the station the President gave a hearty handshake to the engine crew.

WASHINGTON, May 30. -- The possibility that international complications may grow out of the effort of the United States to rescue one of its citizens. Mr. Perdicaris, and his kinsman, the Englishman Varley, who have been abducted by Raisuli, the Moroccan bandit, is not taken as a matter to be seriously considered at this stage of the affair.

NUTLEY, N.J., May 30. -- The happiest man in this town to-day is Charles Keith, and the happiest woman is Mrs. Keith, for after eighteen years of married life a baby -- such a blue-eyed, handsome little girl baby -- has come to their handsome home in Chestnut Street. The baby was four days old when it arrived, on Friday.

NEWARK, N.J., May 30. -- Frank L. Kramer, the National cycling champion, won the half-mile professional event easily at the Vailsburg track to-day. Kramer crossed the tape four feet in front of Iver Lawson, riding easily. The real contest was between Fenn and Lawson for second place, and Lawson just managed to defeat Fenn by a half a wheel for the place.

One who watched the semi-military, semi-civic Decoration Day parade yesterday, if old enough to remember the parades of the period before the war, missed something -- several things, indeed -- which he is likely to recall with a sense of regret. Primarily, he misses the uniforms which once delighted the eye and made our militia regiments gorgeous.

GREENWICH, Conn., May 30. -- The first yacht races of the season of the Indian Harbor Yacht Club to-day finished in a heavy squall. The club was formally opened for the yachting season, the new Commodore, George Lauder, Jr., being present with Vice Commodore Shearson and ex-Commodore Willis.

The Executive Board of the Atlantic Marine Firemen's Union, which has been in session for several days at the Clarendon Hotel, announced yesterday evening that it had taken action on the grievances of the firemen on the boats of the coastwise steamship companies. Secretary James Sullivan of the union then made a statement in which he said that committees would call on the managers of the coastwise lines early to-day and submit the demands.

PARIS, May 30. -- Just arrived from Morocco is Jean Hess, whose fame as an explorer is European, and whose recent work, "La Question du Maroc," is the most living exposition of Moorish affairs which has appeared in the French language.

TANGIER, May 30. -- The United States armored cruiser Brooklyn, flying the flag of Rear Admiral Chadwick, arrived here to-day. The United States cruiser Atlanta arrived later and joined the Brooklyn. Two other American warships are expected shortly.

ATLANTIC CITY, N.J., May 30. -- Nothing remarkable in the way of high speeding qualities was shown by the French locomotive built for the Pennsylvania Railroad, in its test runs over the West Jersey and Seashore system between Camden and this city to-day. The engine was tested in speed power, in endurance, and in making steady time, and the crews say to-night that she did not touch the fliers built in the Pennsylvania Railroad shops.

LONDON, May 31. -- The Times publishes a long article by an American correspondent the purpose of which is to show that there is nothing in Russia's oft-repeated assertion that the United States is vastly indebted to her for kindness and support rendered in critical periods of the Republic's history.

No changes occurred in any of the positions of the clubs in either of the major leagues yesterday, but the Boston Americans were the only players to win both of their games. Rain played havoc with the arrangements made for large crowds at Cleveland and Detroit, as no games were played at either city. At Pittsburg the National League champions managed to have a game with St. Louis in the afternoon and were overwhelmingly defeated.

LONDON, May 31. -- Gen. Kuropatkin, says The Daily Telegraph's St. Petersburg's correspondent, is fighting two enemies -- one at home, the other in Manchuria. While his military reputation is undergoing a terrible ordeal, he is also accused of failure as Minister of War to make proper preparations for war.

Manhasset Bay was alive with automobile boats yesterday, and the way they skimmed over the water in front of the clubhouse of the Manhasset Bay Yacht Club was a caution to the "squareheads" who know no boats but sailing boats. There were six automobile boats entered in various classes in the first championship regatta of the American Power Boat Association.

CINCINNATI, May 30. -- The two games between the local team and the Chicagos attracted over 16,000 persons to the grounds to-day. In the morning contest the Cincinnatians bunched their hits and won. Six persons were slightly burned and a panic of passengers was caused by the explosion of a motor on a Fulton Street car in Brooklyn yesterday afternoon. The car was bound down town. When it was opposite Glenada Place a muffled explosion was heard, and blue flames shot from the controller box, directly in front of the motorman, William Cornelius of 2,196A Fulton Street.

More than 20,000 children from various sections of the city attended May Day parties in Central Park yesterday. They romped and played on the grassy lawns, lest themselves in the roadway tunnels, poked sticks at the lions in the menagerie, and all but the few who met with accidents enjoyed the day's outing.

Edward J. McCallum of New York, despite the fact that his number was "13," flashed past the judges the winner of the twenty-five-mile Irvington-Millburn road race, the sixteenth running of which was decided yesterday over the time-honored course. McCallum had a handicap of six minutes, and his actual time for the twenty-five miles was 1:16:29.

BALTIMORE, May 30. -- Robert M. McLane, Mayor of Baltimore, shot himself through the head at 3 o'clock this afternoon at his home, 29 West Preston Street, and died two hours later. Coroner Benjamin F. Hayden of the Central District, after making an investigation, decided that it was case of suicide, and deemed an inquest unnecessary.

ST. PETERSBURG, May 31. -- The reported defeat of Cossacks at Ai-Yang was the only news and almost the only topic of conversation in St. Petersburg last night. No official dispatches were given out last evening, but officers at military headquarters were reluctant in accepting the Japanese dispatches.

Coney Island crowds established a record for Memorial Day, and it was estimated in the afternoon that fully 225,000 persons were at the resort, causing the managers of the various transportation lines to shudder at the thought of the problems that will confront them when the weather gets really hot.

About 4,000 spectators witnessed the first annual out-door athletic games of the Inter-Settlement Athletic Association, which were held yesterday at Columbia Oval, William's Bridge, N.Y. There were 360 entries received for the nineteen events.

Seventeen of the twenty motor cyclists who started in the second annual hill-climbing contest of the New York Motor Cycle Club on Fort George hill yesterday finished. Two others finished, but were disqualified, and H. Taylorsen, who used the only French machine in the race, stopped half way up the hill. The race was won by F.W. Rogers, his time being one minute.

As a result of the sudden collapse of an old four-story building at 65 East Eighth Street yesterday morning a young woman is in danger of death at St. Vincent's Hospital, and three men are lying painfully injured in a neighboring ward. The collapse, according to the officials of the Building Department, was one of the most remarkable that ever occurred in the city.
ROME, May 30. -- The Chamber of Deputies was crowded to-day when the interpellation on the attitude of the Government toward the Vatican's protest against President Loubet's visit was debated.

Columbia University oarsmen scored a sweeping victory in the annual regatta of the Harlem Regatta Association, held over the Speedway course on the Harlem River yesterday, winning five of the six events in which they were entered, including the intermediate and the senior eight-oared races and all three four-oared events, in competition with the best crews of the New York Athletic Club and of the Harlem River rowing clubs.

The Agricultural Department makes an interesting announcement of the discovery by one of its experts in the province of Alta Vera Paz, Guatemala, of an ant which devotes its energies to the systematic destruction of the boll weevil. The cotton fields of the Indians of that province are not immune from invasion by the weevil, but they have been so fully protected that the plants have suffered no injury.

ST. LOUIS, Mo., May 30. -- The dead body of C.M. Dewey, formerly of New York, a St. Louis clothing manufacturer and jobber, who disappeared a week ago, was found to-day hidden by weeds in a vacant lot on Bircher Road, near the city limits.

NEWARK, N.J., May 30. -- The Justices of the Supreme Court of New Jersey will take advantage of the authority vested in them by the last Legislature and completely rearrange the judicial districts of the State. Five of the nine circuits already have been changed.

Vice President Loomis of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad Company said yesterdy that it would be impossible for several days to come to estimate the exact loss caused by the fire that on Sunday swept six piers in the Jersey City freight yards. The company, he said, had made all necessary arrangements to maintain its service unimpaired and would start the rebuilding of the burned piers immediately.

LONDON, May 30. -- The Royal Yacht Squadron has been obliged to decline the challenge of Commodore Morton F. Plant of the Larchmont Yacht Club for the Cape May Cup with his schooner-yacht Ingomar because the Britannia (which won the Cape May Cup) is too antiquated to defend it. The trophy therefore will be returned to the New York Yacht Club at the earliest possible moment.

GETTYSBURG, Penn., May 30. -- On historic Cemetery Hill, near the spot where, on Nov. 19, 1869, President Lincoln delivered his immortal address, President Roosevelt to-day spoke to an immense and eager assemblage upon the legacy of the civil war and the part that devolves upon each citizen to-day in keeping the Nation great.

RALEIGH, N.C., May 30. -- An order to show cause why he should not be held in contempt of court has been served on Josephus Daniels, editor of The News and Observer, and National Democratic Committeeman from North Carolina, by Federal Judge Purnell because of editorials and paragraphs issued in The News and Observer Sunday morning.

RALEIGH, N.C., May 30. -- News has been received here that Lucama, a little town near this city, has been in a state of ferment for the past week. On Monday a passenger train was wrecked near the station and several of the cars were destroyed by fire, among them the express car.

PARIS, May 31. -- Foreign Minister Delcasse, in consequence of a communication from the State Department at Washington, transmitted through Ambassador Porter, has telegraphed instructions to the French Minister at Tangler to use his utmost endeavors to obtain the release from the brigand Raisuli of Ion Perdicaris and Cromwell Varley.

BALTIMORE, Md., May 31. -- Mayor McLane's suicide puts the Republicans in control of the City Government under a provision for the centralization of power provided by the new city charter. The Republicans now also control the burned district commission and all improvements from this time on.

Subway work in Forty-second Street will be completed and the surface of the street will be restored to a passable condition by Monday of next week, as the result of orders issued last evening through the contractor and Commissioner Oakley of the Department of Water Supply, Gas, and Electricity.

At a public hearing held by the Committee on Elementary Schools of the Board of Education yesterday afternoon on the advisability of reintroducing corporal punishment into the schools, both the ethical and practical questions involved were thrashed out, and the preponderance of opinion seemed to be that moral suasion was a rather roundabout way of reaching the divine side of a bad boy's nature.

For the first time in more than a week Leader Charles F. Murphy of Tammany Hall was at the Fourteenth Street headquarters yesterday, having come in from Atlantic City early in the morning. He had very little to say.

Princeton's greatest doubles tennis players, Frederick B. Alexander and Raymond D. Little, the intercollegiate ex-champions, yesterday gave an excellent exhibition of speedy play in the beginning of the Manhattan Doubles Championship. The contest was a part of the annual open tournament of the New York Lawn Tennis Club on their courts at One Hundred and Twenty-third Street and St. Nicholas Avenue.

VINELAND, N.J., May 31. -- The greatest surprise that Vineland has had in a long time is the wedding announcement of Miss Susan P. Fowler, one of the original dress reformers, who has been photographed as a lecturer and farmer, for newspapers for years.

John R.
