Some little time since, when subjects of more immediate excitement but certainly not of greater intrinsic importance were engaging attention, The Constitution of Atlanta published, with warm approval, a letter from Judge JOHN L. HOPKINS, formerly of the Superior Court of Georgia, on the subject of the suppression of lynching.

Some curious facts are brought out in regard to American influence on the industries of the United Kingdom in the controversy over Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S vague but exciting propositions. Among the grievances brought up against the present regime is the allegation that a number of British trading establishments have been "expatriated," that is have been compelled to change their works to America, in order to get access to American markets.

The head of the public health administration of Philadelphia not long since made himself responsible for the statement that typhoid fever germs may be removed from water, without boiling or filtering, by letting it stand for four hours in a copper vessel at the ordinary temperature of a living room, or twenty-four hours in that of a refrigerator.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 16. -- Gen. John C. Black of Illinois, Civil Service Commissioner, is slated to succeed Capt. Eugene F. Ware as Commissioner of Pensions, but not until President Roosevelt's second Administration begins.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 16. -- As the result of an investigation made by Assistant Attorney General Day in Alaska, the President to-day removed from office Frank H. Richards, Marshal for the Second or Nome Division of Alaska, and asked for the resignations of Judges Alfred S. Moore of the Nome District and Melville C. Brown of the Juneau or First Division.

Charles T. Yerkes, the London underground railway magnate, arrived in New York yesterday morning on the North German Lloyd liner Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse. Mr. Yerkes was much interested in New York's new subway. After hearing about the experiences over here he talked about subway conditions in England.

Airships are a serious proposition. Since the division of $100,000 among airship inventors by the managers of the St. Louis Exposition and the prophetic hope of Inventor Baldwin that he will soon circle about in the atmosphere far above the heights of New York's loftiest buildings, aerial navigation has vindicated its right to receive official recognition.
SHANGHAI, Nov. 16. -- The rebels have repulsed the imperial troops at Liu-Chow, in the Province of Kwang-Si, Southern China.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 16. -- A long conference between Gov. Odell and the President, at which no one else was present, excited the curiosity of political gossips here today.

CHE-FOO, Nov. 16. -- The Port Arthur newspaper, Novy Krai, of Nov. 11, copies of which were brought to Che-Foo by the destroyer Rastoropny, prints details of a daring exploit which resulted in the sinking of a four-funneled Japanese destroyer.

The Duke of Manchester and his Duchess, formerly Miss Zimmerman of Cincinnati, were at the Horse Show last night, guests of I. Henry Smith, in Box 28, on the south side of the Garden, on the turn in the row of arena boxes. With the Duke and Duchess were the Viscountess Maitland, Mr. and Mrs. W. Rhinelander Stewart and Theodore Frelinghuysen, besides their host.

LONDON, Thursday, Nov. 17. -- The Daily Telegraph's St. Petersburg correspondent, who, throughout, has expressed somewhat alarmist views regarding the outcome of the North Sea dispute, in a telegram printed this morning, asserts that the Russian Admiralty has gained an ascendency which compels the Foreign Office to repudiate its agreement with Great Britain, and that Count Benckendorff, Ambassador to Great Britain, will be made the scapegoat and will probably be recalled.
LONDON, Nov. 16. -- The State banquet at Windsor Castle to-night in honor of the King and Queen of Portugal equaled in brilliancy similar previous functions in the historic St. George's Hall.

NYACK, N.Y., Nov. 16. -- Rockland County is much interested in a case tried here in the Supreme Court to-day before Justice Gaynor and a jury. It was a suit brought by Miss Jessie E. Tate of Piermont against Charles Bell, a Sparkill young man, for $25,000 damages for breach of promise.

CHE-FOO, Nov. 16. -- The Novy Krai of Nov. 12 contains the story of Haritena Korotkiewitch, who, although a woman, served valorously in many fights at Port Arthur, until death closed her strange career.

ELIZABETH CITY, N.C., Nov. 16. -- Boats coming into the city to-day reported the loss of the auxiliary yacht Roberta of Providence, R.I., which was said to have foundered in Pimlico Sound Sunday morning, with all her crew and passengers, numbering six or eight in all. A dispatch from Southport, N.C., however, says that the Roberta arrived there to-day with all on board safe.

PARIS, Nov. 16. -- A new play in four acts by Alfred Capus, entitled "Our Youth," was produced with great success to-night at the Comedie Francaise. The rights for England have already been purchased, and the piece will also be produced in America.
CHE-FOO, Nov. 16. -- The Russians to-day blew up the torpedo boat destroyer Rastoropny, which had arrived from Port Arthur at 6:50 A.M.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 16. -- The fifteen-day race meeting of the Washington Jockey Club, which begins to-morrow at the Bennings track, has attracted excellent fields of horses in the various events. The card for to-morrow comprises six races, including the fourth Columbia Handicap at seven furlongs, and the third Bladensburg Steeplechase Handicap over a course about two miles and a half long. The day's entries follow:

CHEYENNE, Wyo., Nov. 16. -- A Thermopolis posse this evening came upon one of the Cody bank robbers, who killed Cashier Middaugh, near the mouth of Owl Creek in the Bad Lands, six miles below Thermopolis, and captured the outlaw without firing a shot. On the bandit was found a quantity of the money taken from the bank, and jewelry and guns stolen yesterday morning in the raid on Edwards' gambling house at Thermopolis.

The seat sale for the first week of the Grand Opera season will open this morning at the Metropolitan Opera House. "Aida" will be the opening attraction next Monday. Mme. Nordica's appearance will be on Thursday in "Parsifal." For the last week she has been rehearsing two widely different roles, Gioconda and Kundry, every day.

After Police Commissioner McAdoo had said that perhaps the Brooklyn police needed a "tonic," and after he had indulged in what he later described as "a clear-cut, square talk" with seven Brooklyn Captains, six detectives of Inspector Brooks's staff went over from Mulberry Street to the borough across the bridge and conducted two lively policy shop raids.

The group of eight-story apartment houses known as the Antoinettes on the west side of Park Avenue, with frontages also on Fifty-eighth and Fifty-ninth Streets, have been sold by Vennette F. Pelletreau Co. for Peter Herter to the Realty and Personalty Corporation of New York. Mr. Herter takes in exchange a large plot of lots on Eighth Avenue, between Seventh and Eighth Streets.

Whether Harvard and Princeton will meet on the football field next Fall is the question of interest in Princeton at the present time. For the two colleges to come together again in the great Fall sport is the earnest hope of most of the undergraduates, while those who argue against the renewal of relations are few.

Yesterday was the flattest day the Street had seen in some months. Although transactions well exceeded the 1,000,000 share mark there was a distinct lack of enthusiasm. The market acted as if it were sobering up. Its appearance was decidedly "spotty." There were some good-sized declines, and for the first time in many days there were at the end more stocks which showed net losses than there were issues which showed gains.
ST. PETERSBURG, Nov, 16. -- Advices from Gen. Stoessel and Rear Admiral Wiren brought by the destroyer Rastoropny to Che-Foo reached the Emperor to-day.

W. Wickham Smith, as counsel for the Pattern Makers' Union, appeared before the Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday and announced that he had been retained to assist the Government in fighting the attempt of R. Hoe Co. to obtain free duty for their wooden patterns used in ironmoulding.

As to the reduction, he says that the heads of departments have fallen into the habit of making their estimates large, with the idea that Congress would cut them anyway.

DENVER, Nov. 28 -- Another woman, Mrs. Rosa Snyder, was arrested to-day on warrants charging her with buying votes at the late election. Lizzie Cummings and other women have made affidavits that Mrs. Snyder gave them $5 each to vote the Republican ticket. Mrs. Snyder is a complainant in one of the cases against Democrats arrested on warrants charging conspiracy to intimidate voters.

The Health Department steamboat Franklin Edson was taking a scarlet fever patient up the East River to North Brother Island yesterday when, as the boat was near the south end of Blackwell's Island, she had to swing around quickly to dodge a big float. When she tried to turn in again her rudder chains snapped and the steamboat went upon the rocks near the island.
I was very much interested in your editorial of to-day entitled "Reciprocity and Annexation, and believe your readers might possibly be interested by comments upon it from a different point of view.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 28. -- The Supreme Court of the United States to-day affirmed an opinion of the Supreme Court of Missouri limiting an interest charge under the National banking law.

Dr. Peter Hughes of' 469 Bedford Avenue, Williamsburg, was riding past the apartment house at 574 Bedford Avenue yesterday afternoon when Mrs. Mortimer D. Metcalfe thrust her head from the window of her apartment and shouted to the doctor to catch a thief who had just left the Metcalfe apartment with his pockets bulging with booty.

PRINCETON, N.J., Nov. 28. -- After an illness of about two weeks the Rev. Dr. William M. Paxton, who was lately President of the Faculty of Princeton Theological Seminary, died at his home in Library Place this morning. His death was caused by a paralytic stroke which he suffered directly after the Yale-Princeton football game, on Nov. 12.

It is plain that the contest for the restoration of the "canteen feature" of the army post exchange must shortly again be brought up before Congress for decision. It is so clearly a contest in behalf of the temperance, the morality, the discipline, and the contentment of the United States Army.

The admirable handling of the audience during a causeless alarm of fire in the Harlem Opera House on Saturday afternoon is an object lesson which theatrical managers generally would do well to take to heart. The moment the hysterical woman in the gallery called "Fire!" -- because, forsooth, she heard the noise of department apparatus in the street -- every employe of the house went to his place and did exactly the right thing.

A well-dressed woman who said she was Mrs. Caroline Hobart of Jersey City Heights was arrested outside a department store in Twenty-third Street yesterday afternoon by Detective Eva Peyser on a charge of stealing two brooches valued at $15.50.

The Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday sustained a protest by F.W. Myers Co. of Plattsburg, N.Y., claiming free duty for concentrated copper ore. The ore had been assessed at 20 per cent. as a non-enumerated manufactured article. It is held that the concentration of the ore, while removing some of the impurities, still leaves it copper ore, which is provided for in the free list.

BENNING. D.C., Nov. 29. -- Favorites won three of the six races at the Benning course to-day. The steeplechase was taken in a driving finish by Woden, a 12 to 1 shot, which reduced the track record for two miles and a half from 5:08 to 5:07. Cousin Jess established the former record three years ago. Australina had an easy victory over the big field that started in the first race.

Baron Alphonse Rothschild, head of the French branch of that famous family of financiers, who is now on a visit to this city, was the guest last evening at a dinner given by August Belmont. The Baron is understood to be in this country for an inspection of the Subway system, in the financing of which his firm is reported to be interested through Mr. Belmont's connection with the Interborough Company and the construction company.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 29. -- The appointment of a representative of this Government on the tribunal which is to examine into the firing upon the British trawlers by the Baltic fleet and a report from Attorney General Moody that he had decided against the legality of the guessing contests in newspapers and magazines and held them to be illegal were considered at a meeting of the Cabinet after President Roosevelt's return this morning.

Charles Teshlin of 357 East Thirty-eighth Street, a chauffeur employed by Charles E. Smith, a dealer in antiques, living at 135 East Thirtieth Street, is believed to be dying at the Presbyterian Hospital from injuries received in a smash-up on the East Drive in Central Park last night between the touring car he was driving and a three-seated surrey belonging to Frank Cohn of 52 East One Hundredth Street.

Controller Grout has begun a controversy with other city officials, in connection with the excavation work for the tunnel and station of the Pennsylvania Railroad, which may hamper the excavating contractors, the New York Contracting and Trucking Company, of which Charles F. Murphy's brother, John J. Murphy, is President.

The cotton market suffered a severe break yesterday, and the worst that has occurred since the days of the Sully regime. From the high prices of Monday the decline measured from 50 to 55 points, the latter in the May option, which was most seriously affected. The result was that cotton, in the case of the November option, which declined to 8.91, for the first time in three years sold below 9 cents.

That Mrs. Chadwick is staying at the Holland House in this city was made clear late last night when a rumor reached the Tenderloin police to the effect that she had committed suicide in her apartments there.

After being delayed nearly two hours at Quarantine, owing to the fact that the Hamburg-American liner Bluecher had got there first, the North German Lloyd liner Kaiser Wilhelm II, arrived at her pier in Hoboken late yesterday afternoon. While at Quarantine there occurred an accident that resulted in the fatal injury of one and the injury of three others of the steerage passengers.

MIDDLETOWN, Nov. 29. -- E.H. Harriman has just added a choice tract of land to his estate of 3,000 acres at Arden, Orange County, by the purchase of the adjoining dairy farm of the late Isaac H. Thompson, located in the town of Monroe and comprising about 200 acres.

LONDON, Nov. 29. -- Elverton R. Chapman, Jr., aged twenty-three, of New York City, committed suicide last night at the Carlton Hotel here by throwing himself from the third floor landing to the vestibule. His skull was crushed, one arm was shattered, and there were other injuries, from which he died within a few minutes.

-- It is very probably true, as Mr. F.B. THURBER gently intimated in the letter we printed yesterday, that more than a few of the people who are now exclaiming angrily over the Subway advertisements as barbarous blemishes on the artistic decorations of the stations, make their moan in the hope of proving an aesthetic sensitiveness of which they really haven't a trace.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 29. -- The final hearing by the Inter-State Commerce Commission in the matter of the complaint of William R. Hearst against the coal carrying roads was begun here to-day.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Nov. 29. -- When Mrs. Chadwick married Dr. L.S. Chadwick, in 1896, she was Mrs. C.L. Hoover, a West Side woman and a reputed widow. After her marriage she went to live at the family home of the Chadwicks on Euclid Avenue, in the most aristocratic part of the city. She has her own automobile and carriages and a retinue of servants.

ALBANY, Nov. 29. -- By a decision of the Court of Appeals to-day, the Interurban and the Brooklyn Rapid Transit systems of street railways will be required to give transfers to points on any of two lines which they operate in the City of New York.

Admiral BARKER'S report that "the Navy is to be congratulated that the department has remained firm in excluding wine and beer from the canteens of ships" doubtless expresses the sentiments of the great majority of naval officers. The present condition of things is a great change from the old times when "grog" was a constituent of the ration of every navy.

Pastor WAGNER -- he is Dr. WAGNER now, but the more familiar term seems to fit him better -- returns to his beloved France to-morrow. He leaves behind him a remarkable number of friends who have learned during his stay what an extraordinarily lovable man he is, and the impression he has made on the thousands he has addressed in all parts of the country, if less in degree, has been of the same kind.

After several weeks of uncertainty and an inability to bring all of the legal billiard organizations into harmony the dead-lock has been broken by a compromise, and the National amateur championship tournament will be played at the Chicago Athletic Association. This is the first time in the history of playing a National championship that the event has been held outside of New York and Brooklyn.

We are confronted, in the case of the woman PATTERSON, accused of murder, with an absurd but not unusual consequence of the actual administration of the august institution of trial by jury. It seems that a juror who had already had two strokes of paralysis, had another as soon as he was impaneled, and is evidently unfit to try the case.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 29. -- William Loeb, Jr., secretary to the President, to-day issued an official statement denying that President Roosevelt's children had cruelly treated the Thanksgiving turkey sent to the President by Mr. Vose of Rhode Island. In the statement Mr. Loeb says:
WINSTED, Conn., Nov. 29. -- Beginning Dec. 1 the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad Company will assume the lease of the Dutchess County Railroad and operate it as part of its system.

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J., Nov. 29. -- The properties of the Great Eastern and National Clay Manufacturing Companies at South River, which recently went into bankruptcy, were sold this afternoon by the receivers, J.K. Rice of this city and Otto T. Bannard, President of the New York Security and Trust Company.

Breeding stock made up the greater part of the 125 trotters and pacers that passed through the sales ring at the "Old Glory" horse auction in Madison Square Garden yesterday, but nevertheless the high average of the offering was maintained straight through, and at the close of the selling last night $44,600 had been added to the total of the sale, bringing the amount of the sale to date up to $417,235.

That the owners of winning harness racers received liberal treatment at the hands of track managers during the year is shown by the money they won at the eleven big trotting meetings. Throughout the nine Grand Circuit meets and the special racing events at Lexington and Memphis there were no less than $286,425 distributed among horsemen.

The most interesting question before the people of this country is, not where President ROOSEVELT now stands in regard to tariff revision, but where he will stand after the 4th of March next. Unless all the signs and portents are at fault, the President has had it in mind to urge upon Congress and upon the country some amendments of the Dingley act.

CHE-FOO, Nov. 29. -- Chinese and Japanese advices received here to-day, while not beyond question, indicate the practical certainty that another general assault on Port Arthur began on Nov. 24 and was continuing Nov. 27.

President Woodrow Wilson of Princeton University, speaking as a guest at the third annual banquet of The Virginians, held last night in the Astor Gallery at the Waldorf-Astoria, called for the South to get rid of the radical element of the Democratic Party and rehabilitate that party on good old-fashioned lines.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 29. -- Speaker Cannon visited the Capitol to-day and talked regarding tariff revision with characteristic frankness and bluntness. He evidently does not expect that any movement will be made at the approaching session to disturb existing conditions. When questioned on this point he said:

BOSTON, Nov. 29. -- Herbert D. Newton of Brookline, the plaintiff in the suit against Mrs. Cassie L. Chadwick, refused to-night to discuss the case in any phase, but referred inquirers to his counsel, Percy W. Carver.

MOUNT VERNON, Nov. 29. -- Mrs. William Taylor of Stamford, Conn., went to the harbor in front of the Larchmont Yacht Club this afternoon for the purpose of donning a diving suit and going to the bottom of the harbor on a "dare." Mrs. Taylor is the wife of an engineer employed by Peter J. Kane, the contractor who is laying a sewer in the harbor, and she is a fairly heavy woman.

Directors of corporations who pay dividends in preferred stock out of capital instead of net earnings were scored roundly yesterday by Justice Clarke in a decision in the Supreme Court, the Justice holding that the Directors of the American Malting Company did this, and ruling that each of them is liable individually for the amount so paid out.

LONDON, Wednesday, Nov. 30. -- According to a Tokio dispatch to The Standard there is an unofficial rumor that the Japanese have hauled large calibre guns to the top of 203-Metre Hill, from where their fire has a sweep of the whole harbor.

RIVERHEAD, L.I., Nov. 29. -- Dr. Albert E. Payne has placed his father and mother in charge of his home here, put his practice, one of the best in Riverhead, in charge of other physicians, and is now on his way across the country, acting as escort to his wife, who is on her way to South Dakota to obtain a divorce from him.

Just before adjournment last evening Justice Gaynor in the Supreme Court in Brooklyn committed to jail for perjury James Corcoran of Manhattan and William H. Larowe, one of Corcoran's witnesses. Corcoran was suing the Brooklyn Heights Railroad Company for $10,000. He alleged that on Dec. 2, 1902, he was injured by a car at Grand and Havemeyer Streets, Brooklyn, and that his left ankle had been made practically useless.

The Broadway-Reliance Realty Company, of which Henry Hellman is President, has bought from the Marsh estate, through William P. Mangam, the plot of fifteen lots, including the entire block front on the west side of Amsterdam Avenue, between Ninety-fourth and Ninety-fifth Streets, and extending 182 feet in depth on the former and 193 feet on the latter.

The market yesterday continued the irregular path which it has been pursuing for a week or more. The underlying tone was firm, but the price movement were irregular. New York Central, which had been strong on the day before, advanced to new high prices. At one time it sold at 141 1/4, and it finally closed at very near the top for a net advance of 2 7/8 points.

BENTON, Ill., Nov. 29. -- The mining war at Zeigler reached its height last night, when the town was fired upon from sundown to daylight. It is estimated that no less than 500 shots were fired at the town.

The "open shop" idea was explained and unionism severely criticised at the second convention of the Citizens' Industrial Association of America, which began yesterday forenoon in the Hotel Astor. The Socialists also came in for left-handed compliments by some of the speakers; including President D.M. Parry of the association.

When the President of the Citizens' Union is asked by newspaper reporters to give his views upon the possibility of an indorsement of the Tammany Mayoralty ticket by the Union, it is evident that our local politics have entered upon an entirely new stage. At the meeting of the City Committee of the Citizens' Union on Monday evening it was stated that the Union's attitude in the next Mayoralty campaign will be defined next April.

ALBANY, Nov. 29. -- By a decision to-day in the action of the People ex rel. Cossey, appellant, vs. Controller Grout of New York, the Court of Appeals declared unconstitutional Chapter 415 of the Laws of 1897, (the labor law,) which prohibits a contractor from employing his men more than eight hours a day on city, county, or State work.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 29. -- Belgium is among the nations which have not yet accepted the invitations sent by the United States to all the signatory powers to The Hague Convention to sign with this Government arbitration treaties similar to the Anglo-French treaty.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Nov. 29. -- Within a few hours Cleveland expects to see disclosures in the Chadwick mystery that will rival in their startling details the famous Humbert case that not long ago astounded Europe.

PARIS, Nov. 29. -- M. Bos, Reporter in the Chamber of Deputies of this year's Admiralty budget, prefaces a detailed account of the French Navy by an interesting comparison of that navy and the navies of the world.

Charges were openly made in the Supreme Court in Brooklyn yesterday that H.J. Bebro, who says that his chosen mission is to get from sanitariums persons wrongfully committed, had been a convict and that he had in his pay many trained nurses who had been discharged from private hospitals, and who gave him family secrets that might be of value.

PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 29. -- The will of Edward L. Wentz, the young Philadelphian who was mysteriously slain in the mountains of West Virginia a year ago, was filed to-day at the office of the Register of Wills. The bulk of the estate, valued at $500,000, is devised in trust for the benefit of the testator's fiancee, Cornelia Brookmire of St. Louis, Mo.

ST. PETERSBURG, Nov. 29. -- According to information which has reached the War Office here, Field Marshal Oyama's strength is much smaller than heretofore believed, tending to confirm the theory that a large force has been withdrawn to assist in storming Port Arthur.

An editorial in THE TIMES of Nov. 28 points out the obvious evils that have arisen in connection with intercollegiate football, and concludes that, in order to eliminate these evils the game itself must be discontinued. But there are many persons who see these evils as clearly as you do, and yet feel that the game has good features that should not be lost in a general abolition.

When a National election is more than three weeks back in history it is a difficult thing to work up post-election enthusiasm, but there was plenty to go around among the 600 and odd diners who attended the Roosevelt-Fairbanks-Higgins-Bruce jubilee dinner last night at the Waldorf-Astoria.

After more than two hours of heated discussion between Controller Grout and Alderman McCall the Sinking Fund Commission yesterday laid aside for one week the application of the New York Central Railroad to divert its tracks in Twelfth Avenue so that the Pennsylvania Railroad could get possession of the Thirty-second Street pier for the purpose of expediting its tunnel and station work.

Thousands of commuters and other travelers over the main line of the New York Central Railroad were delayed for hours when at 4:45 o'clock yesterday afternoon the brick barge "Three J's" tried to pass through the Cromwell's Creek draw, and stuck fast on the bottom on a falling tide.

TOKIO, Nov. 30. -- The Emperor formally opened the second war Diet to-day. He rode through the crowded streets in a state coach escorted by a troop of lancers and accompanied by the Crown Prince, his staff, and some members of the imperial household, to the House of Parliament, where both houses were assembled in the Chamber of Representatives.

If ex-Gov. Frank S. Black announces himself a candidate to succeed Senator Depew there will be two other candidates in the field, according to the declaration yesterday of those close to Mr. Depew. It was said that Timothy L. Woodruff would be one of the candidates and that the other would come from the Western part of the State.

The eighth and most expensive annual dinner of the Rockefeller Bible Class was held at the Hotel Majestic last evening. In 1903 members of the class paid $1 a plate. Last night's dinner cost $1.25 a plate, with Turkish cigarettes, a cigar apiece, and an illustrated cartoon talk thrown in. No fewer than 253 men, young and old, were present.

ORANGE, N.J., Nov. 30. -- An enterprising stranger visited East Orange to-day and did a rushing business with the school children in the Elmwood district. At recess time he unfolded his plan to a crowd of wondering young folks. For old rubbers, rubber boots, and rubber goods he would give jewels of fabulous value, absolutely free.

Wallace Downey of the Townsend Downey Shipbuilding Company and President of the New York Metal Trades Association gave the delegates to the convention of the Citizens' Industrial Alliance in the Hotel Astor yesterday some points as to the progress of the open shop idea in this city. He spoke at the last session of the convention.

BOSTON, Nov. 30. -- Since January, 1901, Mrs. Dagmar Baagoe of New York, wife of Frederick Baagoe, a chemist of that city, and daughter of Gen. Christensen of Brooklyn, has been an inmate of a private sanitarium in Worcester, having been committed as insane at the alleged instigation of her husband.

DUQUOIN, Ill., Nov. 30. -- It became known here to-day that three weeks ago Joseph Leiter was indicted on three counts on the charge of bringing armed men into the State, contrary to recently passed statutes. Although the indictment was returned Nov. 12, no attempt has been made to serve the capias or to arrest Leiter, because State's Attorney Scott, who will retire to-morrow, wishes to leave the case over to his successor.

BENNING, D.C., Nov. 30. -- Go Between, the speedy three-year-old gelding who broke the record in capturing the Washington Cup on Thanksgiving Day, to-day as a 1-to-2 favorite won the Fifth Benning Special and lowered the track record of 2:40 for a mile and a half, made by Rochester four years ago, to 2:37 3-5.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 30. -- Rear Admiral Charles Henry Davis has been chosen by the President, after consultation with Secretaries Hay and Morton, to be a member of the international tribunal which is to investigate the firing upon the British trawling fleet in the North Sea by the Baltic fleet under Admiral Rojestvensky.

The claim is made on behalf of Senator DEPEW that he has pledges to vote for his re-election of seventy-six members of the Legislature, or five more than the majority of the caucus which is necessary to secure that re-election.

CAPE TOWN, Nov. 30. -- With reference to the discovery of alluvial gold in Fern Spruit, Rhodesia, I understand that the Chartered Company's engineer will arrive in Cape Town next week and will proceed at once to inspect the locality.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 30. -- Senator Hale of Maine, whose recently published interview in opposition to tariff revision attracted widespread attention, had an extended conference with the President to-day. It is understood that the subject discussed was the tariff. When he came out of the White House Mr. Hale said he was quite sure that there would be no tariff revision either at this session on during that of the Fifty-ninth Congress.

Police Inspector Richard Walsh has been officially reprimanded by Commissioner McAdoo. This is the first action of the kind on the part of Mr. McAdoo since he became the head of the Police Department.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, Nov. 30. -- One man holds the key to the Chadwick mystery. He may talk to-morrow when the case comes up for a hearing in the court here on a motion for a receiver to take charge of the securities Mrs. Chadwick is said to have.

A number of old paintings and engravings of famous race horses that formerly belonged to the late Col. S.D. Bruce, well known to horse lovers and for many years editor of Turf, Field and Farm, drew a large number of bidders last night to the Anderson auction rooms, 5 West Twenty-ninth Street, where the entire library of the late horseman was disposed of.

SALT LAKE, Utah, Nov. 30. -- The official canvass of the vote of Utah was completed to-day. The vote for President on each Electoral ticket was as follows: Roosevelt, 62,444; Parker, 33,413; Debs, 5,767. No other candidate for President was voted for.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 30. -- Russia is unwilling to join the powers in a second peace conference at The Hague until her war with Japan is ended.

A definite acceptance of the arrangement entered into between the attorneys for Mrs. Chadwick and Henry D. Newton of Boston was made at a midnight conference held at the Park Avenue Hotel last night. Present were Mr. Newton and his Boston counsel, Mr. Carver, and Mr. Ryall. They announced that they had perfect confidence in the ability of Mrs. Chadwick to meet their claims.

As one who has devoted a large part of his life to the study of art, I feel impelled to say that "The Comparative Art Exhibition" now being displayed in the galleries of the American Fine Arts Society, in Fifty-seventh Street, is the most important and the most interesting art exhibition ever held in the United States.

The Directors of the Interborough Rapid Transit Company yesterday declared a dividend of 3 per cent. on the company's stock, payable Jan. 3 next to holders of record on Dec. 10. This is the second dividend declared by the company, and with the first, amounting to 2 per cent., paid in July last, makes a total of 5 per cent. for the present year.

Recalling his own misfortune in having come into the leadership of the Wine, Liquor, and Beer Dealers' Association simultaneously with a reform administration of the city, Fritz Lindinger, now an ex-President of the organization, said last night that District Attorney Jerome was the only member of that administration who had treated the liquor dealers fairly.

Emanuel Tannenbaum, who lives at 345 West Seventy-first Street, brought down a thief with a pistol shot in his back yard yesterday morning, and the occupants of several handsome four-story dwellings in the same block hope that what they describe as a reign of terror caused by the frequent visitations of burglars is at an end.

We remarked yesterday morning that the public interest in the issue raised by Senator HALE'S scantily respectful declaration on tariff revision would centre in the attitude of the President. Something like an official response to the semi-challenge of the Maine Senator is contained in the Washington dispatches of The Tribune, sent from that city on the day that Senator HALE issued his manifesto.

WASHINGTON, N.J., Nov. 30. -- A heap of powdered bituminous coal containing not less than 100 tons is on fire in one of the largest buildings of the plant of the Edison Cement Company at New Village. The fire is an exceedingly dangerous one to handle. It is worse than useless to throw water on the burning coal, as the water causes it to throw off more gases.

LANCASTER, Penn., Nov. 30. -- The Rev. Dr. William T. Manning, Vicar of St. Agnes's Chapel, Trinity Parish, New York City, was to-day elected Bishop of the newly organized Protestant Episcopal diocese of Harrisburg.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 30. -- Secretary Morton announced to-day that he will take up and decide the whole question of titles in the navy. This means the final disposition of a question that has caused more heart burning and bad feeling than any other issue of its size. The old quarrel between the line and staff figures in it, and also the resentment of fighting officers over the giving of high titles to bureau chiefs.

TOPEKA, Kan., Nov. 30. -- At a conference of members of the Kansas Legislature here to-day it was decided to push a bill making pipe lines common carriers. This is a movement in opposition to the Standard Oil Company, which has a monopoly of the Kansas field.

ST. PETERSBURG, Nov. 30. -- The statement that Russia is concentrating troops on the Afghan frontier is denied. Nevertheless it is undoubtedly true that Russia is watching with some misgivings the British plans for the reorganization and increase of the Indian Army as well as the dispatch of a deputation to Persia.
CHICAGO, Nov. 30. -- Peter Nissen is believed to have been either smothered or frozen to death in his rolling balloon Fool Killer, in which he started for a trip across the lake yesterday.

The annual "Old Glory" auction sale of harness bred horses, held by the Fasig-Tipton Company in Madison Square Garden, came to a close last night, with a total realized by the sales that was second only to one auction held by the company, the aggregate sum of the sales for the nine days reaching $447,775 for 987 head.

BERLIN, Nov. 30. -- In the Prussian Diet to-day Herr Moeller, Minister of Commerce and Industry, spoke of the trust question as it exists in the United States, and warned Germany against copying the American system.

Hundreds of Japanese gathered at the Twenty-third Street station of the Pennsylvania Railroad yesterday afternoon to give welcome in a thousand-throated "Banzail" to Prince Sadanaru Fushimi, the head of one of the four royal families of Japan, and a brother, by adoption, of the present Mikado. Many who were not Japanese were present, and everybody cheered.

PITTSBURG, Nov. 30. -- Announcement is made here to-day that, beginning to-morrow, a large advance in the price of wire products will go into effect. No official figures are at hand, but the advance will be between $2 and $4 per ton.

In your issue of to-day is an article on United States Steel earnings which shows an "extremely satisfactory" condition of the business. Yet you quote "a leading official of the Steel Corporation" as saying, "we hear reports that within two years the common stock will be on a stable dividend-paying basis."

The Court of Appeals has practically wiped out the law forbidding contractors for public work to employ their men for more than eight hours a day. But the decision does not leave it very clear how or why the law is unconstitutional.
LONDON, Nov. 30. -- The Times's Paris correspondent sends a summary of a document purporting to be an account of a secret conference recently held in Paris by Russian reformers and revolutionaries.

It was announced the other day that the Government and the importers are in a fair way to procure from the Supreme Court a final decision determining the value of the Indian rupee as used in invoices of dutiable merchandise. Between the importers and the Secretary of the Treasury there has been a long contention over the rupee, and much litigation has resulted.

The announcement that Commissioner GARFIELD of the Bureau of Corporations is about to resume the investigation of the Beef Trust is not likely to send a thrill of apprehension along the nerves of those connected with the packing interest. It is more than doubtful whether any such combination as is forbidden by law exists between the several corporations which control the meat business of this country.

MOUNT VERNON, N.Y., Nov. 30. -- Mrs. Naomi Duncombe Ring, whose elopement on Sept. 10 caused a sensation at Mount Vernon, has begun a suit in the Supreme Court to set aside the deeds of $30,000 worth of property which she gave to her husband, Patrick J. Ring, immediately after their marriage.

The Sully creditors accomplished what had been considered the impossible yesterday and agreed. The hearing before Referee MacGrane Coxe was one of harmony, induced by a pronounced general desire to get something out of the estate at an early date.

BOSTON, Dec. 1. -- Vice President-elect Charles W. Fairbanks and John D. Long, ex-Secretary of the Navy and ex-Governor, discussed the protective tariff at the dinner of the Home Market Club to-night.

CHICAGO, Dec. 1. -- If an agreement just entered into by the trunk lines in the Central and Western Freight Association is firmly maintained, there will hereafter be no more cutting of freight rates, paying of rebates, or granting of concessions of any kind to shippers. The agreement covers both import and domestic traffic east and west bound.

Business men who received their mail through Post Office Station U at Third Avenue and One Hundred and Third Street are rejoicing in the arrest of Herman Fronkers, twenty-five years old, of 43 West One Hundred and Fourteenth Street, a distributing clerk in that sub-station. Fronkers is frantic with grief because it means that he will in all probability never see his old mother again, to whom he is devotedly attached.

His professional position is assured, and it is distasteful to him to be considered a fixture in the office which he has filled with such distinguished ability and with which his reputation is so closely connected.

The stock market had its usual Thursday afternoon reaction yesterday. Close observers of the market have noticed for some weeks that whenever prices showed a tendency to hesitate around 1 o'clock on a Thursday the market was sure to sell off at the end. Almost invariably, also, the market has continued reactionary Friday morning, with a tendency to harden and a final rally in the late afternoon.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 1. -- The long-expected effort to amend the present law taxing oleomargarine has made its appearance. Representative Boutelle of Illinois has framed a bill to make the tax uniform by imposing 4 cents a pound on the product, whether colored or not. At present there is a tax of 10 cents a pound on colored and one-quarter of a cent on uncolored oleo.

Black can now be said to be fairly on.

The first witness was the Rev. J.M. Buckley, editor of The Christian Advocate, of New York, who told of a Mormon meeting he attended in Salt Lake, Utah, last Summer.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 12. -- A somewhat difficult situation is presented by the fact that the House Committee on Judiciary, which has been investigating the case of Judge Swayne of Florida, unanimously recommends his impeachment. Either Swayne, who is charged with being a tyrant, a corrupt Judge, and unfit for his office in every way, must be allowed to hold office for another year, or there must be an extra session of Congress to try him.

Dr. Weber, one of the most eminent members of the commission, reported on the work which that body has already done.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 18. -- Determined opposition to the proposed reduction of the duty on sugar and tobacco imported from the Philippines has developed among those interested in the production of these commodities in the United States. LONDON, Dec. 25. -- The most notable feature of Christmas Day in the United Kingdom was the large amount of charity distributed as the result of the generous sums collected for this purpose through the newspapers and other channels.

PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 25. -- Four men were suffocated and eight other persons were rescued from fire in three different parts of the city early to-day. At a boarding house at 1545 Wood Street, Charles McCusker, aged forty-four years; James Merry, forty-eight years, and Joseph McGill, twenty-four years, died in a trap made by themselves.

James W.S. Langerman, formerly United States Vice Consul General at Tangier, Morocco, is in New York on his way to report to the Sultan of Morocco, whose personal representative he was at the St. Louis Exposition. He talked of Morocco and its desire for American trade at the Waldorf last night.

Just as Mrs. Lillian Bullerton's boarders took their seats in the dining room of her establishment at 380 St. Nicholas Avenue for Christmas dinner yesterday a crash sounded in the kitchen, and the guests started as if to flee.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 25. -- Workingmen's gardens in France are discussed in a recent report by United States Consul Atwell of Roubaix. The evil of intemperance has so undermined the health and usefulness of workmen that this means is sought of interesting them in such healthful employment outside of mill hours as shall bring them increased comfort and attach them to the soil which they cultivate.

DENVER, Col., Dec. 25. -- If the fifteenth General Assembly of Colorado, which is to meet Wednesday, Jan. 4, shall effectuate the plans formulated by the managers of the Republican post-election campaign, Gov. James H. Peabody may serve as Chief Executive of this State for two years more, despite the fact that Alva Adams still has nearly 10,000 plurality.

The Hon. PAUL MORTON, Secretary of the Navy, avers that America, in order to build up a big shipping interest, "will be obliged to meet the competition of all nations." That is quite true. He predicts that we shall be forced "to recognize the mail contracts, the subsidies, and the premiums of Germany, and of England, and of other Governments" to effect this consummation.

SYRACUSE, N.Y., Dec. 25. -- Mr. and Mrs. Charles R. Kemter of this city believe that the mutilated body of the young woman found Nov. 19 in North Cheyenne Canon, near Colorado Springs, is that of their daughter, Mrs. Bessie Boston.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Dec. 25. -- The passenger train which left St. Louis at 9 o'clock last night on the Southern Railway collided to-day head on near Mauds Station, Ill., with the passenger train which left Louisville about the same hour. One passenger and six employes were killed and two passengers and eight employes were slightly injured.

Irvine, who was unfrocked by Bishop Talbot, said to-night that he had no official relation with the case.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 25. -- The members of the Russian Embassy conducted a raffle last night for the benefit of the Russian wounded in Manchuria.

ORANGE, N.J., Dec. 25. -- A young woman, who declined to tell her name, was run down by a trolley car at Main and Day Streets, Orange, about midnight last night, and escaped injury by an acrobatic feat which called forth the admiration of all who saw it. Kathrine Breschkovsky, who for more than twenty-two years was a Siberian exile.

CLEVELAND, Dec. 25. -- It was an exceedingly gloomy Christmas for Mrs. Chadwick, who remained alone in her cell most of the day, not taking advantage of the Christmas custom of allowing to the prisoners unusual freedom in the jail.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 25. -- Henry Casson, Sergeant-at-Arms of the House, was connected with the Speaker's Bureau of the Republican Congressional Committee in the late campaign, and his friends out in his home district, the Second Iowa, ascribe to him all the credit for the Republican sweep in the Nation last month.
TOKIO, Dec. 25. -- Tokio is again a great military camp, and the scenes of last Spring, when the first armies were mobilized and dispatched, are being duplicated.

The valuation last year was $198,702,924.

Adolph Herschkopf, after serving eight years of a life sentence in Sing Sing, became a free man yesterday by pardon of Gov. Odell. Herschkopf was not the most miserable man in New York last night. He had been employed in the prison tailor shop, and had not felt the touch of snow on his face since entering the prison gates.

The list of the telephone's utilities lengthens as time goes on and it is found subservient to the most various and unexpected uses. It is only lately that it has been employed for conducting religious services, when for any reason the congregation could not come together, but it is found on trial to do the business acceptably and to the edification of those to whom it is made to minister.

The cold wave from the Ohio Valley predicted by the Weather Bureau struck New York with full force yesterday morning. It came in sections, each section a fraction colder than its predecessor. This continued up to about 10 o'clock, when the temperature began to rise, the clouds became heavy, and the weather sharps knew that a snowstorm was imminent.

In to-day's issue of THE TIMES I notice a letter from a navy yard clerk with reference to the "Rights of Government Employes." The only right about which he seemed anxious was a longer vacation. Government clerks are amply protected under the civil service laws and regulations, and if the rights of letter carriers, navy yard clerks, , are infringed upon, they have their recourse to the courts and numerous civil service commissions.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 26. -- Representative Robert Baker of Brooklyn was asked to discourse on how it feels to be regarded as "the kicker of the House." He has maintained his reputation in this respect in this session, as he did in the last, and just as Congress adjourned for the holidays he succeeded in defeating by well timed objections the proposition to turn over the Pension Office to the inaugural ball.

It was the first production of the piece in this country, although in London "The Money Makers" has had a successful run at the Royalty Theatre.

The situation is most acute in Moscow, where the university is closed, and the students and the pedagogic and other societies are in a constant state of ferment.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 26. -- Mrs. Leslie Carter scored a success to-night with "Adrea" at Convention Hall, which David Belasco has adopted as the place for his Washington presentations. In "Adrea" Mrs. Carter abandoned her accustomed class of plays and made her debut in tragedy.

Debutantes will be out in full force and in full glory to-night, for there are three private dances on the social programme, one to be given at Sherry's by Mrs. Howard Page for Miss Lily Lee Page; another at Dodworth's by Mrs. Amos Morrill for Miss Elsie Morrill, and a third by Mrs. John Claflin of Washington Square at her home for Miss Wilhelmine Claflin.

Edward Terry, the English actor, who made his first appearance in this country yesterday afternoon, was received in a spirit of generous warmth that must have gone far toward reconciling him to the fact that the season of good cheer finds him far away from home. The audience that assembled in the Princess Theatre had obviously come in a fine holiday mood, and this fact was reflected in an abundance of laughter and applause.

BALTIMORE, Dec. 26. -- President Roosevelt could not have given a greater surprise to Congressman Frank Wachter and other leaders of the local Republican organization than he did by his choice to-day of W. Hall Harris as Postmaster of Baltimore to succeed S. Davies Warfield.

Eighteen Chinamen, charged with being common gamblers, were arraigned in the Tombs Court yesterday, but Magistrate Breen discharged all except one. On the promise of the police to produce more evidence against Sing Moh, said to be one of the proprietors of the place, the Magistrate held him in $1,000 for examination to-morrow.

A little while before Mrs. Williams had a slight tiff with her daughter Margaret, sixteen years old, about the dress which the girl was to wear this evening at a Christmas dance for young folks at the South Orange Field Club.

The interior of the structure is almost an absolute wreck.

After a lapse of three years, the Seventh Regiment handicap and championship competitions in indoor tennis were revived yesterday afternoon, on the large floor of the armory, Park Avenue and Sixty-seventh Street. A number of the best players in the regiment turned out, and while the contests did not advance beyond the first rounds in the events, there were several lively and well-contested matches.

HALIFAX, N.S., Dec 26. -- A portion of the Acadia Powder Company's works, at Waverly, ten miles from this city, blew up to-day and the concussion shook the country and broke windows for twenty miles around. No one was killed or even seriously injured, although about twenty of the employes who had just left the building, which was demolished, were thrown violently to the ground and stunned.

Replying to the request of the City Club for facts concerning the new lighting contracts Commissioner Oakley of the Department of Water Supply, Gas and Electricity announced last night that he had made a full report to Mayor McClellan in a letter to the Mayor in reply to one addressed to the Mayor by Lawrence Veillier, Secretary of the City Club.

With their trotters and pacers hooked to featherweight speeding cutters, road drivers held an impromptu sleighing carnival in the Park and on the Harlem River Speedway yesterday. The footing was all that could be desired, as the snow which fell Sunday just put a nice covering on the roads that have been ice bound for several days past, without making them too heavy for fast work.

MOSCOW, Dec. 26. -- The Zemstvo Congress of the Moscow Government opened to-day. Prince Trubetzkoi, the President, in his opening address, dwelt upon the serious condition of Russia and the regretable war with Japan, the end of which could not be anticipated in the near future, as well as the grave economical crisis through which the country was passing, and the internal disorganization of the empire.

It was not until early yesterday morning, however, that her predicament was observed by the Oak and Fire Island Life Saving stations, the crews of both of which went to the assistance of the vessel.

Warren in Seaview Avenue, facing Long Island Sound, was burned to-day, a candle which was a part of the decoration of a Christmas tree starting the blaze. Col. and Mrs. Warren were entertaining a party of children at the time.

White went to see a friend aboard the warship and took with him, it is said, a quart bottle of fine old whisky.

PERU, Ind., Dec. 27. -- A fast train on the Wabash Railroad, east bound, came in collision with a freight train at 9 o'clock to-night at Fort Wayne, and it is believed that one man was killed, two persons fatally injured, and twelve or fourteen more or less seriously hurt. Much of the produce intended for the London Christmas market was unloaded. The loss, however, through its late arrival aggregates several hundred thousand pounds.

In a decision written by Gen. T.S. Sharretts, the Board of United States General Appraisers yesterday overruled a protest by the Alfred H. Smith Company of New York against the classification as manufactures of rubber at 30 per cent. of so-called India rubber sponges. The importers contended that they were dutiable at 20 per cent. as sponges.

The new Anchor liner Caledonia, from Glasgow, finished her maiden voyage across the Atlantic late yesterday afternoon. Capt. Archie Baxter, her commander, after telling how smoothly the engines of the big ship worked and how easily the liner plowed her way through giant seas, told a story of a wonderful field of icebergs south of which the Caledonia passed last Thursday.

In THE NEW YORK TIMES of March 7 there was published a telegram giving the views of the Council of Foreign Bondholders with regard to the treatment of the English holders of the bonds of the external debt of Santo Domingo in the proposed arrangement of the Dominican debt.

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J., June 1. -- George Yepsen, a prominent resident of Perth Amboy, was arrested there this morning by Detective Peltier on a warrant issued yesterday by Justice Sedam of this city, in which he was charged by the officers of the Second People's Building and Loan Association of this city with forgery for the purpose of making a bogus transfer of stock.

I note your very timely comment in this morning's TIMES in which you so ably take to task him who "is content to live on the alms extorted by the insolence or servility of others." On first thought the one whom we will accuse as being that person in the present controversy is the head porter in any one of the large hotels.

In his last annual message President ROOSEVELT declared that "combination of capital, like combination of labor, is a necessary element of our present industrial system." He therefore thought it "unfortunate that our present laws should forbid all combinations, instead of sharply discriminating between those combinations which do good and those combinations which do evil."

When the big Cunard turbine steamer Lusitania arrives in this port about the middle of September it is probable she will come up to the city through the new Ambrose channel The matter of the vessel entrance has been a question which has been agitating the Cunard line, the engineers who have been working on the channel, and the War Department for some time.

ODESSA, Sept. 2. -- The Black Hundreds began rioting hers this afternoon, alleging that the Jews were responsible for the explosion of the bomb in the courtyard of the Central Police Station here on Saturday morning, which resulted in the killing of an artillery officer and four policemen, although it was stated at the time that the bomb was accidentally dropped by the officer.

ASBURY PARK, Aug. 31. -- Dwight Gibb, of the firm of Mills Gibb, of New York, and William Gullington, a cigar manufacturer of Red Bank, were seriously injured in an automobile collision at Como, near Spring Lake, this evening. The accident occurred at the intersection of the Allaire and Manasquan turnpikes.

The address of President ROOSEVELT at the unveiling of the monument to Mr. McKINLEY yesterday was in nearly all respects a fitting one The virtues of his predecessor were recounted in simple and dignified phrase, and his career was traced briefly in terms of deserved eulogy.
